41 — A four-word clause that will not sit still

Ki-Eun Jang, "The Problems of Sons of Gods, Daughters of Humans, and the Nephilim in Genesis 6:1-4: A Reassessment," Religions 16, no. 8 (2025): article 972. Jang works through the grammatical difficulty of Genesis 6:4's claim that the Nephilim were on the earth "in those days, and also afterward": the Hebrew syntax describing the sons of God going in to the daughters of humans uses a verb form regularly read as iterative or durative rather than strictly punctiliar, meaning the verse describes a recurring pattern rather than a single sealed-off episode. On this reading the grammar itself, independent of any question of sources or editors, already resists treating the Nephilim's appearance as confined to the years immediately before the flood.

42 — A passage that reads like a fragment because it may be one

Claus Westermann, Genesis 1-11: A Continental Commentary, trans. John J. Scullion (Minneapolis: Augsburg Publishing House, 1984), ad loc. Genesis 6:1-4. Westermann treats the unit as one of the most obviously composite, least fully integrated passages in the primeval history: a terse, mythologically dense fragment that sits between the genealogies of chapter 5 and the flood announcement of 6:5-8 without being smoothly stitched to either. He reads the notice that the Nephilim existed "in those days, and also afterward" as exactly the kind of loose end this kind of fragment leaves behind, a detail original to whatever older tradition supplied the verse, retained by the compiler of Genesis without being reconciled to the flood narrative's implication that the pre-flood world, Nephilim included, was wiped out entire.

43 — Not Israel's invention, but Israel's version of a wider story

Ronald S. Hendel, "Of Demigods and the Deluge: Toward an Interpretation of Genesis 6:1-4," Journal of Biblical Literature 106, no. 1 (1987): 13-26. Hendel reads Genesis 6:1-4 against a broad ancient Near Eastern and Aegean backdrop in which divine beings visit the earth and leave demigod offspring behind, comparing the Nephilim to figures such as the heroes of the Sumerian King List tradition and the demigods of Greek epic. On his account, Genesis preserves a compressed, second-hand version of an old mythological pattern rather than composing the Nephilim from scratch for this one scene, which is part of why the verse reads as oddly self-contained: it is quoting, in miniature, a larger inherited story the author assumed the audience already knew well enough not to need explained.

44 — One tenth left loose, forward-pointing to Jubilees' own chapter

James C. VanderKam, trans., The Book of Jubilees, Corpus Scriptorum Christianorum Orientalium 511, Scriptores Aethiopici 88 (Louvain: Peeters, 1989), Jubilees 10:1-11. This book gives Jubilees its own full treatment later (Chapter 18), but the detail matters here: in Jubilees' retelling, unclean demons begin afflicting Noah's grandsons after the flood, and when Noah prays for their removal, Mastema, described as chief of the spirits, petitions God to let some remain, arguing he could not otherwise exercise his intended power over corrupted humanity. God grants that one tenth of the spirits stay active while the remaining nine tenths are bound in the place of condemnation. The flood, on Jubilees' own telling, did not fully clear the field.

45 — Qumran was still writing new chapters about them

Loren T. Stuckenbruck, The Book of Giants from Qumran: Texts, Translation, and Commentary, Texts and Studies in Ancient Judaism 63 (Tubingen: Mohr Siebeck, 1997). This book covers the Qumran Book of Giants fully in Chapter 17; noted here only as evidence that the question this chapter is asking was still alive for Second Temple readers. Stuckenbruck's edition of the Qumran fragments shows scribes centuries after Genesis was written still composing new narrative material about individual giants by name, their fates, and their visions, material that complicates any assumption that the giants' story was considered closed, tidy, or fully resolved by the flood within the Enochic tradition itself.

46 — A theodicy of evil in general, not of these giants in particular

Irenaeus, Proof of the Apostolic Preaching 18, trans. Joseph P. Smith, S.J., Ancient Christian Writers 16 (Westminster, MD: Newman Press, 1952). Irenaeus writes that "wickedness extended and spread, and reached and laid hold upon the whole race of mankind, until a very small seed of righteousness remained among them: and illicit unions took place upon the earth, since angels were united with the daughters of the race of mankind; and they bore to them sons who for their exceeding greatness were called giants," continuing that the angels taught their human wives sorcery, cosmetics, and idolatry, by which evil spread further still. This is a genuine patristic theodicy of persistent evil, tracing corruption's durability in the world to the Watchers' teaching rather than to human weakness alone, drawing directly on 1 Enoch. It explains why evil continues in general; it does not, in this passage or any other located for this chapter, address the specific question of why the Anakim, Rephaim, or Og of Bashan continued to exist after a flood supposedly sent to end their kind.

47 — The one patristic source that engages this exact verse, and answers a different question

Augustine, Concerning the City of God against the Pagans, Book XV, chapter 23, trans. Henry Bettenson (London: Penguin Classics, 2003; Latin original c. 426 CE). Augustine addresses Genesis 6:4's "and also afterward" directly, writing that giants existed both before and after the flood, noting "even after the flood they existed; as a matter of fact, in our own day there have also been some individual humans incredibly large," while adding that not all children of the union described in the verse were giants, and that there were more giants before the flood than after it. His explanation, however, is not a theodicy of evil serving a purpose; it is closer to a naturalistic and genealogical one, folded into his larger argument that the "sons of God" were the godly line of Seth, who fell from righteousness by intermarrying with the line of Cain. Unusually large humans, on Augustine's reading, are simply a trait that recurs across human history at uneven rates; no supernatural mechanism is required to explain their reappearance after the flood.

48 — A commentary tradition split on how much to trust frightened men

Jacob Milgrom, Numbers = Ba-midbar: The Traditional Hebrew Text with the New JPS Translation, JPS Torah Commentary (Philadelphia: Jewish Publication Society, 1990), ad loc. Numbers 13:31-33. Milgrom situates the spies' report within the broader pattern of the "evil report," noting that the ten spies' account escalates from a description of a land whose inhabitants are simply large (13:32) to the specific, loaded claim of Nephilim descent (13:33), a term carrying the full mythic weight of Genesis 6:4. Commentary in this tradition treats the escalation as a diagnostic of the spies' own fear rather than a reliable ethnographic claim, while granting that the text gives readers no independent means of confirming or disproving an actual genealogical connection between the Anakim and the antediluvian Nephilim.

49 — A medieval reading already calling this hyperbole

Ramban (Nachmanides), Commentary on the Torah, vol. 4, Numbers, trans. Charles B. Chavel (New York: Shilo Publishing House, 1975), ad loc. Numbers 13:33. Ramban observes that the spies first describe the land's inhabitants only as men of great size (13:32), then, in reporting to the assembled people, sharpen this into the specific claim of Nephilim descent, a rhetorical escalation Ramban reads as deliberate exaggeration meant to terrify the Israelites out of the invasion rather than a considered genealogical claim. The hyperbole reading is not, in other words, a modern historical-critical import; it has a documented pedigree in medieval Jewish exegesis centuries before Westermann or Milgrom.

50 — One people, or one category, under three names

Jeffrey H. Tigay, Deuteronomy = Devarim: The Traditional Hebrew Text with the New JPS Translation, JPS Torah Commentary (Philadelphia: Jewish Publication Society, 1996), ad loc. Deuteronomy 2:10-23. Tigay reads this passage as an antiquarian aside inserted into the itinerary, explaining to the audience that the Emim the Moabites displaced and the Zamzummim the Ammonites displaced were, in the text's own accounting, both instances of the broader category Rephaim, the same category to which the Anakim belong and against which each is measured for comparison. Tigay treats "Rephaim" here as functioning less like a single ethnic label and more like a taxonomic term, of a kind: a way of naming a recognized class of unusually large, formerly widespread pre-Israelite inhabitants under whatever local name a given neighboring nation happened to use for them.

51 — The same word also means the dead

Laura Quick, "Og, King of Bashan: Underworld Ruler or Ancient Giant?" TheTorah.com, July 22, 2020. Quick, associate professor of Hebrew Bible at the University of Oxford, notes that rephaim carries two distinct senses across the Hebrew Bible: shades or spirits of the dead in the underworld (Isaiah 26:14; Proverbs 9:18; Psalm 88:11), and, separately, the pre-Israelite giant inhabitants of Transjordan and Canaan named in Deuteronomy 2 and Genesis 14:5. She argues the Deuteronomic use is the older, historically literal sense, giants who "lived long ago, but are now dead," and that the underworld sense developed as a later, separate extension of the same word rather than the reverse; she also cites Alan Millard's argument that an iron bed is plausible as a genuine decorative luxury object in the relevant period, supporting a literal rather than symbolic reading of Deuteronomy 3:11.

52 — A nine-cubit bed and what it was actually for

Timo Veijola, "King Og's Iron Bed (Deut 3:11) — Once Again," in Studies in the Hebrew Bible, Qumran, and the Septuagint Presented to Eugene Ulrich, ed. Peter W. Flint, Emanuel Tov, and James C. VanderKam, Supplements to Vetus Testamentum 101 (Leiden: Brill, 2006), 60-76. Veijola surveys the live proposals for what Deuteronomy 3:11's "iron bed," preserved as a museum piece in Rabbah of the Ammonites, actually was: a genuine royal bed captured as war booty and displayed as a trophy, a funerary bed or sarcophagus (the Hebrew word can carry either sense), or, on a minority reading, a basalt slab whose dark color and weight led later observers to describe it as "iron." None of the three readings requires or forecloses supernatural size; all agree the verse presents the object as a physically verifiable relic available for inspection by the book's original audience, which is part of why it functions as such a concrete anchor for Og's otherwise legendary stature.

53 — The base translation used for the second cosmic tour

George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch: A New Translation (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2004), translation of 1 Enoch 17-19, 21, 24-27, 32-33. This translation, prepared in tandem with Nickelsburg's Hermeneia commentary volume, is the only English rendering of 1 Enoch that weighs the full textual base now available: the Ethiopic manuscript tradition, the Greek fragments (including Codex Panopolitanus), and the Aramaic fragments recovered at Qumran. Quotations and paraphrases of 1 Enoch 17-36 in this chapter follow this translation's wording and versification unless otherwise noted.

54 — Two journeys, not one, and what the seam tells a reader

George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001), commentary on 1 Enoch 17-19 and on the composite structure of chapters 17-36 generally. Nickelsburg reads chapters 17-19 and 20-36 as two originally distinct journey accounts, stitched together by the roster of angelic names in chapter 20, which serves the redactor as a hinge: the anonymous angelic guides of the first tour give way to named, individually commissioned angels for the second, longer tour. The commentary treats this seam as a genuine literary join rather than a unity composed at one sitting, though it stops short of resolving every detail of the two accounts' relative dating.

55 — A specialist study of exactly this cosmography

Kelley Coblentz Bautch, A Study of the Geography of 1 Enoch 17-19: "No One Has Seen What I Have Seen," Supplements to the Journal for the Study of Judaism 81 (Leiden: Brill, 2003). Coblentz Bautch's monograph is the standard specialist treatment of the cosmic geography narrated in this section of the Book of the Watchers, working through how the storehouses of the winds, the ends of the earth, the mountains of fire, and the placement of the luminaries relate to one another as a coherent mental map, and situating that map against background drawn from the Hebrew Bible, the ancient Near East, and the wider world of Hellenistic Judaism. She does not claim the itinerary corresponds to any real, traversable route; her argument is about the cosmological picture the text assumes, not about ancient travel writing as a genre, and this chapter follows her on that narrower claim.

56 — Seven names, seven jobs

Nickelsburg and VanderKam, 1 Enoch: A New Translation (2004), translation and notes ad loc. 1 Enoch 20; see also Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1 (Hermeneia, 2001), commentary ad loc. 1 Enoch 20 supplies a formal register of seven angels, each assigned a cosmic portfolio: Uriel over the world and Tartarus, Raphael over the spirits of human beings, Raguel who exacts vengeance on the world of the luminaries, Michael set over the better part of humankind, Sariel (also transliterated Saraqael) over the spirits who sin against the spirit, Gabriel over Paradise, the serpents, and the cherubim, and Remiel, whom God set over those who rise — read by most commentators as an office concerned with resurrection. The list functions in the narrative as a formal roster before the second tour begins, naming who among the angels will do what.

57 — Even the roster of seven is not textually settled

Nickelsburg and VanderKam, 1 Enoch: A New Translation (2004), textual notes ad loc. 1 Enoch 20. The two principal textual witnesses do not agree on the full list. The Greek witness, Codex Panopolitanus (the Akhmim manuscript), preserves all seven names including Remiel, while part of the Ethiopic manuscript tradition lacks that seventh name. The translators reconstruct a full roster of seven from the combined witnesses rather than from any single manuscript standing alone, which means the tidy number seven is itself a text-critical judgment call, not a reading directly available in any one surviving copy.

58 — Four names first, then seven

Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1 (Hermeneia, 2001), commentary ad loc. 1 Enoch 9:1 and 20:1-8. Earlier in the Book of the Watchers, only four angels are named as the ones who look down on the bloodshed the Watchers' offspring have caused and carry the complaint to God: Michael, Sariel (Uriel in some witnesses), Raphael, and Gabriel (9:1). 1 Enoch 20's register of seven repeats three of those four names — Michael, Raphael, Gabriel — and adds Uriel, now distinguished from Sariel/Saraqael as a separate figure, along with Raguel and Remiel. Nickelsburg treats the expansion from four to seven as evidence of growth within the angelological tradition across the Book of the Watchers' own composite history, not as a contradiction requiring harmonization.

59 — A second, independent seven

Carey A. Moore, Tobit, Anchor Bible vol. 40A (New York: Doubleday, 1996), commentary ad loc. Tobit 12:15. In the book of Tobit, the angel Raphael identifies himself as "one of the seven holy angels who present the prayers of the saints and enter into the presence of the glory of the Holy One" (Tobit 12:15). Moore treats this as an independent witness to the same broader Second Temple tradition of seven principal angels of the divine presence that 1 Enoch 20 names in full; Tobit supplies only the number and Raphael's own place within it, not the other six names. Whether Tobit drew directly on an Enochic source or on a wider shared tradition is not something Moore's commentary claims to settle.

60 — Why this chapter matters more than its length suggests

Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1 (Hermeneia, 2001), commentary ad loc. 1 Enoch 22. Nickelsburg treats chapter 22's vision of a differentiated post-mortem holding place — one mountain, several hollow compartments, each reserved for a distinct category of the dead awaiting a still-future judgment — as a documented early step in the development of Jewish and, later, Christian afterlife belief away from an undifferentiated Sheol and toward the idea that the dead are already sorted, prior to a final resolving judgment, by the moral character of the life they led. He is careful to describe this as one datable witness within a developing picture rather than as the origin point of Jewish afterlife belief as a whole.

61 — A specific case among the general categories: Abel, again

Nickelsburg and VanderKam, 1 Enoch: A New Translation (2004), translation ad loc. 1 Enoch 22:7, compared with Genesis 4:10. Among the four categories of dead Enoch is shown, one compartment holds a specific named case rather than a class: "the spirit which went forth from Abel, whom his brother Cain slew," pleading its case against Cain until Cain's "seed is destroyed from the face of the earth" (22:7). This directly extends Genesis 4:10, where Abel's spilled blood already "cries out" from the ground to God. 1 Enoch 22 takes that single biblical image of blood crying from the earth and turns it into an ongoing legal petition lodged by a waiting spirit, a considerably more developed picture of postmortem agency than Genesis itself supplies.

62 — A parable and a documented literary neighborhood

Richard Bauckham, "The Rich Man and Lazarus: The Parable and the Parallels," New Testament Studies 37 (1991): 225-246. Bauckham situates Jesus's parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31) within a documented ancient narrative pattern of a reversal of fortune after death and a request that a dead person return with a warning for the living, a pattern he traces across several ancient sources. This chapter flags the parallel only briefly and points forward: the fuller treatment of how Luke 16's compartmentalized afterlife imagery relates to 1 Enoch 22's hollow places belongs to this book's later chapter on New Testament citation and allusion, not here.

63 — "Spirits in prison": one reading traces straight back here

William J. Dalton, Christ's Proclamation to the Spirits: A Study of 1 Peter 3:18-4:6, 2nd rev. ed., Analecta Biblica 23 (Rome: Pontifical Biblical Institute, 1989). Dalton's monograph, the standard specialist treatment of this notoriously difficult passage, surveys the major interpretive options for 1 Peter 3:19's "spirits in prison," including the reading, with real scholarly support, that identifies those spirits with the imprisoned Watchers of the Enochic tradition rather than with human dead generally. Dalton does not treat that reading as the only defensible one. As with the Lazarus parallel, this chapter notes the connection and reserves the full argument for the later chapter on New Testament citation.

64 — Tree of life, or tree of wisdom by another name?

Veronika Bachmann, "Rooted in Paradise? The Meaning of the 'Tree of Life' in 1 Enoch 24-25 Reconsidered," Journal for the Study of the Pseudepigrapha 19 (2009): 83-107. The tree Enoch is shown in chapters 24-25, fragrant beyond any tree he has known, reserved until the final judgment for the righteous and the chosen, is generally read as a straightforward tree-of-life image, an eschatological counterpart to Eden's own tree of life (Genesis 2:9; 3:22-24) and to Revelation 22:2's tree standing at the center of the New Jerusalem. Bachmann argues instead that the tree's original resonance in the Book of the Watchers is closer to a wisdom symbol, drawing on the wisdom-as-tree imagery found in Proverbs and Sirach, than to a literal replaying of Eden's tree of life. She does not deny the later, straightforwardly tree-of-life reading became dominant; she argues only that it may not have been the earliest one.

65 — A second tree, and this time the text names its source

Nickelsburg and VanderKam, 1 Enoch: A New Translation (2004), translation ad loc. 1 Enoch 32:3-6. Later in the tour, Enoch reaches a garden he calls the garden of righteousness and asks about a strikingly beautiful tree there. The angel with him — Raphael, per the same office assigned him in chapter 20 — answers plainly that this is the tree of wisdom, of which Enoch's own distant forebears, "old in years," ate, "and they learnt wisdom and their eyes were opened, and they knew that they were naked, and they were driven out of the garden" (32:6), an unmistakable retelling of Genesis 3:6-7's tree of the knowledge of good and evil rather than of Eden's separate tree of life. 1 Enoch 32, in other words, names its own source text far more directly than chapter 24-25's tree does.

66 — The center of the earth, and the valley just past it

Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1 (Hermeneia, 2001), commentary ad loc. 1 Enoch 26-27. Enoch is brought to a mountain range at what the text calls "the center of the earth," identified by the surrounding geography as Jerusalem and its Temple mount (26:1-2), and then to an adjoining "accursed valley" reserved for those who speak evil against the Lord and where the condemned will be gathered and punished in full view of the righteous (27:1-3). Nickelsburg identifies this accursed valley with the Valley of Hinnom directly south of the city, the same site whose name (Hebrew ge-hinnom) underlies the later term Gehenna; the identification rests on the valley's real, known location just outside Jerusalem's walls, not on anything internal to Enoch's own account.

67 — Eleven Aramaic manuscripts, not twelve

Jozef T. Milik, in collaboration with Matthew Black, The Books of Enoch: Aramaic Fragments of Qumran Cave 4 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1976). Milik's edition identifies eleven Aramaic manuscript copies of Enochic material recovered from Qumran Cave 4: seven copies of the Book of the Watchers, the Book of Dreams, and the Epistle of Enoch (catalogued 4Q201, 4Q202, 4Q204, 4Q205, 4Q206, 4Q207, and 4Q212), plus four further copies of the separate Astronomical Book (4Q208-4Q211). Milik's paleographic analysis dates the oldest of the group, 4Q201, to approximately 200-150 BCE on the evidence of its Hasmonean-period semi-cursive hand, with the remaining copies distributed across the following two centuries down toward the turn of the era.

68 — A twelfth catalogue number that belongs to a different book

Jozef T. Milik, The Books of Enoch: Aramaic Fragments of Qumran Cave 4 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1976), where the Book of Giants material is published alongside the Enoch fragments proper. The manuscript numbered 4Q203 falls within the same run of Cave 4 catalogue numbers as the eleven Enoch copies but is not a twelfth copy of 1 Enoch itself: it preserves fragments of the Book of Giants, a related Enochic composition concerning the offspring of the Watchers that circulated at Qumran as its own distinct work. The Book of Giants was later excluded from the Ethiopic 1 Enoch collection altogether and survives today only in scattered Aramaic fragments and later Manichaean adaptations.

69 — One section of the book, missing from every Qumran fragment

George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch: A New Translation (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2004), introduction; Jozef T. Milik, The Books of Enoch: Aramaic Fragments of Qumran Cave 4 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1976). No fragment of the Book of Parables (1 Enoch 37-71) appears among any of the eleven Aramaic Enoch manuscripts recovered from Cave 4, although every other major section of the work is represented there in some form. Scholars have debated the reason for this absence for decades; the most widely held explanation ties it to a later date of composition for the Parables than for the rest of the Enochic collection, placing it outside the period in which the Qumran community was copying and depositing Enochic texts. This book takes up that debate directly in the next chapter.

70 — A monk's grave, four texts, one archaeological mission

Urbain Bouriant, ed., "Fragments du texte grec du livre d'Enoch et de quelques ecrits attribues a saint Pierre," Memoires publies par les membres de la Mission archeologique francaise au Caire, vol. 9, fasc. 1 (Paris: Ernest Leroux, 1892). The manuscript, recovered in 1886-87 by the French Archaeological Mission at Akhmim (ancient Panopolis) in Upper Egypt from a grave in the town's ancient cemetery, reportedly a monk's, contains a Greek text of 1 Enoch 1-32 alongside a Greek text of the Gospel of Peter, a Greek text of the Apocalypse of Peter, and a fragment of the Martyrdom of Saint Julian.

71 — A manuscript scholars still cannot agree on the century of

Discussed in George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001), in the introductory survey of the Greek witnesses. Paleographic proposals for the date of Codex Panopolitanus, the Akhmim manuscript, span roughly two centuries: specialists working from the same handwriting have argued for dates as early as the late fifth century and as late as the first half of the seventh, with "sixth century" the figure most commonly cited in general reference works. The spread reflects genuine, unresolved paleographic disagreement rather than a settled consensus that has simply been rounded off to one date.

72 — The last chapters, published apart from the first

Campbell Bonner, with the collaboration of H. C. Youtie, The Last Chapters of Enoch in Greek (London: Christophers, 1937); plates subsequently issued as Frederic G. Kenyon, ed., Enoch and Melito, Fasciculus VII of The Chester Beatty Biblical Papyri: Descriptions and Texts of Twelve Manuscripts on Papyrus of the Greek Bible (London: Emery Walker, 1941). The papyrus codex, since divided between the Chester Beatty Library, Dublin, and the University of Michigan, preserves the closing chapters of 1 Enoch, approximately 97:6 through the book's end at 107 or 108, bound together with a homily on the Passion by the second-century bishop Melito of Sardis, a text likewise previously unattested in Greek before this discovery. Paleographers date the codex to the fourth century CE.

73 — Nine-odd chapters, quoted twice over, and nothing else for two centuries

William Adler and Paul Tuffin, trans., The Chronography of George Synkellos: A Byzantine Chronicle of Universal History from the Creation (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2002); the underlying Greek excerpts were first published in the West by Joseph Justus Scaliger in 1606. George Syncellus's Chronographia, a world-chronicle compiled around 810 CE, quotes 1 Enoch 6:1-9:4, then separately duplicates 8:4-10:14 from an apparently different exemplar than the first excerpt, and finally quotes a further short passage, 15:8-16:1. From Scaliger's 1606 publication of these excerpts until James Bruce's return from Ethiopia with complete Ge'ez manuscripts in 1773, this handful of quoted chapters was the only text of 1 Enoch that Western scholarship possessed in any language.

74 — Eighty-one uncontested books, and a broader list beyond them

R. W. Cowley, "The Biblical Canon of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church Today," Ostkirchliche Studien 23 (1974). Cowley distinguishes a narrower canon of eighty-one books recognized in Ethiopia, forty-six Old Testament and thirty-five New Testament, whose contents are uncontested within the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church today, from a broader canon that additionally includes works such as the Book of Enoch, the Book of Jubilees, and Meqabyan among others distinctive to the Ethiopian tradition. 1 Enoch's canonical standing in Ethiopia belongs to this broader list, not to the narrower eighty-one that most printed Ethiopian Bible editions present as the core text.

75 — Thirty-three manuscripts, and the oldest known at the time

Michael A. Knibb, in consultation with Edward Ullendorff, The Ethiopic Book of Enoch: A New Edition in the Light of the Aramaic Dead Sea Fragments, 2 vols. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1978). Knibb's critical edition drew on thirty-three Ethiopic manuscripts, the oldest of which he identified as dating to the fifteenth century, the earliest known complete witness to 1 Enoch's text available at the time of publication.

76 — The oldest complete copy anyone has identified, so far

Ted M. Erho and Loren T. Stuckenbruck, "A Manuscript History of Ethiopic Enoch," Journal for the Study of the Pseudepigrapha 23, no. 2 (2013): 87-133. Erho and Stuckenbruck's survey of the Ethiopic manuscript tradition identifies MS Lake Tana 9, copied in the first half of the fifteenth century, as the oldest known complete Ethiopic manuscript of 1 Enoch, refining rather than substantially overturning Knibb's earlier fifteenth-century dating.

77 — Why the mainstream church let it go, in bare outline

James C. VanderKam, Enoch: A Man for All Generations, Studies on Personalities of the Old Testament (Columbia: University of South Carolina Press, 1995). VanderKam traces the reception of Enoch and Enochic literature from the Second Temple period through the fourth and fifth centuries CE, when influential Latin fathers including Jerome and Augustine ceased to treat 1 Enoch as scripture, contributing to its exclusion from most canonical lists in both the Western and Eastern churches by that period. The fuller range of theological reasons behind that shift, rather than the bare transmission fact of it, is the subject of a later chapter of this book.

78 — Three manuscripts home, a fourth left behind in Rome

Ariel Hessayon, "James Bruce and His Copies of Ethiopic Enoch," and the companion study, published separately, "James Bruce's 'Fourth' Manuscript: Solving the Mystery of the Provenance of the Roman Enoch Manuscript (Vat. et. 71)." Hessayon's research establishes that James Bruce returned to Europe in 1773 with three Ge'ez manuscripts of the complete Book of Enoch: one presented to the Bodleian Library, Oxford; one presented to the Royal Library in Paris, later absorbed into the Bibliotheque Nationale; and one retained by Bruce himself, which eventually also reached the Bodleian. Hessayon's further archival research identifies a previously unaccounted-for fourth manuscript, given by Bruce to a cardinal's library in Rome during a stop on his return journey after meeting Pope Clement XIV, resolving the long-uncertain provenance of the Vatican Library's own Enoch manuscript, shelf-mark Vat. et. 71.

79 — The first Enoch an English reader could actually read

Richard Laurence, The Book of Enoch the Prophet: An Apocryphal Production, Supposed to Have Been Lost for Ages (Oxford: Parker, 1821). Laurence, Regius Professor of Hebrew at Oxford, produced this translation from one of the Ge'ez manuscripts James Bruce had deposited in the Bodleian Library, making it the first complete English-language translation of 1 Enoch to appear in print.

80 — The edition that stood for most of a century

R. H. Charles, The Ethiopic Version of the Book of Enoch (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1906); R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1912). Charles's 1906 volume presented a critical edition of the Ethiopic text drawn from a considerably larger manuscript base than Laurence had used, incorporating the Greek and Latin fragments known at the time; his 1912 second edition supplied a fully revised English translation and commentary. The Charles edition and translation remained the standard scholarly reference for most of the twentieth century.

81 — The first translation to weigh all three witnesses together

George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001); George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch 2: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 37-82, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2012); George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch: A New Translation (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2004). This project, completed across these volumes, was the first to produce a critical translation and commentary weighing the Aramaic Qumran fragments, the scattered Greek witnesses, and the complete Ethiopic textual tradition together, superseding Charles's early-twentieth-century edition as the field's standard reference.

82 — Four titles, one figure: the standard modern catalog

George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch 2: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 37-82, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2012), excursus "The Chosen One of Righteousness and Faith . . . Also the Righteous One, the Son of Man, and the Anointed One," pp. 113-23. Nickelsburg and VanderKam, who divided authorship of the two-volume Hermeneia commentary (VanderKam on chapters 1-36 and 81-108, Nickelsburg on 37-82, the Parables), devote a dedicated excursus to cataloging every occurrence of the four titles applied to the same heavenly judge across the three parables and arguing that they function as synonyms for one figure rather than as four distinct characters.

83 — Three parables, one book, and an ending that will not sit still

George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch 2: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 37-82, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2012), introduction and commentary on 1 Enoch 37-71. The commentary divides the Parables into an introduction (37:1-5), the first parable (38:1-44:1), the second parable (45:1-57:3), the third parable (58:1-69:29), and a concluding section (70:1-71:17) narrating Enoch's own final ascent — five structural units total, framing three sustained "similitudes" rather than three short fables in the folk sense.

84 — Daniel's own "one like a son of man": collective symbol, or individual being?

John J. Collins, Daniel: A Commentary on the Book of Daniel, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 1993), commentary on Daniel 7:13-14, 27. Collins surveys a genuine, still-unresolved split among Daniel scholars over whether the phrase "one like a son of man" who comes "with the clouds of heaven" and receives "dominion and glory and a kingdom" (Daniel 7:13-14) originally names a collective symbol for "the people of the holy ones of the Most High" (Daniel 7:27), or an individual heavenly being — an angel, or a "second" divine figure distinct from the Ancient of Days. Both readings have serious scholarly defenders; Daniel's own text does not adjudicate the question, and it is this same ambiguous figure that both 1 Enoch's Parables and, later, the New Testament Gospels draw on.

85 — A book that ends by telling Enoch he is the very figure he has been watching

George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch 2: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 37-82, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2012), commentary on 1 Enoch 70:1 and 71:14. Through seventy chapters the son of man Enoch describes is a figure distinct from Enoch, seated on a throne Enoch only observes from outside. Then, in the closing ascent narrative, an angel tells Enoch directly, "You are the son of man who was born for righteousness" (71:14), an identification apparently in tension with 70:1, which still speaks of Enoch approaching "that son of man" as someone other than himself. Nickelsburg reads chapter 70 as probably the Parables' original conclusion, with chapter 71's identification a secondary addition; VanderKam instead proposes that Enoch is being shown his own heavenly double or counterpart, so that the identification is not a late insertion but the intended climax all along. Neither position commands unanimous assent among specialists.

86 — The Watchers story again, with a different cast and a cosmic oath added

Jonathan Ben-Dov and Eshbal Ratzon, "The Oath and the Name in 1 Enoch 69," Journal of Semitic Studies 60, no. 1 (2015): 19-51. The Parables retell the Watchers-and-giants narrative on their own terms within 1 Enoch 54:1-6, 55:3-4, and 64:1-69:29, rather than simply repeating the account already given in 1 Enoch 6-11 earlier in the book. Ben-Dov and Ratzon's study focuses on the distinctive material unique to this retelling: a named angel, Kasbeel, identified as "the chief of the oath" and holder of a hidden name called Biqa, who compels Michael to disclose that name so that it can anchor a cosmic oath binding creation itself (69:13-25) — a cosmological function for the Watchers' transgression that has no counterpart in the earlier Book of Watchers, alongside its own list of angels and the specific forbidden arts each discloses (69:4-12), a list that overlaps with but does not simply duplicate the roster given in 1 Enoch 8.

87 — The one section of 1 Enoch that Qumran never gave up

J. T. Milik, with the collaboration of Matthew Black, The Books of Enoch: Aramaic Fragments of Qumrân Cave 4 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1976). Milik, who edited the eleven Aramaic Enoch manuscripts recovered from Qumran Cave 4 discussed in the preceding chapter, found fragments of the Book of Watchers, the Astronomical Book, the Book of Dreams, and the Epistle of Enoch — every other major section of 1 Enoch — but not one fragment, however small, of the Parables (1 Enoch 37-71). From that absence Milik argued the Parables were composed considerably later than the rest of the corpus, assigning them to the third century CE and identifying the work as a Christian, or Jewish-Christian, composition rather than a product of the same Second Temple Jewish milieu that produced the rest of 1 Enoch.

88 — The revision begins: a "recent discussion" survey that pushed back

David W. Suter, "Weighed in the Balance: The Similitudes of Enoch in Recent Discussion," Religious Studies Review 7 (1981): 217-21. Writing only five years after Milik's edition of the Qumran Aramaic fragments, Suter surveyed the scholarship responding to Milik's late, third-century Christian dating of the Parables and found most specialists already unpersuaded, arguing that the absence of Parables material at Qumran is better explained by the text circulating within a different scribal or sectarian circle than the one that assembled the Qumran caves' Enoch collection, not by a late composition date.

89 — A case for reading the Parables as pre-Christian after all

James C. VanderKam, "Righteous One, Messiah, Chosen One, and Son of Man in 1 Enoch 37-71," in The Messiah: Developments in Earliest Judaism and Christianity, ed. James H. Charlesworth (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 1992), 169-91. VanderKam argues for a date in the latter part of Herod the Great's reign or shortly after, roughly the last decades of the first century BCE to the early first century CE, pointing to internal evidence such as the Parables' apparent allusion to a Parthian and Median invasion of the land (1 Enoch 56:5-7), which fits attested first-century-BCE incursions, and the complete absence of any reflection on the Jerusalem Temple's destruction in 70 CE anywhere in the text — a silence VanderKam judges hard to explain in a work as concerned with judgment and vindication as the Parables, had it in fact been composed after that catastrophe.

90 — A book-length case that the field changed its mind

Darrell L. Bock and James H. Charlesworth, eds., Parables of Enoch: A Paradigm Shift, Jewish and Christian Texts in Contexts and Related Studies 11 (London: Bloomsbury T&T Clark, 2013). This edited volume, gathering roughly two dozen specialists, documents what its editors call a paradigm shift away from Milik's 1976 late-Christian dating and toward a consensus placing the Parables' composition in the late first century BCE or the early-to-mid first century CE, prior to the Gospels, on the strength of internal historical allusions, calendrical data, and the absence of any recognizably Christian content in the text itself. The volume presents this as the current majority position rather than a closed question; a minority of scholars, discussed elsewhere in this chapter, continue to argue for a later date.

91 — Not everyone signed on: a dissenting later date

James D. G. Dunn, Christology in the Making: A New Testament Inquiry into the Origins of the Doctrine of the Incarnation (London: SCM Press, 1980; 2nd ed., Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1989), chapter on Son of Man Christology. Dunn represents the ongoing minority position that the Parables postdate 70 CE, arguing that a fully pre-existent heavenly "Son of Man" as an individual figure cannot be securely traced within non-Christian Jewish circles before that date, and treating the Parables' version of the figure as more plausibly influenced by, rather than prior to, earliest Christian Son of Man language. The disagreement between Dunn and the "paradigm shift" scholars remains a live one; this book does not adjudicate it.

92 — A rival account: the same Danielic well, not the same bucket

Maurice Casey, The Solution to the 'Son of Man' Problem, Library of New Testament Studies 343 (London: T&T Clark, 2007). Casey argues that the underlying Aramaic phrase bar (e)nash(a), "son of man," functioned as an ordinary idiom for "a man" or "someone" rather than a fixed messianic title, and that in the Parables themselves the figure so named is most plausibly Enoch himself rather than a separately conceived pre-existent Messiah. On this reading, the Gospels' use of "the son of man" for Jesus need not derive from the Parables at all; both could draw independently on the same Danielic idiom and imagery (Daniel 7:13) without one text influencing the other, a position standing at the opposite end of the spectrum from those who argue for direct literary dependence.

93 — Same canon, same eighty-one books, as already noted

R. W. Cowley, "The Biblical Canon of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church Today," Ostkirchliche Studien 23 (1974): 318-23. As this survey has already discussed with respect to the rest of 1 Enoch, the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's canon draws no distinction between the Book of Watchers, the Parables, and the other constituent sections of 1 Enoch; the Parables belong to the single Ge'ez Mets'hafe Henok read and preserved as scripture within that eighty-one-book canon, the only Christian tradition to have carried the Parables continuously as canonical text rather than losing and recovering it.

94 — An angel with a specific portfolio

George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch 2: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 37-82, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2012), commentary ad loc. 1 Enoch 72:1. Enoch introduces this whole section as "the book of the courses of the luminaries of heaven," shown to him by "Uriel, the holy angel who was with me, who is their leader." Nickelsburg and VanderKam note that this is a distinct office from Uriel's other appearance earlier in 1 Enoch as one of the four archangels who intercede with God over the earth's corruption (see Chapter 5 of this book); here Uriel functions specifically as the angel of instruction over the sun, moon, stars, and winds, and chapters 72-82 amount to his own extended technical lecture.

95 — The standard modern commentary on this section

George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch 2: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 37-82, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2012). This volume, completing Nickelsburg's earlier 1 Enoch 1 (Fortress Press, 2001) covering chapters 1-36 and 81-108, is the standard critical commentary treating chapters 72-82 verse by verse against both the Ethiopic textual tradition and the Aramaic Qumran fragments; citations to "Nickelsburg and VanderKam" throughout this chapter refer to this volume unless otherwise noted.

96 — Four Aramaic copies, and a text longer than what survived

Henryk Drawnel, The Aramaic Astronomical Book (4Q208-4Q211) from Qumran: Text, Translation, and Commentary (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2011). Four Aramaic manuscripts from Qumran Cave 4 — 4Q208, 4Q209, 4Q210, and 4Q211 — preserve portions of the Astronomical Book. Drawnel's edition shows that 4Q208 and 4Q209 in particular contain far more numerical and tabular detail about the moon's waxing and waning than survives in the later Ethiopic translation, which appears to have compressed or dropped material during transmission; the Aramaic fragments therefore give a fuller, more technical picture of the underlying astronomical scheme than the complete Ethiopic text does by itself.

97 — How old is the oldest copy — and is it the oldest Enoch fragment of all?

J. T. Milik, The Books of Enoch: Aramaic Fragments of Qumran Cave 4 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1976), 273-297. On paleographic grounds Milik dated 4Q208 to the late third or early second century BCE, which he took as a terminus ante quem placing the Astronomical Book's composition itself in the third century BCE or earlier — among the earliest material anywhere in the Enochic corpus. This claim needs a caution the popular literature often drops: 4Q201, the oldest surviving copy of the separate Book of Watchers, has been dated by Milik and by subsequent paleographers to a closely comparable window (roughly 200-150 BCE, with some more recent assessments pushing it as early as the late third century). The two earliest Enoch manuscripts at Qumran are close contemporaries on the current evidence; the Astronomical Book's claim to priority is genuine but not undisputed, and no consensus verdict names it the single oldest.

98 — Not, in fact, the best-attested section — a needed correction

Percentages as calculated by J. T. Milik, The Books of Enoch: Aramaic Fragments of Qumran Cave 4 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1976), and cited in Michael A. Knibb, in consultation with Edward Ullendorff, The Ethiopic Book of Enoch: A New Edition in the Light of the Aramaic Dead Sea Fragments, 2 vols. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1978). By these widely cited calculations, the Qumran Aramaic fragments cover roughly 50 percent of the Book of Watchers (chapters 1-36), against roughly 30 percent of the Astronomical Book (chapters 72-82), 26 percent of the Book of Dreams, and 18 percent of the Epistle of Enoch. By that measure the Astronomical Book is well attested and unusually early, but it is the Book of Watchers, not the Astronomical Book, that is the most extensively preserved section of 1 Enoch at Qumran in terms of raw proportion of text recovered.

99 — Twelve months, thirty days, four more

1 Enoch 72:32; 74:10-17; 82:4-6, 11-20, discussed in Nickelsburg and VanderKam, 1 Enoch 2, commentary ad loc. The Astronomical Book lays out a year of twelve months of thirty days each (360 days), with four additional days inserted at the turn of each of the four seasons — one after every third month — bringing the total to 364 days across four equal quarters of 91 days. 1 Enoch 82 assigns each 91-day quarter its own "leader," a named star governing that portion of the year, and states plainly that this reckoning, not any lunar count, is the correct one.

100 — A warning built into the astronomy

1 Enoch 74:10-17; 80:2-8; 82:4-6, discussed in Nickelsburg and VanderKam, 1 Enoch 2, commentary ad loc. Having laid out the solar 364-day reckoning, the text turns polemical: it describes "the days of the sinners" as a coming time when the calendar itself will fall into disorder — the moon will shift from its proper order and appear at the wrong times — and warns that those who set festivals by lunar observation, rather than by the fixed solar scheme just described, will miscalculate months, years, and the timing of sacred occasions. This is presented in the text as established fact about calendrical error, not as a claim this chapter is positioned to adjudicate; it is reported here as what the Astronomical Book itself says, and why.

101 — The math the text does not solve

Jonathan Ben-Dov, Head of All Years: Astronomy and Calendars at Qumran in their Ancient Context, Studies on the Texts of the Desert of Judah 78 (Leiden: Brill, 2008); Eshbal Ratzon and Jonathan Ben-Dov, "A Newly Reconstructed Calendrical Scroll from Qumran in Cryptic Script," Journal of Biblical Literature 136, no. 4 (2017): 905-936. The true solar year is approximately 365.2422 days; a 364-day calendar therefore runs roughly 1.24 days short every year, drifting against the actual seasons at a rate that would displace fixed festival dates by weeks within a few decades and by months within a century or two if left uncorrected. Neither the Astronomical Book itself nor 4Q324d, an independent Qumran sectarian calendrical scroll using the same 364-day scheme reconstructed and published by Ratzon and Ben-Dov, describes an intercalation mechanism or any other method for correcting this drift; the silence is worth reporting as silence rather than filling with a solution no surviving source actually states.

102 — The same scheme, attested independently

James C. VanderKam, Calendars in the Dead Sea Scrolls: Measuring Time (London: Routledge, 1998), chapters on the 364-day tradition in Enoch, Jubilees, and the Qumran sectarian calendrical texts. VanderKam traces the same 364-day, 12-month-plus-4-day solar scheme independently through the Astronomical Book, the Book of Jubilees, and a distinct family of Qumran sectarian documents — among them mishmarot priestly-course texts and mentions in the Community Rule tradition — that presuppose or spell out this calendar for organizing festivals, sabbaths, and priestly rotations. That three independent bodies of text converge on the identical scheme is the strongest evidence that this was a real, operative calendrical tradition among some Second Temple Jewish groups, not merely a literary conceit unique to one book.

103 — Where did the scheme come from? A live, contested question

Annie Jaubert, "Le calendrier des Jubilés et les jours liturgiques de la semaine," Vetus Testamentum 7 (1957): 35-61; discussed in VanderKam, Calendars in the Dead Sea Scrolls (London: Routledge, 1998). Jaubert argued that the 364-day scheme she reconstructed from Jubilees matches a calendar implicit in the Bible's own priestly source material, making the 364-day tradition older and more mainstream than a sectarian invention. VanderKam has partly endorsed this priestly-calendar hypothesis, while other scholars — for instance Roger Beckwith — have argued the relationship runs the other way, that the biblical chronologies were later read through the lens of an Essene-era calendar rather than the calendar deriving from them. The question of where the 364-day scheme originated remains genuinely open; this chapter reports the competing positions rather than adjudicating between them.

104 — A calendar that could not agree with the Temple's

VanderKam, Calendars in the Dead Sea Scrolls (London: Routledge, 1998); Ben-Dov, Head of All Years (Leiden: Brill, 2008). The mainstream Jerusalem Temple calendar of the Second Temple period was lunar-solar, fixing months by observed new moons and periodically intercalating a thirteenth month to stay aligned with the seasons — a fundamentally different mechanism from the fixed 364-day solar scheme found in the Astronomical Book, Jubilees, and the Qumran sectarian texts. A community keeping the 364-day calendar would mark its festivals, including Passover and the Day of Atonement, on different calendar dates than the Jerusalem priesthood in most years. Some scholars treat this calendrical incompatibility as one documented factor among several in the Qumran community's separation from the Jerusalem priesthood; this chapter reports that scholarly discussion without asserting a single settled cause for the historical split.

105 — Four named leaders, spelled differently in different manuscripts

1 Enoch 82:11-20, discussed in Nickelsburg and VanderKam, 1 Enoch 2, commentary ad loc. The text names four stars as "leaders" of the four 91-day quarters of the year, commonly rendered in translation as forms close to Milkiel, Helemmelek, Melekiel, and Narel. Nickelsburg and VanderKam note that the underlying Ethiopic manuscript tradition is unstable at exactly this point, with meaningful spelling variation for each of the four names across surviving witnesses — a reminder that even a passage as arithmetically precise as this one rests on a textual transmission that was not itself perfectly stable.

106 — The standard specialist commentary on this one section of 1 Enoch

Patrick A. Tiller, A Commentary on the Animal Apocalypse of I Enoch, Early Judaism and Its Literature 4 (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1993), a lightly revised version of his 1991 Harvard Divinity School doctoral dissertation. Tiller's remains the only book-length, verse-by-verse specialist commentary devoted solely to 1 Enoch 85-90 (the Animal Apocalypse), and it is cited throughout this chapter for the allegorical scheme's details, the periodization of the seventy shepherds, and the arguments for dating the work's composition. George W. E. Nickelsburg's Hermeneia commentary, cited alongside it throughout, covers the same chapters as part of its full-book treatment of 1 Enoch 1-36 and 81-108.

107 — Where this chapter's material sits inside 1 Enoch as a whole

George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001), commentary ad loc. 1 Enoch 83-90. Nickelsburg treats chapters 83-90 as a single composite unit, the Book of Dream Visions, addressed by Enoch to his son Methuselah: a first, shorter dream (83-84) in which Enoch foresees the Flood, and a second, much longer dream (85-90), conventionally called the Animal Apocalypse, in which the entire span of history from Adam to an idealized future is recast as a history of animals. This chapter covers only the second, longer vision.

108 — Why the first humans are cattle, and why their color matters

Patrick A. Tiller, A Commentary on the Animal Apocalypse of I Enoch, Early Judaism and Its Literature 4 (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1993), commentary ad loc. 1 Enoch 85:3-10; see also George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001), commentary ad loc. the same verses. The vision opens with a white bull (Adam) and a heifer (Eve); the two bulls born to them are one black (Cain) and one red (Abel), and the black bull gores the red one to death, retelling Genesis 4 in code. A further white bull, Seth, continues the line afterward. Both commentators read the color scheme as load-bearing rather than decorative: white consistently marks the righteous line running from Adam through Seth and eventually to Israel, while darker colors mark the line that diverges from it, a distinction the text sustains for the rest of the vision.

109 — Why the imagery changes species partway through

Patrick A. Tiller, A Commentary on the Animal Apocalypse of I Enoch, Early Judaism and Its Literature 4 (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1993), commentary ad loc. 1 Enoch 89:10-12; George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001), commentary ad loc. the same verses. From Adam through Isaac, the righteous line is consistently pictured as cattle. At Jacob, the imagery shifts: Jacob and his twelve sons become sheep, and Israel remains sheep for the rest of the vision, all the way through the exile and into the seventy-shepherds material covered later in this chapter. Both commentators treat the switch as a deliberate demotion in the text's own zoological hierarchy, from the more powerful, semi-wild bull to the defenseless, herded sheep, matching Israel's emerging status as a people perpetually vulnerable to larger predators.

110 — Wolves, dogs, wild boars, and the sheep's own rams

Patrick A. Tiller, A Commentary on the Animal Apocalypse of I Enoch, Early Judaism and Its Literature 4 (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1993), commentary ad loc. 1 Enoch 89:10-90:1, surveying the vision's working bestiary. Once Israel becomes sheep, surrounding and rival peoples are given their own fixed animal identities: Egyptians as wolves, Philistines as dogs, Edomites as wild boars, and later Hellenistic-era powers as birds of prey (eagles, kites, and ravens, discussed further below). Within Israel's own flock, kings are marked out as rams rather than ordinary sheep; Tiller identifies Saul, David, and Solomon by name among the named rams, with Solomon singled out as the ram who builds "the house" for the sheep, the vision's code for the Jerusalem Temple.

111 — The same fallen-angels story, told a second time in code

George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001), commentary ad loc. 1 Enoch 86:1-4; see also Patrick A. Tiller, A Commentary on the Animal Apocalypse of I Enoch, Early Judaism and Its Literature 4 (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1993), commentary ad loc. the same verses. Nickelsburg treats 86:1-4 — a single star falling from heaven to "eat and pasture" among the cattle, followed by many more stars descending, becoming bulls, and mating with the cows — as an explicit second retelling, in animal allegory, of the Watchers narrative already told discursively earlier in 1 Enoch (chapters 6-11, covered earlier in this book): the falling stars are the same rebel angels there called the Watchers, and their mating with cattle is the same forbidden union with human women. Both commentators agree the identification is not merely thematic resemblance but a close, point-by-point correspondence the text itself clearly intends.

112 — What kind of monster the union produces, and why elephants, camels, and donkeys specifically

Patrick A. Tiller, A Commentary on the Animal Apocalypse of I Enoch, Early Judaism and Its Literature 4 (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1993), commentary ad loc. 1 Enoch 86:4-87:1. The offspring of the star-bulls' union with the cows are not more cattle but elephants, camels, and donkeys — three different large, non-domestic-to-Israel animal types grafted onto an otherwise ordinary bovine herd. Tiller reads this deliberate category violation, rather than any specific numeric height, as the allegory's way of signaling monstrousness: where the book's earlier, non-allegorical telling of the same events gave the giants a spectacular physical measurement (three hundred cubits, covered earlier in this book), the Animal Apocalypse gets the same effect by making the giants a visibly wrong kind of animal for the herd they are born into, immediately marking them as violations of the created order rather than merely large specimens of it.

113 — Binding the stars, arming the giants against themselves

Text of 1 Enoch 87:1-88:3, discussed in George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001), commentary ad loc. the same verses, and Patrick A. Tiller, A Commentary on the Animal Apocalypse of I Enoch, Early Judaism and Its Literature 4 (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1993), commentary ad loc. the same verses. A snow-white being descends and briefly shelters Enoch; then four beings, matching the four archangels of the book's earlier, non-allegorical telling of this same story (covered earlier in this book), each seize one of the fallen stars, bind it hand and foot, and cast it into an abyss in the earth (88:1, 88:3). Separately, one of the four draws a sword and gives it to the elephants, camels, and donkeys themselves, "and they began to smite each other, and the whole earth quaked because of them" (88:2) — an allegorical restaging of the giants' self-destroying violence against one another already narrated in the book's earlier telling. Both commentators read this as confirmation that the Animal Apocalypse is not merely alluding to the earlier Watchers narrative but deliberately reproducing its full plot sequence — descent, illicit union, monstrous birth, angelic response, binding, self-destruction — move for move, in a different code.

114 — Seventy overseers, sorted into four blocks

Patrick A. Tiller, A Commentary on the Animal Apocalypse of I Enoch, Early Judaism and Its Literature 4 (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1993), commentary ad loc. 1 Enoch 89:59-90:19, the chronology chapter of his commentary. After the sheep are handed over to lions and other predators as punishment (the Babylonian conquest and exile), the Lord of the sheep summons seventy shepherds and gives each a fixed, limited period to pasture — meaning rule over and expose to danger — the flock, warning them in advance that they will be held to account for any sheep destroyed beyond an appointed number; a separate recording figure is secretly instructed to keep a written tally of each shepherd's excesses for later use at judgment. The text itself groups the seventy shepherds into four blocks, and Tiller's widely followed periodization divides them 12, 23, 23, and 12, corresponding approximately to the Babylonian, Persian, Ptolemaic (Macedonian-Ptolemaic), and Seleucid periods of foreign rule over Judea. He and other commentators caution that no single, fully agreed correspondence exists between individual shepherds and identifiable historical rulers or years; only the broad four-period, four-empire alignment commands wide assent.

115 — Lambs that can suddenly see, and who they stand for

Patrick A. Tiller, A Commentary on the Animal Apocalypse of I Enoch, Early Judaism and Its Literature 4 (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1993), commentary ad loc. 1 Enoch 90:6; George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001), commentary ad loc. the same verse. Small lambs are born among the still-blind sheep and "begin to open their eyes and to see, and to cry to the sheep" (90:6), though most of the flock does not heed them and they are attacked by ravens. Both commentators identify these newly sighted lambs with the Hasidim, the pious Jewish resistance movement attested independently in 1 and 2 Maccabees as active before and alongside the Maccabean revolt — the text's way of marking the appearance of an internal reform party within Judea shortly before the revolt proper begins.

116 — The lamb whose horn cannot be broken

Patrick A. Tiller, A Commentary on the Animal Apocalypse of I Enoch, Early Judaism and Its Literature 4 (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1993), commentary ad loc. 1 Enoch 90:9-16. A great horn grows on one of the lambs, and the birds of prey harassing the flock try and fail to break it (90:9-12); this lamb goes on, in the following verses, to lead the sheep in active, organized resistance against their oppressors. Tiller identifies this figure with Judas Maccabeus, the revolt's military leader from 167 BCE until his death in battle in 160 BCE, a reading widely, though not quite universally, followed in the subsequent literature. The identification is the single detail that lets the vision's otherwise generic periodization be anchored to a specific, datable figure and campaign.

117 — Matching specific verses to specific, datable battles

Patrick A. Tiller, A Commentary on the Animal Apocalypse of I Enoch, Early Judaism and Its Literature 4 (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1993), in his discussion of the work's date of composition. Tiller matches 1 Enoch 90:13b-14 to the Battle of Beth-Zur (early 164 BCE) and 90:15 to the Battle of Carnaim (summer 163 BCE), both independently attested in 1 Maccabees. On this basis he concludes the bulk of the Animal Apocalypse was composed between roughly 165 and 160 BCE, nearer the earlier end of that range, with the possibility that verses 90:13-15 specifically were added slightly later than the surrounding material — after the 163 BCE battle they describe, but still before Judas Maccabeus's death in 160 BCE. This is among the more precisely arguable composition dates for any Second Temple Jewish text outside the Hebrew Bible, because the vision's own narrated events can be checked against an independently attested political and military timeline.

118 — A more recent full commentary, not identical to Tiller's at every point

Daniel C. Olson, A New Reading of the Animal Apocalypse of 1 Enoch: "All Nations Shall Be Blessed," With a New Translation and Commentary, Studia in Veteris Testamenti Pseudepigrapha 24 (Leiden: Brill, 2013). Olson produces an independent full translation and verse-by-verse commentary two decades after Tiller's, and while he concurs with the general placement of the vision's composition in the Maccabean period, he proposes some different correspondences for individual details within the seventy-shepherds and Maccabean-crisis material and argues for more caution than Tiller allows in a few places where the text's own historical allusions are genuinely ambiguous. His work is a useful check against treating Tiller's reading, however standard, as the only one available.

119 — A courtroom scene, then a bigger house

George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001), commentary ad loc. 1 Enoch 90:20-29; Patrick A. Tiller, A Commentary on the Animal Apocalypse of I Enoch, Early Judaism and Its Literature 4 (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1993), commentary ad loc. the same verses. A throne is set up and books are opened (90:20); the fallen stars, the unfaithful shepherds, and the blinded sheep are judged in turn from those records and cast into a fiery abyss (90:21-27). A "new house," greater and loftier than the first, is then built (90:28-29), which both commentators read as the vision's symbol for an eschatological Jerusalem or Temple, replacing the "house" earlier built by the ram Solomon, into which the surviving sheep and other now-included peoples are gathered.

120 — A bull is born, and scholars do not agree on who he is

George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001), commentary ad loc. 1 Enoch 90:37-38; David C. Mitchell, "Firstborn Shor and Rem: A Sacrificial Josephite Messiah in 1 Enoch 90:37-38 and Deuteronomy 33:17," Journal for the Study of the Pseudepigrapha 15, no. 3 (2006): 211-28. At 90:37, a white bull with great horns is born, feared and petitioned by all the other beasts and birds; at 90:38, all the other animals present are said to be transformed into white bulls in turn, with one among them singled out by a difficult and disputed word in the Ethiopic text for special mention and the particular rejoicing of the Lord of the sheep. Three distinct readings circulate in the scholarship without any one having driven out the others: a restoration-of-Adam (or Seth) reading, in which the vision's entire proliferation of colors since 85:3 is finally undone and all creatures return to the single white-bull condition the vision began in; a Davidic-messianic reading, connecting the figure by proposed textual emendation to an earlier passing reference to a man identified with David at 89:46; and Mitchell's more recent, closely argued proposal that the disputed final word should be read against Deuteronomy 33:17's blessing of Joseph as a firstborn bull with the horns of a wild ox, yielding a distinct "Josephite messiah" reading. This book takes no position on which, if any, is correct.

121 — Coding real history as animals was not this book's invention

John J. Collins, The Apocalyptic Imagination: An Introduction to Jewish Apocalyptic Literature, 2nd ed. (Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1998), in his treatment of the Animal Apocalypse alongside the book of Daniel. Collins situates the Animal Apocalypse and Daniel together as the two major historical apocalypses to survive from the Maccabean crisis, both narrating recent, identifiable political history through sustained symbolic imagery rather than naming rulers or peoples outright: Daniel does this across two beast-visions, the four beasts of chapter 7 and the ram and goat of chapter 8, both texts converging independently on the same events (the Seleucid persecution under Antiochus IV and the response to it) encoded in animal images rather than direct political commentary. The technique itself, narrating history as beast-symbol rather than as chronicle, is a recognized convention of the apocalyptic genre in this period, not a device unique to 1 Enoch.

122 — A periodization whose middle third arrives in the wrong place

George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch: A New Translation (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2004), Introduction, section "The Epistle of Enoch with an Introduction (Chaps. 91-105)," and the volume's own sigla page, which states that "chapter and verse numbers in boldface type indicate text that has been transposed from its place in the manuscripts." The translators print 91:11-17 immediately after 93:10, relocating it from the position it actually occupies in every surviving Ethiopic manuscript: earlier in chapter 91, inside Enoch's opening testamentary speech to his sons, well before chapter 93 even introduces the numbered-weeks scheme. No Ethiopic witness preserves the two halves of the Apocalypse of Weeks in their logical numerical sequence; the correction found in modern translations is an editorial judgment built on independent evidence, not a straightforward transcription of any single manuscript.

123 — The one Aramaic copy that settles the question

J. T. Milik, The Books of Enoch: Aramaic Fragments of Qumran Cave 4 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1976), pp. 247-259. Milik's edition of the Qumran Aramaic manuscript catalogued as 4Q212 (4QEnoch-g) shows it preserving a continuous run of text corresponding to 1 Enoch 91:18-19, 92:1-2, 92:5-93:4, 93:9-10, 91:11-17, and 93:11-94:2 — with 93:9-10 (the close of "week seven") running directly into 91:11-17 (the opening of "week eight") with no intervening material. This is the concrete Aramaic evidence behind the now near-consensus view that the Ethiopic tradition's placement of 91:11-17 earlier in chapter 91 is a secondary disruption of an original sequence the Qumran copy still preserves intact.

124 — The internal case for the correction, independent of Qumran

George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001), ad loc. 93:1-10 and 91:11-17. Nickelsburg lays out the argument that source critics had available before any Qumran evidence surfaced: chapter 93 numbers weeks one through seven and stops mid-count, while 91:12-17, as transmitted in the Ethiopic manuscripts, numbers weeks eight through ten and appears many chapters earlier, disconnected from the sequence it plainly continues. Read in the transmitted order, the ten-week countdown runs backward. Milik's Aramaic evidence confirmed, rather than originated, a rearrangement that internal logic had already made probable.

125 — Ten weeks, and the seventh is the author's own generation

George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch: A New Translation (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2004), translation ad loc. 93:3-10; identifications of the individual weeks with Noah (week two), Abraham (week three), the Sinai covenant (week four), the Solomonic temple (week five), and the Babylonian exile (week six) follow George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001), ad loc. Enoch narrates his own place in the scheme in the first person — "I was born the seventh in the first week, and until my time righteousness endured" (93:3) — before the countdown reaches "the seventh week," described as a "perverse generation" out of which "the chosen will be chosen, as witnesses of righteousness" and given "sevenfold wisdom and knowledge" (93:9-10): almost certainly the author's own community, addressed as living at history's hinge.

126 — Weeks eight through ten: sword, temple, new heaven

George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch: A New Translation (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2004), translation ad loc. 91:12-17. The three future weeks proceed from armed judgment ("a sword will be given to all the righteous, to execute righteous judgment on all the wicked," 91:12) through the construction of "the temple of the kingdom of the Great One... for all the generations of eternity" (91:13) and the revelation of "righteous law... to all the sons of the whole earth" (91:14) to a final, cosmos-wide renewal in which "the first heaven will pass away... and a new heaven will appear" (91:16) — the same new-creation ending narrated in allegorical form by the Animal Apocalypse's new house and white bull (1 Enoch 90:28-38), told here as a numbered sequence instead.

127 — Woes, exhortations, and judgment-scenes: a recognizable prophetic kit

George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch: A New Translation (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2004), Introduction, section "The Epistle of Enoch with an Introduction (Chaps. 91-105)." The translators' own summary states that the central portion of the epistle "is composed almost entirely of three literary forms well known from the biblical tradition, especially from the prophets" — woe oracles, exhortations to the righteous, and descriptions of the coming judgment, all three "carr[ying] the theme of the coming judgment." The superscription itself frames the whole address as revelation given "to all my sons who will dwell on the earth, and... to the last generations who will observe truth and peace" (92:1), meaning the actual audience is the author's own contemporaries rather than Enoch's literal children.

128 — A form borrowed from Isaiah and Amos

George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001), discussion of the woe-oracle form underlying 1 Enoch 94:6-104:8. The "Woe to you who..." construction, followed by an indictment and a sentence, is not original to the Epistle; it is the same prophetic form that opens six successive denunciations in Isaiah 5:8-23 (each beginning "Woe to those who...") and structures the series of oracles commentators call Amos's "Book of Woes" (Amos 5:18-20; 6:1-3; 6:4-14), directed there as here against the complacent and the wealthy. The Epistle deploys the inherited form with the same directness, aiming it repeatedly at named categories of the rich and powerful rather than at Israel as a whole.

129 — Built on someone else's labor

George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch: A New Translation (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2004), translation ad loc. 99:13: "Woe to those who build their houses not with their own labors, and make the whole house of the stones and bricks of sin. Woe to you; you will have no peace." The translators note (ad loc.) that the wording of the verse is uncertain in places, but the accusation itself is plain: houses raised on labor the builder did not perform and did not pay for are houses built out of sin, and are cursed on that basis rather than for the wealth they display.

130 — A weeping-and-wailing address the Epistle of James may already have known

William Barclay, The Letters of James and Peter, rev. ed., The Daily Study Bible (Philadelphia: Westminster Press, 1976), commentary ad loc. James 5:1-6. Barclay quotes 1 Enoch 97:8, in the older Charles translation then current, as a documented precedent for James's own denunciation of the rich: "Woe to you who acquire silver and gold in unrighteousness... they shall perish with their possessions, and in shame will their spirits be cast into the furnace of fire." The wording differs from the Nickelsburg-VanderKam rendering of the same material quoted elsewhere in this chapter, and the verse numbering for this stretch of the Epistle is not perfectly stable across translations and manuscript traditions; the substance of the parallel Barclay draws — a woe-form denunciation of the rich for hoarded, unrighteous wealth awaiting imminent judgment — holds regardless of which translation supplies the wording.

131 — Spirit vindicated, not explicitly flesh restored

George W. E. Nickelsburg, Resurrection, Immortality, and Eternal Life in Intertestamental Judaism and Early Christianity, expanded ed., Harvard Theological Studies (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2006). Nickelsburg treats the closing chapters of the Epistle of Enoch (102:4-104:8) as a genuine and distinctive data point in the unsettled Second Temple argument over what happens to the vindicated dead: the passage promises that the souls of the pious "will come to life" and "will not perish" (103:4) and that the righteous "will shine like the luminaries of heaven" (104:2), consistently describing the survival, vindication, and glorification of the spirit rather than describing bodies rising from graves. This leaves the Epistle's own position closer to spirit-survival and astral transformation than to the more explicitly bodily model attested elsewhere in the period.

132 — Shining like the stars: two texts, one image, read differently

John J. Collins, Daniel: A Commentary on the Book of Daniel, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 1993), commentary ad loc. Daniel 12:1-3. Daniel promises that "many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life," and that "those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky... like the stars forever and ever" (Dan 12:2-3), pairing an image of bodily waking with a separate image of astral transformation drawn from the wider ancient association of the exalted dead with the heavenly host. Collins reads the star-imagery specifically as evidence of that astral-immortality background. The Epistle of Enoch's "you will shine like the luminaries of heaven" (1 Enoch 104:2) reuses the second half of Daniel's pairing — the shining — without the first half's explicit language of bodies waking from the dust.

133 — Two short appendices closing a five-part book

George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch: A New Translation, Based on the Hermeneia Commentary (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2004), section headings "The Birth of Noah" (106-107) and "Another Book by Enoch" (108); see also George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001), commentary ad loc. 1 Enoch 106:1-108:15. Nickelsburg and VanderKam's edition structures the whole of 1 Enoch as five major booklets — the Book of the Watchers (1-36), the Book of Parables (37-71), the Astronomical Book (72-82), the Book of Dreams (83-90), and the Epistle of Enoch (91-105) — followed by two short appendices: the birth of Noah (106-107) and a final testamentary word attributed to Enoch (108). This chapter covers both appendices, the last material in the book.

134 — The public-domain translation quoted for this chapter's verses
