R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch or 1 Enoch, translated from Professor Dillmann's Ethiopic Text (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1893; rev. 1912), chs. 106-108. Charles's century-old translation remains in the public domain and is quoted directly in this chapter for its verse-numbered wording of the Noah birth account and the closing testament; its readings are consistent in substance with the modern Nickelsburg/VanderKam translation used elsewhere in this survey.

135 — The birth of Noah, attested in Aramaic at Qumran

J. T. Milik, The Books of Enoch: Aramaic Fragments of Qumran Cave 4 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1976), 208-217; updated in Henryk Drawnel, in consultation with Emile Puech, Qumran Cave 4: The Aramaic Books of Enoch: 4Q201, 4Q202, 4Q204, 4Q205, 4Q206, 4Q207, 4Q212 (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2019). The Aramaic manuscript 4Q204 (4QEnoch(c) ar), which Milik dated on paleographic grounds to roughly the turn of the era and judged a copy of an older exemplar, preserves fragments corresponding to portions of 1 Enoch 106:13-107:2 — meaning the Noah birth appendix covered in this chapter is not a late addition known only from the complete Ethiopic translation but is directly attested, in part, in the same Aramaic Qumran cave that yielded the earliest Enoch material generally.

136 — A lost "Book of Noah" behind more than one surviving text

Michael E. Stone, "The Book(s) Attributed to Noah," Dead Sea Discoveries 13, no. 1 (2006): 4-23. Stone argues that 1 Enoch 106-107, several passages in Jubilees (7:20-39; 10:1-15), and material in the Qumran Aramaic corpus all draw, independently, on an older and now-lost work or cluster of works attributed to Noah himself — a hypothetical source scholars conventionally call the "Book of Noah," no complete copy of which survives under that title. On this reconstruction, the birth account in 1 Enoch 106-107 is not an isolated invention but one surviving witness to source material that circulated more widely across Second Temple Jewish literature.

137 — The same birth story, four columns deep in another scroll

Joseph A. Fitzmyer, The Genesis Apocryphon of Qumran Cave 1 (1Q20): A Commentary, 3rd rev. ed., Biblica et Orientalia 18B (Rome: Editrice Pontificio Istituto Biblico, 2004), commentary on columns II-V. Fitzmyer's standard commentary on the Genesis Apocryphon — a first-person Aramaic retelling of Genesis found in Qumran Cave 1 — shows that its opening columns narrate essentially this chapter's crisis at much greater length: Lamech, alarmed by his newborn son's unearthly appearance, confronts his wife Bitenosh directly, and she answers with an extended sworn oath of fidelity, the most developed speech given to any woman in the entire Dead Sea Scrolls corpus, before Methuselah is sent to Enoch exactly as in 1 Enoch 106.

138 — Bitenosh's oath, quoted

Joseph A. Fitzmyer, The Genesis Apocryphon of Qumran Cave 1 (1Q20): A Commentary, 3rd rev. ed., Biblica et Orientalia 18B (Rome: Editrice Pontificio Istituto Biblico, 2004), text and translation of column II; see also Daniel A. Machiela, The Dead Sea Genesis Apocryphon: A New Text and Translation with Introduction and Special Treatment of Columns 13-17, Studies on the Texts of the Desert of Judah 79 (Leiden: Brill, 2009), translation of cols. I-V. Where 1 Enoch 106 gives Lamech's fear and Enoch's reassurance but no direct speech from the mother, the Genesis Apocryphon supplies exactly that: Bitenosh answers her husband's suspicion with a sworn oath — "I swear to you by the Great Holy One, by the King of the Heaven, that this seed is from you, that this pregnancy is from you, that you planted this fruit, and that it is not from any foreigner, nor from any of the Watchers, nor from any son of heaven" — a scene 1 Enoch's own version of the story never narrates.

139 — Borrowed from each other, or both older than either?

Loren T. Stuckenbruck, "The Lamech Narrative in the Genesis Apocryphon (1QapGen) and 1 Enoch 106-107: A Tradition-Historical Study of Two Ancient Accounts about Noah's Birth," in The Myth of Rebellious Angels: Studies in Second Temple Judaism and New Testament Texts, Wissenschaftliche Untersuchungen zum Neuen Testament 335 (Tuebingen: Mohr Siebeck, 2014), 58-77. Stuckenbruck lays out the genuine, unresolved spectrum of scholarly positions on how the Genesis Apocryphon's Noah-birth columns relate to 1 Enoch 106-107: some read the Apocryphon as directly dependent on and expanding the Enochic account; others read the relationship in the opposite direction; and others, Stuckenbruck among them, judge the overlapping wording and shared structure best explained by both texts drawing independently on a common earlier tradition (compare the "Book of Noah" hypothesis) rather than either copying the other outright. No consensus has settled the question, and the shared material itself does not supply the missing evidence that would.

140 — The Watchers' story, still feared generations later

George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001), commentary ad loc. 1 Enoch 106:4-107:1; compare Genesis 6:1-4 and 1 Enoch 6:1-9:11. Lamech's fear that his own newborn son might be "not sprung from me but from the angels" (106:6) only makes sense against the book's own earlier narrative of angelic Watchers descending, marrying human women, and fathering giants (chs. 6-11). Nickelsburg reads the appendix as a deliberate, in-world extension of that anxiety: 1 Enoch's own narrative logic allows an ordinary human father, generations after the primordial Watcher crisis, to suspect the same violation could have happened again inside his own household. The fear the Watchers narrative established as a live danger for the antediluvian world has not, within the book's own timeline, gone away by the time of Noah's birth.

141 — The appendix's own aftertaste of what chapters 15-16 already promised

1 Enoch 106:19 and 1 Enoch 15:8-16:1 (Nickelsburg/VanderKam translation; compare R. H. Charles's rendering of both passages). Enoch's word to Methuselah does not end with reassurance alone: even after Noah is confirmed as the flood's righteous remnant, Enoch adds that "there shall be still more unrighteousness than that which was first consummated on the earth" (106:19). The appendix never explains this line in its own words, but the book's earlier chapters already have: chapters 15-16 describe the slain giants' spirits becoming "evil spirits" who "afflict, oppress, destroy, attack, do battle, and work destruction on the earth" and will keep doing so "until the day of the consummation of the great judgement" (15:8-16:1). Read against that earlier material, 106:19's throwaway line reads as this closing appendix quietly acknowledging, in its last verses, that the flood does not fully close the account the Watchers narrative opened.

142 — A luminous child in a wider tradition of glorified figures

Crispin H. T. Fletcher-Louis, All the Glory of Adam: Liturgical Anthropology in the Dead Sea Scrolls, Studies on the Texts of the Desert of Judah 42 (Leiden: Brill, 2002), esp. chs. 1-3 (on Noah and cognate glory traditions) and chs. 4-6 (on angelomorphic and divine Moses traditions in Qumran texts including 4Q374 and 4Q377). Fletcher-Louis situates the Noah birth account's description of a newborn whose eyes "lighted up the whole house like the sun" within a broader Second Temple Jewish habit of describing especially favored human figures — Adam, Enoch, Noah, and in some Qumran fragments Moses himself — in luminous, quasi-angelic terms. He does not claim 1 Enoch 106 directly quotes or alludes to Moses's shining face in Exodus 34:29-35; the connection he draws is broader, a shared idiom for marking a human being as touched by the divine, of which both the Sinai account and the Noah birth account are separate instances rather than one text borrowing from the other.

143 — A third, unrelated Aramaic "birth of Noah" text

Daniel A. Machiela, A Handbook of the Aramaic Scrolls from the Qumran Caves: Manuscripts, Language, and Scribal Practices, Studies on the Texts of the Desert of Judah 140 (Leiden: Brill, 2022), manuscript profiles for 4Q534-536. Beyond 1 Enoch 106-107 and the Genesis Apocryphon, the Qumran Aramaic corpus preserves yet a third, textually independent set of fragments conventionally labeled Birth of Noah(a-c) (4Q534-536), which describe a marked, physically distinguished child in terms scholars have connected to Noah though the fragments never name him outright. Their existence, alongside the two fuller accounts this chapter compares directly, indicates that some version of an extraordinary, physically marked birth attached to Noah's name circulated widely enough in Aramaic-speaking Second Temple Judaism to generate at least three separately transmitted tellings.

144 — The book's last word, addressed past its own narrative

George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch: A New Translation, Based on the Hermeneia Commentary (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2004), section heading "Another Book by Enoch" (108); George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001), commentary ad loc. 1 Enoch 108:1-15. 1 Enoch 108 opens by naming itself "another book" Enoch wrote for Methuselah and later readers (108:1), stepping outside the birth-of-Noah narrative entirely to address, directly and in the second person, "those who will come after him, and keep the law in the last days." Nickelsburg and VanderKam's edition treats it as a self-conscious closing appendix rather than a continuation of any preceding narrative thread — the book's final assurance to the righteous and warning to sinners, sealing the whole collection rather than advancing its story.

145 — The standard modern translation and introduction

F. I. Andersen, "2 (Slavonic Apocalypse of) Enoch," in James H. Charlesworth, ed., The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, vol. 1 (Garden City, NY: Doubleday & Company, 1983), 91-221. Andersen's paired introduction and translation, printing the longer and shorter recensions in parallel columns, is the standard modern critical source cited throughout this chapter. His introduction lays out the manuscript situation, the recension question, and the case for an underlying Greek original later translated into Old Church Slavonic.

146 — A book that survives in a language it probably was not written in

F. I. Andersen, introduction to "2 (Slavonic Apocalypse of) Enoch," in James H. Charlesworth, ed., The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, vol. 1 (Garden City, NY: Doubleday & Company, 1983), 91-97. No Hebrew, Aramaic, or Greek manuscript or fragment of 2 Enoch has ever been recovered; the work survives complete only in Old Church Slavonic. Andersen nonetheless argues the underlying composition was almost certainly first written in Greek, pointing to internal evidence that only works in Greek — most strikingly 2 Enoch 30:13's etymology of Adam's name from the initial letters of the four Greek compass-point words (anatole, dysis, arktos, mesembria) — a wordplay with no equivalent in Hebrew, Slavonic, or any other candidate original language.

147 — Twenty-some manuscripts, and two different shapes of the same book

F. I. Andersen, introduction to "2 (Slavonic Apocalypse of) Enoch," in James H. Charlesworth, ed., The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, vol. 1 (Garden City, NY: Doubleday & Company, 1983), 92-97. Just over twenty Old Church Slavonic manuscripts and fragments of 2 Enoch survive, the earliest no older than the fourteenth century, almost always copied as part of larger devotional miscellanies rather than circulating as independent books. They divide into a longer recension (represented chiefly by manuscripts labeled J, R, and P) and a shorter recension (represented chiefly by manuscripts labeled A, U, B, V, and N); both preserve material judged original by different scholars, and neither can simply be discarded in favor of the other.

148 — A French critical edition reverses the original presumption

Andre Vaillant, ed. and trans., Le Livre des secrets d'Henoch: Texte slave et traduction francaise (Paris: Institut d'Etudes Slaves, 1952). The earliest modern editors of 2 Enoch treated the longer recension as closest to the original, reasoning that texts more often get abridged over time than expanded. Vaillant's critical edition reversed that presumption: he identified vocabulary and phrasing in the longer recension's additional material that reads as later medieval Slavic elaboration rather than early Jewish substance, and argued instead that the shorter recension preserves the more ancient text — a position most subsequent specialists, including Andersen, have followed at least in part, though without full unanimity.

149 — A Nubian monastery yields four leaves in Coptic

Joost L. Hagen, "No Longer 'Slavonic' Only: 2 Enoch Attested in Coptic from Nubia," in Andrei A. Orlov, Gabriele Boccaccini, and Jason Zurawski, eds., New Perspectives on 2 Enoch: No Longer Slavonic Only, Studia Judaeoslavica 4 (Leiden: Brill, 2012). Four Coptic parchment leaves excavated decades earlier at Qasr Ibrim, a Christian-period Nubian site in what is now southern Egypt, were identified by Hagen in 2009 as a translation of 2 Enoch chapters 36 through 42, corresponding to the shorter recension. The find confirmed that 2 Enoch circulated well beyond the Slavic world in antiquity and gave scholars, for the first time, a documented witness to the text in a language other than Slavonic — though still not in the Greek most scholars believe stands behind both the Coptic and the Slavonic.

150 — The first English translation, and an argument for a first-century date

W. R. Morfill, trans., and R. H. Charles, ed., The Book of the Secrets of Enoch (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1896), introduction. This first full English translation, made from Slavonic manuscripts by Morfill with introduction and notes by Charles, argued for a composition date in the second half of the first century CE, chiefly on the strength of the text's own assumption that Temple sacrifice is still ongoing — it gives detailed regulations for animal offerings (2 Enoch 59:1-2) and commands visiting the sanctuary three times a day (51:4) without a hint that the Temple has already fallen, which Charles read as evidence the book was written before 70 CE.

151 — An astronomer argues the whole case is backwards

A. S. D. Maunder, "The Date and Place of Writing of the Slavonic Book of Enoch," The Observatory 41 (1918): 309-316. Maunder, a British astronomer, rejected the first-century dating outright, arguing from the text's calendrical and astronomical content, together with its portrait of two rival heavenly princes, Satanail and Michael, that 2 Enoch is a specimen of Bogomil propaganda — the product of a medieval Slavic dualist sect — composed no earlier than the twelfth century and possibly as late as the fifteenth. On her reading, nothing in the book requires, or even strongly suggests, a Jewish first-century origin at all.

152 — The original translator answers back

R. H. Charles, "The Date and Place of Writing of the Slavonic Enoch," Journal of Theological Studies 22 (1921): 161-163. Charles rejected Maunder's Bogomil attribution directly, arguing that a text which credits the entire creation to God and treats the Mosaic law as itself divinely given — as 2 Enoch does throughout — could not have originated among the Bogomils, whose theology divided the created order between a good spiritual creator and an evil material one. The exchange between Maunder and Charles fixed the two poles historians of 2 Enoch have argued between ever since, without either side landing a decisive blow.

153 — Twenty-first-century scholarship revives the early case

Andrei A. Orlov, "The Sacerdotal Traditions of 2 Enoch and the Date of the Text," 103-116, and Crispin H. T. Fletcher-Louis, "2 Enoch and the New Perspective on Apocalyptic," 127-148, both in Andrei A. Orlov, Gabriele Boccaccini, and Jason Zurawski, eds., New Perspectives on 2 Enoch: No Longer Slavonic Only, Studia Judaeoslavica 4 (Leiden: Brill, 2012). Both essays argue, independently, that 2 Enoch's priestly and sacrificial material reflects genuine, detailed familiarity with Second Temple-period practice unlikely to have been invented from scratch by a later Byzantine or Slavic Christian author, reinforcing an early Jewish core beneath whatever later editorial layers the surviving Slavonic manuscripts have added.

154 — A second, independent line of argument reaches the debate from Germany

Christfried Bottrich, Das slavische Henochbuch, Judische Schriften aus hellenistisch-romischer Zeit V/7 (Gutersloh: Gutersloher Verlagshaus, 1995). Bottrich's German critical translation and commentary, produced independently of the French and English lines of scholarship, likewise concludes that the shorter recension is closer to an ancient core while allowing that the manuscripts as they now stand carry substantial later Christian and Slavic reworking — a judgment that has not, on its own, settled the dating question so much as narrowed the range of positions serious scholars still hold.

155 — Ten heavens, and a scribe who comes back down

F. I. Andersen, "2 (Slavonic Apocalypse of) Enoch," in James H. Charlesworth, ed., The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, vol. 1 (Garden City, NY: Doubleday & Company, 1983), commentary ad loc. 2 Enoch 3-22, 39-67. Andersen's translation and notes lay out the book's architecture: chapters 1 through 38 narrate Enoch's ascent through ten successive heavens, ending at the tenth, where God dictates the contents of three hundred and sixty-six books to Enoch through the angel Vrevoil; chapters 39 through 67 narrate Enoch's return to earth for thirty days to instruct his sons in what he has seen, before his final, permanent removal to heaven. The Watchers material this chapter covers, chapter 18, is one stop inside that much longer itinerary.

156 — The Grigori and their prince get a dedicated modern study

Andrei A. Orlov, "The Watchers of Satanail: The Fallen Angels Traditions in 2 (Slavonic) Enoch," in Andrei A. Orlov, Dark Mirrors: Azazel and Satanael in Early Jewish Demonology (Albany: State University of New York Press, 2011). Orlov reads 2 Enoch 18's naming of a single prince, Satanail, over the fallen Grigori as a development beyond 1 Enoch's Book of the Watchers, where the rebel host acts under named group leaders such as Shemihazah and Asael but no single figure yet carries a name recognizable as "Satan." He also connects 2 Enoch 18:3's count of two hundred Grigori and its naming of the place "Ermon" directly back to the tradition of a two-hundred-strong band of Watchers descending on Mount Hermon under a mutual oath — the same episode covered in Chapter 2 of this survey — reading it as evidence that 2 Enoch assumes its audience already knows the fuller 1 Enoch story and only needs to gesture at it.

157 — A hinge text between an ancient patriarch and an angel with many names

Andrei A. Orlov, The Enoch-Metatron Tradition, Texts and Studies in Ancient Judaism 107 (Tubingen: Mohr Siebeck, 2005). Orlov traces the transformation of the human patriarch Enoch into the archangel Metatron across Second Temple and later Jewish literature, arguing that 2 Enoch marks a critical transitional stage: it already gives Enoch exalted titles and roles — heavenly scribe, knower of secrets, one who stands before God's face — that later Hekhalot and Merkabah texts apply directly to Metatron, without yet making that identification explicit. The fuller identification of Enoch with Metatron is the subject of 3 Enoch, covered in the next chapter of this survey.

158 — A transliteration, not a translation

F. I. Andersen, "2 (Slavonic Apocalypse of) Enoch," in James H. Charlesworth, ed., The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, vol. 1 (Garden City, NY: Doubleday & Company, 1983), 130, note 18b. "Grigori" is not a Slavonic word; it is a Slavonic transliteration of the Greek egregoroi, "wakeful ones" or "watchers," the same Greek term underlying 1 Enoch's own designation for the rebel angels. Andersen treats this transliteration, rather than translation, as itself a small piece of evidence that the Slavonic text was rendered from a Greek intermediary that already used this term as a fixed technical name rather than an ordinary descriptive word.

159 — The nineteenth-century translation quoted for this chapter's ascent scene

W. R. Morfill, trans., and R. H. Charles, ed., The Book of the Secrets of Enoch (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1896), ad loc. ch. 18. Direct quotations from 2 Enoch 18 in this chapter follow Morfill's original English rendering, the same public-domain translation whose introduction argued for a first-century date. Andersen's later, modern OTP translation renders the same verses with different word choices but does not differ from Morfill in any of the substantive details — giant stature, withered and silent faces, the prince Satanail, the descent to Ermon — that this chapter relies on.

160 — Three names, one book, none of them the book's own

Philip Alexander, "3 (Hebrew Apocalypse of) Enoch," in James H. Charlesworth, ed., The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, Volume 1: Apocalyptic Literature and Testaments (Garden City, NY: Doubleday & Company, 1983), 223-315, esp. 223. Alexander catalogs the work's several manuscript titles — Sefer Hekhalot ("Book of the Palaces"), "the Hebrew Book of Enoch," and, from its content, "the Revelation of Metatron" — and notes that "3 Enoch" itself is a modern scholarly label, coined by Hugo Odeberg for his 1928 critical edition, chosen only to distinguish this work from 1 (Ethiopic) Enoch and 2 (Slavonic) Enoch. The text does not refer to itself by any of these names.

161 — The standard English critical translation

Philip Alexander, "3 (Hebrew Apocalypse of) Enoch," in James H. Charlesworth, ed., The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, Volume 1: Apocalyptic Literature and Testaments (Garden City, NY: Doubleday & Company, 1983), 223-315. Alexander's introduction and annotated translation remains the standard English-language critical edition used outside specialist Hekhalot circles; it situates the work within the Hekhalot ("heavenly palaces") corpus of Jewish mystical ascent literature rather than among the earlier Enochic apocalypses.

162 — How late is "late"? A range, not a date

Philip Alexander, "3 (Hebrew Apocalypse of) Enoch," in Charlesworth, ed., Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, vol.1 (1983), Introduction, 223-228. Alexander surveys proposals for 3 Enoch's date of composition ranging from as early as the second century to as late as the tenth, but favors, on the basis of the work's place within the broader development of Merkabah mysticism and its vocabulary, a window of roughly the fifth to sixth century CE — centuries after 1 Enoch, and later still than 2 Enoch. No single manuscript or external witness fixes the date more precisely than that range; Alexander presents it as a scholarly judgment, not a certainty.

163 — The standard monograph on the Enoch-to-Metatron transformation

Andrei A. Orlov, The Enoch-Metatron Tradition, Texts and Studies in Ancient Judaism 107 (Tübingen: Mohr Siebeck, 2005). Orlov traces the titles and celestial roles applied to "the seventh antediluvian hero" across Mesopotamian lore, the Second Temple Enochic corpus, and later Hekhalot literature, arguing that the shift from human patriarch to supreme angel is already underway within 2 (Slavonic) Enoch and reaches its fullest expression in 3 Enoch's Metatron material.

164 — The one verse the whole later dossier builds on

Genesis 5:24 (NRSV): "Enoch walked with God; then he was not, for God took him." This spare notice of Enoch's disappearance without a recorded death is the entire scriptural basis on which 1 Enoch, 2 Enoch, and eventually 3 Enoch's Metatron material each build their own, mutually independent elaborations of what happened to Enoch after he was "taken."

165 — A body enlarged to match the world

3 Enoch 9:2-5, per Philip Alexander's translation in Charlesworth, ed., Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, vol.1 (1983), ad loc. Metatron reports that his body was enlarged "to match the world in length and breadth," that wings were caused to grow on him — the manuscripts Alexander collates disagree on the exact count, some giving thirty-six and others seventy-two, arranged symmetrically on each side — each wing "as the whole world," and that a comparably vast array of eyes was fixed on him, "each like the great luminary." Alexander flags the manuscript disagreement over the wing count explicitly in his notes rather than silently resolving it.

166 — Why a cosmic body, specifically

Andrei A. Orlov, The Enoch-Metatron Tradition (Tübingen: Mohr Siebeck, 2005), chapters on Metatron's bodily attributes and celestial offices. Orlov reads the enlargement, wings, and eyes not as isolated flourishes but as a coherent claim to cosmic-scale mediatorial office — a body built to the scale of the created order Metatron is said to oversee — paralleling comparable claims made for other exalted intermediary figures elsewhere in Second Temple and late antique Jewish literature that Orlov catalogs at length.

167 — "The Lesser YHWH" — and the verse it leans on

3 Enoch 12:5, per Philip Alexander's translation in Charlesworth, ed., Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, vol.1 (1983), ad loc. God clothes Metatron in a garment of glory, sets a royal crown on his head, and, in the text's own words, "called me 'The Lesser YHWH' in the presence of all his heavenly household, as it is written, 'my name is in him.'" The quoted clause is Exodus 23:21, where God warns Israel to obey the angel sent ahead of them because "my name is in him." 3 Enoch reads that clause as a warrant for extending God's own name, in diminished form (Hebrew YHWH ha-qatan, "the Lesser/Younger YHWH"), to the transformed Enoch.

168 — Metatron sits, and a sage draws a heretical conclusion

Babylonian Talmud, tractate Hagigah 15a, in The Babylonian Talmud, ed. Isidore Epstein (London: Soncino Press, 1938). The Talmud narrates that the sage Elisha ben Abuyah — remembered afterward under the epithet "Aher," "the Other," following his apostasy — entered the mystical "orchard" (pardes) and saw Metatron seated, granted permission to sit in order to record Israel's merits. Seated posture, the tradition holds, belongs to God alone in heaven: "no sitting, no rivalry, no back, and no weariness." Aher concluded aloud: "Perhaps there are, heaven forfend, two powers in heaven!"

169 — Sixty lashes, to prove a negative

Babylonian Talmud, tractate Hagigah 15a, in The Babylonian Talmud, ed. Isidore Epstein (London: Soncino Press, 1938). The same passage reports that Metatron was given sixty lashes of fire and made to stand rather than sit, precisely because his seated posture had produced Aher's "two powers" conclusion; the Talmud narrates the punishment as a corrective demonstration that Metatron, however exalted, remains subject to divine discipline and is not himself a second divine power.

170 — The heresy category this story belongs to

Alan F. Segal, Two Powers in Heaven: Early Rabbinic Reports about Christianity and Gnosticism, Studies in Judaism in Late Antiquity 25 (Leiden: E. J. Brill, 1977). Segal's monograph is the standard scholarly treatment of "two powers in heaven" as a named rabbinic heresy category — the charge that scripture or tradition implies a second, co-equal divine power alongside God — and situates the Metatron/Aher episode of b. Hagigah 15a within a broader rabbinic anxiety that also touched early Christian and Gnostic claims about exalted intermediary figures.

171 — Never received into any canon, anywhere

Philip Alexander, "3 (Hebrew Apocalypse of) Enoch," in Charlesworth, ed., Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, vol.1 (1983), Introduction. Alexander notes that 3 Enoch, unlike 1 Enoch — which holds unique canonical status within the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo biblical canon, a status no other Enoch text shares — was never accepted as scripture by any Jewish or Christian community. It survives instead through the specialized manuscript transmission of the Hekhalot literature itself, copied and studied within a narrow mystical circle rather than read liturgically or treated as authoritative scripture.

172 — A more skeptical genealogy for the same material

Peter Schäfer, The Origins of Jewish Mysticism (Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press, 2009). Against readings (including Orlov's) that trace a continuous line of development from the Second Temple Enochic apocalypses through to 3 Enoch's Metatron, Schäfer argues more skeptically that the Hekhalot corpus's Enoch/Metatron material is substantially a product of its own late antique setting, assembled by writers working centuries after 1 and 2 Enoch, rather than a transparent continuation of Second Temple Enochic thought; he cautions generally against assuming Jewish mysticism formed one uniform, continuously transmitted phenomenon across the whole span.

173 — Ten fragmentary copies of a text almost lost entirely

Loren T. Stuckenbruck, The Book of Giants from Qumran: Texts, Translation, and Commentary, Texts and Studies in Ancient Judaism 63 (Tübingen: Mohr Siebeck, 1997), Introduction. Stuckenbruck's critical edition catalogues the Aramaic fragments of the Book of Giants recovered from Qumran caves 1, 2, 4, and 6: 1Q23, 1Q24, 2Q26, 4Q203, 4Q206a, 4Q530, 4Q531, 4Q532, 4Q533, and 6Q8. No single fragment preserves more than a small portion of the work, the ten manuscripts overlap only partially with one another, and the surviving text covers only a fraction of what Stuckenbruck estimates was a considerably longer original composition. The work's own title, if it had one distinct from its content, is not preserved; "Book of Giants" is the modern scholarly label for what the fragments attest.

174 — The Enoch book that never made it into 1 Enoch

J. T. Milik, The Books of Enoch: Aramaic Fragments of Qumran Cave 4 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1976), 298-339. Milik was the first to argue, from the Qumran fragments, that the Book of Giants had circulated alongside the Book of the Watchers, the Astronomical Book, the Book of Dream Visions, and the Epistle of Enoch as part of a five-part Enochic collection, occupying the position the Similitudes of Enoch (the "Son of Man" section) would later occupy in the Ethiopic collection that became canonical 1 Enoch. On Milik's account the Book of Giants was displaced from that later collection rather than never having belonged to one; either way, its Aramaic text disappeared from view until the Qumran discoveries.

175 — The chief Watcher's sons, given voices of their own

Stuckenbruck, Book of Giants from Qumran, commentary ad loc. 4Q531 and 4Q530. Ohyah and Hahyah are identified in the fragments as sons of Shemihazah, the Watcher named at the head of the rebel band in the Book of the Watchers' own list of ringleaders. Where their father is a name in a list in that earlier text, Ohyah and Hahyah are given extended dialogue, competing dream-visions, and distinguishable temperaments across several fragments: quarrelsome, sure of their own strength, and then, as the narrative turns, visibly frightened.

176 — A third giant, and a different father

Stuckenbruck, Book of Giants from Qumran, commentary ad loc. 4Q530 col. ii. Mahaway is identified in the fragments as the son of a different Watcher, Baraqel, distinguishing his parentage from Ohyah and Hahyah's. The text assigns him a narrative role neither brother shares: he alone makes the journey to Enoch, functioning as the giants' chosen emissary rather than as one more voice in their internal debate.

177 — "Mounted up in the air like strong winds"

Stuckenbruck, Book of Giants from Qumran, commentary ad loc. 4Q530 col. ii-iii. The fragment renders Mahaway's flight to Enoch in specific, vivid language: he "mounted up in the air like strong winds, and flew with his hands like eagles," passing beyond the inhabited world and over a wilderness the text names Desolation before Enoch sees him coming and calls out to him. The passage is among the longest continuous stretches of narrative Stuckenbruck's edition preserves from the whole composition.

178 — A monster's name, buried in a list of births

Stuckenbruck, Book of Giants from Qumran, commentary ad loc. 4Q203 fragment 3, line 3. The fragment, part of a passage naming giants alongside their Watcher fathers, records one giant's name as Hobabish. Philologists identify this as an Aramaic rendering of Humbaba (also transliterated Huwawa), the monstrous forest guardian killed by Gilgamesh and his companion Enkidu in the Mesopotamian Epic of Gilgamesh. The name's appearance here, in an Aramaic Jewish text of the last centuries BCE, is a specific and checkable data point rather than a speculative parallel.

179 — A hero recast as a doomed giant, on purpose

Matthew J. Goff, "Gilgamesh the Giant: The Qumran Book of Giants' Appropriation of Gilgamesh Motifs," Dead Sea Discoveries 16, no. 2 (2009): 221-253. Goff examines the appearance of the name Gilgamesh among the giants named in the fragments (4Q530 and 4Q531) and argues the borrowing is not incidental color: the Book of Giants recasts the Mesopotamian epic's hero as one of the violent, doomed giants awaiting the flood, which Goff reads as a deliberate literary inversion rather than mere name-recycling. On his argument, the author needed real, specific familiarity with the Gilgamesh tradition to invert it this precisely.

180 — Two dreams, and the same number surviving each

Stuckenbruck, Book of Giants from Qumran, commentary ad loc. 4Q530 col. ii. The surviving fragments describe two closely related dream-visions troubling the giants. In one, gardeners water an orchard that produces abundant new growth, only for the whole planting to be destroyed in what the text describes as a deluge of water and fire. In the other, a great tree is felled and uprooted entirely except for three roots, which survive intact. Both visions resolve on the same detail: near-total destruction, with a remnant of three surviving it. Damage to the fragments leaves the assignment of each specific vision to a specific giant by name less than fully certain.

181 — A tablet goes into the water and comes out nearly blank

Stuckenbruck, Book of Giants from Qumran, commentary ad loc. 2Q26 and 4Q530 fragment 7. A further vision, carried to Enoch alongside the garden and tree material, describes an inscribed tablet submerged in water; when it is drawn out again, everything written on it has been erased except three names. Read together, the tree's three surviving roots, the tablet's three surviving names, and the garden's destruction converge on the same numeral well before Enoch is asked what any of it signifies.

182 — Enoch answers: it is the flood, and you are not in it

Stuckenbruck, Book of Giants from Qumran, commentary ad loc. 4Q206 fragment 4. Enoch's response, preserved only in fragments, reads the destruction common to all three visions as the coming deluge: judgment that will destroy nearly every living thing on earth, sparing only a remnant. The three roots and the three surviving names are identified with Noah and his three sons, the only human survivors of the flood the visions foretell. Enoch does not tell the giants they will be spared; the visions' arithmetic does not include them.

183 — The Manichaean copy was in print before its Jewish source was found

John C. Reeves, Jewish Lore in Manichaean Cosmogony: Studies in the Book of Giants Traditions, Monographs of the Hebrew Union College 14 (Cincinnati: Hebrew Union College Press, 1992), 1-3. Reeves credits J. T. Milik with first recognizing, among the Qumran fragments assigned to him for publication, that this Aramaic work was, in Reeves's word, "unquestionably" the precursor of the Manichaean Book of Giants that W. B. Henning had already published from Central Asian fragments in 1943. The sequence runs backward from how such discoveries usually unfold: the far downstream copy was identified, edited, and translated a full scholarly generation before anyone recognized the upstream Jewish original it depended on.

184 — A prophet formed inside a Jewish-Christian baptizing sect

Reeves, Jewish Lore in Manichaean Cosmogony, 4-8, discussing the Cologne Mani Codex (Universitätsbibliothek Köln, P. Colon. inv. nr. 4780), a miniature Greek parchment codex first described in scholarship in 1970. Drawing substantially on the testimony of Mani's own early followers, the codex records that Mani (216-274 CE) spent his childhood and youth within an Elchasaite community, a Jewish-Christian baptizing sect observing Sabbath law, dietary restriction, and ritual purification, before separating from it as a young man to found his own religion. Reeves treats this documented formation inside a law-observant, apocalyptically oriented Jewish-Christian milieu as the plausible channel through which Enochic literature, including the Book of Giants, first reached Mani.

185 — One of Mani's own seven scriptures

Reeves, Jewish Lore in Manichaean Cosmogony, 8-12, citing the Coptic Kephalaia, a Manichaean catechetical work preserved in Coptic translation, alongside other Manichaean canon lists. Manichaean tradition counted the Book of Giants among Mani's seven canonical writings, together with the Living Gospel, the Treasury of Life, the Pragmateia, the Book of Mysteries, the Epistles, and the Psalms and Prayers, with the Shabuhragan, composed later in Middle Persian for a Sasanian royal audience, sometimes reckoned an eighth alongside them. Mani did not merely echo Jewish Enoch material in passing; he promoted a reworked version of one of its texts to the rank of his own scripture.

186 — The 1943 article that first named the fragments

W. B. Henning, "The Book of the Giants," Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 11, no. 1 (1943): 52-74. Henning's article was the first publication to identify, edit, and translate the Manichaean Central Asian fragments of the Book of Giants, working from Middle Persian, Parthian, and Sogdian pieces recovered decades earlier at Turfan. Writing before the Qumran discoveries existed as a point of comparison, Henning could not yet know he was publishing the far downstream end of a transmission chain that had begun in Aramaic Judea centuries before Mani was born; Milik's identification of that chain's Qumran-era origin came almost thirty years later.

187 — A buried Manichaean library, excavated by German expeditions

Albert von Le Coq, Buried Treasures of Chinese Turkestan: An Account of the Activities and Adventures of the Second and Third German Turfan Expeditions, trans. Anna Barwell (London: George Allen & Unwin, 1928). Von Le Coq's own account documents the four German Turfan expeditions (1902-1914), organized initially under Albert Grünwedel and then largely led by von Le Coq, which excavated the ruined temple libraries of the ancient oasis kingdom of Qocho at Turfan, in what is now China's Xinjiang region, recovering tens of thousands of manuscript fragments in multiple languages and scripts, a substantial share of them Manichaean. The fragments containing the Book of Giants were part of this recovery, catalogued and deposited chiefly in Berlin, where Henning worked on them for his 1943 edition.

188 — Attested in more languages than any other Manichaean scripture

Prods Oktor Skjærvø, "Iranian Epic and the Manichaean Book of Giants: Irano-Manichaica III," Acta Antiqua Academiae Scientiarum Hungaricae 48 (1995): 187-223. Skjærvø's survey situates the Manichaean Book of Giants among the most widely attested of all Mani's scriptures in Central Asian translation: fragments survive in Middle Persian, Parthian, and Sogdian, with an additional leaf in Old Uyghur (Old Turkic) recovered among the Turfan finds. No other text in the Manichaean canon is attested in as many of the languages the religion's eastward missionaries carried it into, a rough index of how central the Book of Giants remained to Manichaean communities as the religion spread along the Silk Road.

189 — The current standard translation of 1 Enoch 7:2 gives no height at all

George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch: A New Translation, based on the Hermeneia commentary (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2004), ad loc. 1 Enoch 7:2. The translation these two scholars produced, drawing on the Ethiopic manuscripts, both surviving Greek witnesses (the Akhmim/Panopolitanus codex and the excerpts quoted by the Byzantine chronographer George Syncellus), and the Aramaic Qumran fragments together, reads: "And they conceived from them and bore to them great giants. And the giants begot Nephilim, and to the Nephilim were born daggerEliouddagger. And they were growing in accordance with their greatness." No number of cubits appears anywhere in this sentence, and the translators' own sigla (explained in their front matter) mark the word "Elioud" itself with daggers, meaning they judge that word to be corrupt. The height figure that most popular accounts attribute to this verse is not present in the base text current scholarship actually prints.

190 — Where the fuller textual apparatus for chapter 7 actually lives

George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001), pp. 182-183. Nickelsburg and VanderKam's 2004 translation volume explicitly refers readers to these pages of Nickelsburg's earlier Hermeneia commentary for "the textual problems in this chapter," rather than reproducing the full apparatus itself. The commentary volume is where Nickelsburg lays out, manuscript by manuscript, why he judges verse 2 too damaged to reconstruct a specific number with confidence.

191 — The reading nearly every casual reader actually encounters online

R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch or 1 Enoch, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1912), ad loc. 1 Enoch 7:2, based on his earlier critical edition of the Ethiopic text, The Ethiopic Version of the Book of Enoch (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1906). Charles's base Ethiopic manuscript reads: "And they became pregnant, and they bare great giants, whose height was three thousand ells." Because Charles's century-old, public-domain translation is the version reproduced on most freely accessible websites (Wikisource, the Christian Classics Ethereal Library, sacred-texts.com), it is the wording most readers actually meet, even though it disagrees by a factor of ten with the "three hundred cubits" figure repeated in most contemporary popular summaries.

192 — The earliest surviving copy of this book at all

J. T. Milik, The Books of Enoch: Aramaic Fragments of Qumran Cave 4 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1976). Milik's edition remains the founding publication of the Aramaic fragments of 1 Enoch recovered from Qumran Cave 4 (sigla 4Q201-4Q212), the oldest surviving textual witnesses to the book, some dating to the late third or early second century B.C.E. — centuries earlier than either the medieval Ethiopic manuscript tradition or the Byzantine excerpts of George Syncellus.

193 — A hole in the parchment exactly where the number would be

Daniel A. Machiela, ed., A Handbook of the Aramaic Scrolls from the Qumran Caves: Manuscripts, Language, and Scribal Practices, Studies on the Texts of the Desert of Judah 140 (Leiden: Brill, 2022), manuscript profile for 4Q202 (4QEnb). The profile confirms that column ii of this manuscript preserves material corresponding to 1 Enoch 6:1-4, 6:7-7:1, and 7:5-8:1 — meaning the surviving Aramaic skips directly from the end of verse 1 to the middle of verse 5. Verses 2 through 4, which contain both the disputed height figure and the giants-to-Nephilim-to-Elioud genealogy, fall in a physical gap in the earliest manuscript evidence. The oldest copy of 1 Enoch cannot settle the question, because the page is torn away at exactly this point.

194 — What a cubit actually was, and was not, in the ancient world

Mark H. Stone, "The Cubit: A History and Measurement Commentary," Journal of Anthropology 2014, Article ID 489757. Stone's survey finds that ancient Near Eastern cubits cluster around two standards, a shorter "common" or anthropological cubit of roughly 42-48 centimeters (the length of a forearm from elbow to fingertip, averaging about 44.5 cm) and a longer "royal" or architectural cubit of about 52.5 centimeters. No single, universally fixed cubit existed across the region and period in which 1 Enoch circulated; any conversion to modern units necessarily gives a range rather than one figure.

195 — Two stories welded into one chapter, first argued in detail in 1977

Paul D. Hanson, "Rebellion in Heaven, Azazel, and Euhemeristic Heroes in 1 Enoch 6-11," Journal of Biblical Literature 96, no. 2 (1977): 195-233. Hanson argued at length that 1 Enoch 6-11 combines two originally separate literary traditions: a "Shemihazah story," in which the watchers' sin is the illicit taking of human wives and the begetting of giants, and an "Asael story" (Asael is also called Azazel), in which the watchers' sin is the revelation of forbidden knowledge — metallurgy, weaponry, cosmetics, and the mantic arts of divination. The two strands are visible in the way chapter 7 briefly anticipates, in a single clause about sorcery and root-cutting, material that chapter 8 develops at much greater length and assigns to named individual angels.

196 — The translators' own description of the seam

George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch: A New Translation (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2004), Introduction, section on "The Book of the Watchers." In their own words: "Interwoven with the myth of the watchers and the women is a second pair of myths, which identify the sin of the watchers as the revelation of forbidden secrets (metallurgy and mining, magic and the mantic arts) that promote violence and promiscuity. Here the rebel chieftain is Asael, a figure who resembles Prometheus, the rebellious divine figure of Greek myth." This is the same compositional layering that Hanson had argued for in 1977; the two most recent editors of the Ethiopic and Aramaic text accept it as the standing scholarly account of how chapters 6-11 took shape.

197 — Twenty names for the angels, none at all for the women

Compare 1 Enoch 6:7 with 7:1 in either R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch or 1 Enoch, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1912), or Nickelsburg and VanderKam, 1 Enoch: A New Translation (2004). 1 Enoch 6 gives a full roster of twenty watchers by name, headed by Shemihazah, before listing them again with functions in chapter 8 and a second time in chapter 69. By contrast, chapter 7's account of the women the watchers marry — "took for themselves wives from among them such as they chose" — names not one of them, in either the Ethiopic or the Aramaic evidence. The asymmetry is verifiable directly from the text itself in every textual tradition surveyed here; no manuscript tradition supplies names for the women.

198 — A different scroll with a similar name

The so-called Book of Giants is a separate Aramaic composition found among the Dead Sea Scrolls (principally 4Q203, 4Q206a, 4Q530, 4Q531, 4Q532, 4Q533, with further fragments from Caves 1, 2, and 6), distinct from 1 Enoch itself, though clearly dependent on the same Genesis 6 tradition and overlapping in its cast of giant offspring. J. T. Milik included provisional material on these fragments in The Books of Enoch: Aramaic Fragments of Qumran Cave 4 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1976); the standard critical edition is now Loren T. Stuckenbruck, The Book of Giants from Qumran: Texts, Translation, and Commentary, Texte und Studien zum Antiken Judentum 63 (Tubingen: Mohr Siebeck, 1997). Popular accounts frequently quote the Book of Giants and 1 Enoch 7 interchangeably, as though they were the same document; they are not, and claims about giants' heights sourced to "Enoch's Book of Giants" should be checked against which of the two compositions is actually being cited.

199 — The giants' hunger, verse by verse

George W. E. Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch: A New Translation (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2004), ad loc. 1 Enoch 7:3-6; and R. H. Charles, trans., "The Book of Enoch," in The Apocrypha and Pseudepigrapha of the Old Testament in English, vol. 2: Pseudepigrapha, ed. R. H. Charles (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1913), 7:3-6. Charles's public-domain rendering of the sequence reads: the giants "consumed all the acquisitions of men," and "when men could no longer sustain them, the giants turned against them and devoured mankind," after which "they began to sin against birds, and beasts, and reptiles, and fish, and to devour one another's flesh, and drink the blood," at which point "the earth laid accusation against the lawless ones." Nickelsburg and VanderKam's later critical translation, produced with access to the Aramaic Qumran fragments unavailable to Charles, renders the same four-stage sequence with no material change to its order or content, which confirms this escalation, human produce, then humans themselves, then the animal kingdom broadly, then one another, as the base text's own deliberate structure rather than a later editorial gloss.

200 — Why the giants' diet matters to Noah's covenant

Matthew Goff, "Monstrous Appetites: Giants, Cannibalism, and Insatiable Eating in Enochic Literature," Journal of Ancient Judaism 1 (2010): 19-42. Goff argues that the specific claim that the giants drink blood functions to make intelligible the post-diluvian food law of Genesis 9:3-4, in which God, immediately after the flood, grants humanity permission to eat animal flesh for the first time but categorically forbids eating flesh with its blood still in it. On Goff's reading, the pre-flood giants' crime is not simply violence but eating wrongly, in a way that anticipates, and retroactively justifies, the specific dietary boundary God draws in Genesis only after this earlier, unlicensed consumption has already crossed it.

201 — A myth that explains why the rules exist

Matthew Goff, "Monstrous Appetites: Giants, Cannibalism, and Insatiable Eating in Enochic Literature," Journal of Ancient Judaism 1 (2010): 19-42. Goff situates the giants' insatiable, boundary-crossing eating within what he classifies as a "monster theory" reading of the Book of the Watchers: the giants' murder, cannibalism ("anthropophagy" in his term), and blood-drinking are presented as the reason the post-diluvian social and dietary order had to be instituted at all. He argues part of the text's ancient popularity lay in this function, giving Second Temple readers a coherent account of how the world came to need rules against murder and rules about food in the first place, with the giants' collapse into eating everything, including each other, standing as the demonstration case for what a world without those rules produces.

202 — One verse, four industries

R. H. Charles, trans., "The Book of Enoch," in The Apocrypha and Pseudepigrapha of the Old Testament in English, vol. 2 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1913), 8:1-2, renders Azazel's teaching: he "taught men to make swords, and knives, and shields, and breastplates, and made known to them the metals of the earth and the art of working them, and bracelets, and ornaments, and the use of antimony, and the beautifying of the eyelids, and all kinds of costly stones, and all colouring tinctures"; the text adds that in consequence "there arose much godlessness, and they committed fornication, and they were led astray, and became corrupt in all their ways." George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001), 193, argues that Azazel's (Asael's) teaching of mining and metallurgy draws on the Greek Prometheus myth, in which Aeschylus's Prometheus Bound credits the rebel Titan with teaching mortals the mining of copper, iron, silver, and gold (lines 500-504); both rebel figures are subsequently bound and exiled to a remote, rocky place, a parallel close enough that Nickelsburg dates the underlying Enochic material to a period, the fourth century BCE or later, when literary contact with Greek tradition had become possible in the eastern Mediterranean.

203 — Whose gaze reads the eye-paint as seduction?

Annette Yoshiko Reed, "Gendering Heavenly Secrets? Women, Angels, and the Problem of Misogyny and 'Magic,'" in Daughters of Hecate: Women and Magic in the Ancient World, ed. Kimberly B. Stratton with Dayna S. Kalleres (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014). Reed examines the gendered language used of sorcery and forbidden knowledge across 1 Enoch, Genesis, and later rabbinic sources; per Maxwell Teitel Paule's review of the volume in Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2015.07.15, Reed's chapter "critiques modern scholarly analyses of these ... texts and the latent perpetuation of gender stereotypes accomplished through assuming an 'active male gaze' therein." On this reading, the common commentary move that treats Azazel's eye-paint and jewelry teaching as self-evidently about inflaming female sexual allure imports an assumption about who adornment is for and what it is for, rather than reading directly off the text, which names cosmetics alongside weapons and mining as one undifferentiated catalogue of Azazel's forbidden technical knowledge and does not itself gender the wearers or specify that the corruption named in 8:2 runs along male-female lines.

204 — An older layer that does not blame women, and a newer one that does

Annette Yoshiko Reed, Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity: The Reception of Enochic Literature (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2005). Reed traces how the Watchers' teaching of forbidden arts was received across centuries of retelling, and argues that the tradition's earliest layers do not single out women for blame, nor identify the forbidden knowledge the Watchers pass on as specifically women's magic; it is only later strata of reception, shaped by a developing Greco-Roman discourse in which magic itself becomes coded as a feminine and morally suspect practice, that recast the story as being especially about women, seduction, and female culpability. Read against Reed's later 2014 essay, the two arguments compound: the cosmetics detail was not gendered in the way later readers, including many modern commentators, have assumed.

205 — Eight teachers, eight subjects

R. H. Charles, trans., "The Book of Enoch," in The Apocrypha and Pseudepigrapha of the Old Testament in English, vol. 2 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1913), 8:3, lists eight further Watchers and their specialties: "Semjaza taught enchantments, and root-cuttings, Armaros the resolving of enchantments, Baraqijal (taught) astrology, Kokabel the constellations, Ezeqeel the knowledge of the clouds, Araqiel the signs of the earth, Shamsiel the signs of the sun, and Sariel the course of the moon." George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2001), commentary ad loc. 8:3, documents that the surviving witnesses to this verse, the continuous Ethiopic text, the Greek excerpts preserved by the ninth-century chronicler George Syncellus, and the fragmentary Aramaic manuscripts from Qumran, do not agree in every particular of spelling and, in some cases, sequence, though the substance of an eight-part division of astral, meteorological, and divinatory knowledge is stable across the witnesses.

206 — A parallel argued at length: Watchers as inverted apkallu

Amar Annus, "On the Origin of Watchers: A Comparative Study of the Antediluvian Wisdom in Mesopotamian and Jewish Traditions," Journal for the Study of the Pseudepigrapha 19, no. 4 (2010): 277-320. Annus argues that the Enochic Watchers and their forbidden-arts catalogue derive from, and function as a deliberate inversion of, the Mesopotamian tradition of the apkallu, seven antediluvian culture-bringing sages credited in cuneiform and later Greek-language Mesopotamian sources with teaching humanity civilization's foundational arts before a great flood. He notes that Akkadian sources call the apkallu massaru, "watchers" or "guardians," a term he reads as directly continuous with the later Aramaic and Hebrew designation of Enoch's fallen angels as Watchers, and argues that some strata of Mesopotamian tradition already regarded the apkallu ambivalently, with ties to demonic and unauthorized knowledge, giving Jewish authors existing material to build a polemical reversal upon rather than inventing the association of these sage-figures with danger from nothing.

207 — The earlier, book-length case for the same connection

Helge S. Kvanvig, Roots of Apocalyptic: The Mesopotamian Background of the Enoch Figure and of the Son of Man, Wissenschaftliche Monographien zum Alten und Neuen Testament 61 (Neukirchen-Vluyn: Neukirchener Verlag, 1988). Kvanvig's earlier and more extensive study first argued in detail that the figure of Enoch and the Watchers narrative surrounding him draw on Mesopotamian traditions about the antediluvian sages, identifying specific points of correspondence between the apkallu and the Watchers despite real differences between the two traditions, since the apkallu are culture heroes in their own mythological right while the Watchers are angels who transgress a specific divine prohibition. Subsequent scholarship responding to both Kvanvig and to Annus's later restatement of a similar thesis has judged some of the specific text-critical arguments for direct literary borrowing as underdetermined by the surviving evidence, even while broadly accepting that a real relationship between the two antediluvian-sage traditions exists; the field's working position supports a genuine structural and conceptual parallel while stopping short of confirming one single, traceable line of textual dependence.

208 — The primary account: a fish-man teaches Babylon to be civilized

Gerald P. Verbrugghe and John M. Wickersham, Berossos and Manetho, Introduced and Translated: Native Traditions in Ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt (Ann Arbor: University of Michigan Press, 1996). Berossus, a Babylonian priest of Bel-Marduk writing in Greek for the Seleucid court around 290-278 BCE, preserved, in fragments quoted centuries later by Alexander Polyhistor and, through him, Eusebius, an account of seven antediluvian sages, part-fish and part-man in form, who emerged one after another from the sea to instruct the kings who reigned before a great flood. The first and most prominent of these, Oannes, is credited with teaching humanity writing, the sciences, city-founding, temple-building, law, and agriculture, the whole apparatus of civilized life, presented in Berossus's account as a benefaction to be honored rather than a transgression to be punished.

209 — The cuneiform record behind the later Greek retelling

Alan Lenzi, "The Uruk List of Kings and Sages and Late Mesopotamian Scholarship," Journal of Ancient Near Eastern Religions 8, no. 2 (2008): 137-169. Lenzi analyzes a Seleucid-era cuneiform tablet excavated at Uruk in the 1959-60 season and first published by Jan van Dijk in 1962, which pairs each of seven antediluvian kings with a corresponding apkallu-sage and then lists further post-diluvian kings paired with human ummanu-scholars, presenting Mesopotamian scribal learning as descending, generation by generation, from the antediluvian sages. Lenzi treats the tablet as the clearest surviving cuneiform evidence, independent of Berossus's later Greek retelling, that Mesopotamian scholars traced their own professional lineage back to these seven pre-flood culture-bringers, which is the specific body of source material Annus and Kvanvig argue the Enochic Watchers narrative works against and inverts.

210 — A book with three names and one complete copy

James C. VanderKam, The Book of Jubilees: A Critical Text, Corpus Scriptorum Christianorum Orientalium 510-511, Scriptores Aethiopici 87-88, 2 vols. (Leuven: Peeters, 1989). VanderKam's critical edition establishes that Jubilees survives complete only in Ge'ez (classical Ethiopic), under the title Mashafa Kufale, "Book of Divisions" — the source of its common English nickname, Kufale. No complete Hebrew, Greek, Syriac, or Latin manuscript survived antiquity; VanderKam's edition reconstructs the text from the Ethiopic witnesses supplemented by the fragmentary versional and Hebrew evidence discussed in a companion volume. The Latin and Greek epithet "Little Genesis" (Leptogenesis), attested in patristic citations, reflects the book's project: retelling Genesis and the opening of Exodus in full.

211 — A translation that dates the book to a generation, not a guess

O. S. Wintermute, "Jubilees," in James H. Charlesworth, ed., The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, Volume 2: Expansions of the "Old Testament" and Legends, Wisdom and Philosophical Literature, Prayers, Psalms, and Odes, Fragments of Lost Judeo-Hellenistic Works (Garden City, NY: Doubleday, 1985), 35-142. Wintermute's introduction places Jubilees' composition in Hebrew in the middle of the second century BCE, on internal grounds (its familiarity with the Maccabean crisis) and its attested use at Qumran, making it roughly contemporary with or somewhat later than the Enochic Book of the Watchers.

212 — Fourteen or fifteen copies, mostly from one cave

James C. VanderKam, The Book of Jubilees, Guides to Apocrypha and Pseudepigrapha (Sheffield: Sheffield Academic Press, 2001), 13-16. VanderKam counts fourteen to fifteen fragmentary Hebrew manuscripts of Jubilees recovered from the Qumran caves, the majority — nine or ten copies — from Cave 4 alone, with further fragments from Caves 1, 2, and 11. A community that owned that many copies of one book, alongside its several copies of 1 Enoch, was treating Jubilees as a text worth preserving and consulting repeatedly, not as a curiosity.

213 — The same 364 days, argued for twice

James C. VanderKam, The Book of Jubilees, Guides to Apocrypha and Pseudepigrapha (Sheffield: Sheffield Academic Press, 2001), 97-104. Jubilees repeatedly insists on a 364-day solar calendar, divisible evenly into fifty-two weeks, and treats lunar reckoning as a source of ritual error — the same calendar this book's earlier chapter on the subject traced through the Enochic Astronomical Book. VanderKam reads Jubilees' Qumran popularity and its calendrical insistence as connected: the community that kept fourteen or fifteen copies of Jubilees is the same community whose own calendar texts match its 364-day scheme.

214 — Sent to teach, not sent to fall

Annette Yoshiko Reed, Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity: The Reception of Enochic Literature (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2005), 87-90. Reed reads Jubilees 4:15 as a genuinely distinct starting point from the Book of the Watchers: the angels who become the Watchers descend, in the days of Jared, on a licit commission "to instruct the children of men, and that they should do judgment and uprightness on the earth." Only afterward does the text report their corruption. Where 1 Enoch's Book of the Watchers presents illicit desire as the descent's driving motive from its opening lines, Jubilees supplies an origin story in which the fall is a later development of a mission that began as obedience.

215 — Enoch, folded into Jubilees' own timeline

James L. Kugel, A Walk through Jubilees: Studies in the Book of Jubilees and the World of Its Creation, Supplements to the Journal for the Study of Judaism 156 (Leiden: Brill, 2012), 51-55. Jubilees 4:22 places Enoch's activity — his time among angels, his comprehensive writing, and his testimony against the Watchers who had defiled themselves with human women — inside its own chronological frame, before the corruption narrated in chapter 5 is allowed to run its course. Kugel treats this as Jubilees' method throughout: absorbing Enochic material as already-known background rather than narrating it fresh, then building its own account on top.

216 — From teaching mission to judgment sentence

Michael Segal, The Book of Jubilees: Rewritten Bible, Redaction, Ideology and Theology, Supplements to the Journal for the Study of Judaism 117 (Leiden: Brill, 2007), 176-183. Jubilees 5:1-11 narrates the Watchers taking human wives, fathering giants, and the resulting spread of lawlessness, followed by God's decree of judgment against both the Watchers and their offspring and, ultimately, the flood. Segal notes Jubilees compresses the Enochic sequence of separate angelic crimes (forbidden marriage, forbidden knowledge) into a single unfolding corruption, consistent with the book's broader habit of streamlining Genesis-adjacent material into a tighter causal chain.

217 — Noah names three causes, and the giants finish each other

James L. Kugel, A Walk through Jubilees, Supplements to the Journal for the Study of Judaism 156 (Leiden: Brill, 2012), 88-93. In Jubilees 7:20-25, Noah instructs his sons and grandchildren directly, naming the fornication of the Watchers, the resulting uncleanness, and the bloodshed and injustice that followed as the three causes of the flood. The same passage describes the giants' offspring destroying one another in a descending hierarchy — giants killing the Naphil, the Naphil killing the Elyo, the Elyo killing human beings, and human beings killing each other — a mutual-annihilation detail with no direct equivalent in 1 Enoch's account of the giants' end.

218 — The spirits do not stay in the ground

O. S. Wintermute, "Jubilees," in Charlesworth, ed., The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, Volume 2 (Garden City, NY: Doubleday, 1985), 74-75, commentary and translation ad loc. Jubilees 10:1-6. After the flood, Jubilees reports that unclean demons — offspring of the Watchers — begin leading Noah's descendants astray into blindness, error, and premature death; the passage this book's earlier chapter on the flood's survivors already flagged as one live answer to how anything demonic could postdate the deluge at all. Noah, alarmed at his grandchildren's suffering, prays directly to God to shut the spirits away.

219 — Mastema's petition, and the fraction God grants him

R. H. Charles, trans., The Book of Jubilees or the Little Genesis, Translated from the Editor's Ethiopic Text (London: Adam and Charles Black, 1902), chapter 10, verses 7-9 — the widely reproduced public-domain rendering, still cited alongside modern translations for its precision on this point; compare the modern critical translation in James C. VanderKam, The Book of Jubilees: A Critical Text, CSCO 511, Scriptores Aethiopici 88 (Leuven: Peeters, 1989), and O. S. Wintermute, "Jubilees," in Charlesworth, ed., OTP Volume 2 (1985), 75-76. Charles renders Mastema's intervention: "the chief of the spirits, Mastema, came and said: Lord, Creator, let some of them remain before me, and let them harken to my voice, and do all that I shall say unto them; for if some of them are not left to me, I shall not be able to execute the power of my will on the sons of men; for these are for corruption and leading astray before my judgment, for great is the wickedness of the sons of men." God's answer, in the same rendering: "Let the tenth part of them remain before him, and let nine parts descend into the place of condemnation." Both the modern critical translations and Charles agree on the substance: nine-tenths of the surviving evil spirits are bound; one-tenth is left free, explicitly placed under Mastema's own command, for the stated purpose of continuing to corrupt and test humanity until the final judgment.

220 — A name built from a Hebrew root for hostility

James C. VanderKam, The Book of Jubilees, Guides to Apocrypha and Pseudepigrapha (Sheffield: Sheffield Academic Press, 2001), 106-110. Mastema's name derives from the Hebrew root s-t-m, "to accuse" or "bear hostility toward," the same root that gives Hebrew its common noun for animosity; VanderKam treats it as functioning almost as a title, "the Hostile One" or "the Accuser," rather than a proper name coined independently of that meaning. Jubilees itself treats Mastema and ha-satan as close enough in function that later interpreters, and some modern commentators, read them as the same figure under two names, though Jubilees never states this identity outright; the text is content to let Mastema act, across the chapters that follow, in the role a reader of Genesis or Job would recognize as the adversary's.

221 — A pharmacy against the one-tenth left behind

O. S. Wintermute, "Jubilees," in Charlesworth, ed., The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, Volume 2 (Garden City, NY: Doubleday, 1985), 76, translation and notes ad loc. Jubilees 10:10-14. Having lost the argument over the nine-tenths, Jubilees has an angel teach Noah the medicinal use of earth's herbs against the diseases the remaining spirits still cause; Noah writes the cures in a book and hands it down to his son Shem. The detail gives the one-tenth Mastema kept a continuing, textually acknowledged reason to exist in the story: without them, Noah's pharmacological inheritance would have no adversary left to counter.

222 — Not a paraphrase — a reworking with its own agenda

Michael Segal, The Book of Jubilees: Rewritten Bible, Redaction, Ideology and Theology, Supplements to the Journal for the Study of Judaism 117 (Leiden: Brill, 2007), 1-9. Segal situates Jubilees within the modern scholarly category "rewritten Bible" — texts that retell scriptural narrative while expanding, reordering, and supplementing it toward the author's own legal and theological ends — and argues, against a one-author consensus, that Jubilees' finished form combines an underlying narrative source with a later editorial layer responsible for the book's legal material and its jubilee-based chronological scaffolding.

223 — Canonical scripture in one church, apocryphal everywhere else

R. W. Cowley, "The Biblical Canon of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church Today," Ostkirchliche Studien 23 (1974): 318-323. Cowley's survey, still the standard Western academic reference on the question, documents Jubilees' inclusion within the broader Old Testament canon recognized by the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, alongside 1 Enoch — the same dual canonical status this book's earlier chapter on Enoch's transmission history already laid out. No other living church tradition treats Jubilees as scripture; its complete survival is owed entirely to a community that kept reading it as such.

224 — A lexicon that calls its own best guess "precarious"

Francis Brown, S. R. Driver, and Charles A. Briggs, A Hebrew and English Lexicon of the Old Testament (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1907), s.v. נפיל. BDB glosses nephilim simply as "giants" at Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33, and explicitly states that proposed derivations of the word — chiefly from the root נפל (naphal, "to fall") — are "all very precarious," declining to commit to an etymology despite the word's obvious visual resemblance to naphal-derived forms.

225 — A modern lexicon that also declines to derive the word

Ludwig Koehler and Walter Baumgartner, The Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon of the Old Testament (HALOT), rev. ed., trans. and ed. M. E. J. Richardson (Leiden: Brill, 1994-2000), s.v. נְפִילִים. HALOT glosses nephilim as "giant, monster, deformed birth" without asserting a derivation from naphal ("to fall"), reflecting the same caution BDB shows nearly a century earlier: the standard modern reference lexicon for biblical Hebrew treats the word's origin as unresolved rather than repeating the popular "fallen ones" etymology as settled fact.

226 — The Nephilim read against their Near Eastern neighbors

Ronald S. Hendel, "The Nephilim Were on the Earth: Genesis 6:1-4 and Its Ancient Near Eastern Context," in The Fall of the Angels, eds. Christoph Auffarth and Loren T. Stuckenbruck (Leiden: Brill, 2004), 11-34. Hendel situates Genesis 6:1-4 among a wider set of ancient Near Eastern traditions about a primeval mixed age of divine-human offspring preceding a catastrophic divine judgment, treating the passage's terse, allusive style — and the unresolved question of what nephilim etymologically means — as itself evidence that the text assumes background knowledge from its earliest audience that no longer survives for modern readers to check.

227 — One verse, two words, and a commentary that will not force a choice

Claus Westermann, Genesis 1-11: A Continental Commentary, trans. John J. Scullion (Minneapolis: Augsburg Publishing House, 1984), commentary and excursus ad loc. Genesis 6:1-4. Westermann's extended treatment of the passage lays out the live grammatical question of whether gibborim in 6:4 restates the identity of the Nephilim just named or designates their offspring as a related but distinct group, without resolving it decisively; his commentary is representative of a broader modern critical tradition that treats the verse's syntax as genuinely ambiguous on this point rather than settled in either direction.

228 — One Greek word for two different Hebrew ones

John William Wevers, Notes on the Greek Text of Genesis, Septuagint and Cognate Studies 35 (Atlanta: Scholars Press for the Society of Biblical Literature, 1993), ad loc. Genesis 6:4. Wevers's verse-by-verse notes on the Greek translation of Genesis record that the Septuagint renders both nephilim and gibborim in 6:4 with the same Greek term, gigantes ("giants"), a single-word translation choice that erases the Hebrew's own internal distinction between the two terms rather than preserving it — a flattening repeated at Numbers 13:33, where nephilim is again rendered gigantes.

229 — One dictionary entry, two biblical meanings

Dictionary of Deities and Demons in the Bible (DDD), 2nd rev. ed., eds. Karel van der Toorn, Bob Becking, and Pieter W. van der Horst (Leiden: Brill / Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1999), s.v. "Rephaim." The entry surveys both biblical senses of Rephaim — an aboriginal giant people-group (Genesis 14:5; Deuteronomy 2:11, 2:20; 3:11) and the shades of the dead in the underworld (Isaiah 14:9; Psalm 88:10; Proverbs 2:18, 9:18, 21:16) — and treats the question of whether the two senses share a common origin, most plausibly in a West Semitic cult of legendary heroic ancestors, as a reasoned scholarly inference rather than a textually confirmed fact.

230 — Dead kings who still ride to the feast

Conrad E. L'Heureux, Rank Among the Canaanite Gods: El, Ba'al, and the Repha'im, Harvard Semitic Monographs 21 (Missoula, MT: Scholars Press, 1979). Drawing on the Ugaritic texts recovered at Ras Shamra (roughly fourteenth century BCE), L'Heureux argues that the Ugaritic rapiuma — the direct cognate of Hebrew Rephaim — name a class of divinized royal ancestors and warrior-heroes who feast with the god El despite belonging to the realm of the dead, addressed in the texts as both "divine ones" and "men"; he reads this as the most plausible common root beneath the Bible's own two senses of Rephaim.

231 — A clan named for its neck

Standard Hebrew lexicography (Francis Brown, S. R. Driver, and Charles A. Briggs, A Hebrew and English Lexicon of the Old Testament [Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1907], s.v. עֲנָק; confirmed in the Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon of the Old Testament [HALOT], s.v. עָנָק) connects the singular 'anaq to a Hebrew root associated with the neck, giving the clan name Anakim a most plausible sense along the lines of "long-necked ones" or "people of the neck-chain," consistent with, though independent of, the giant-stature tradition the biblical narrative separately attaches to them.

232 — A single verse asked to carry a whole genealogy

Robin Routledge, "The Nephilim: A Tall Story? Who Were the Nephilim and How Did They Survive the Flood?" Tyndale Bulletin 66, no. 1 (2015): 19-40. Routledge weighs the parenthetical clause in Numbers 13:33 tying the Anakim to the Nephilim against the fact that it is the only place in the Hebrew Bible making that connection explicitly, and that Moses's own commissioning of the spies and every other biblical reference to the Anakim never repeats it; he treats a later scribal gloss, a genuine older tradition, and the frightened spies' own rhetorical exaggeration as all live possibilities the text does not adjudicate between.

233 — The conquest narrative pauses for an ethnography lesson

Duane L. Christensen, Deuteronomy 1:1-21:9, rev. ed., Word Biblical Commentary vol. 6A (Nashville: Thomas Nelson, 2001), commentary ad loc. Deuteronomy 2:10-12, 2:20-23. Christensen reads these antiquarian notices — which explain that the giant peoples called Rephaim by Israel's narrator were known as Emim to the Moabites and Zamzummim to the Ammonites — as older ethnographic memory retained and folded into the conquest narrative, serving the passage's rhetorical purpose of reassuring Israel that the giant peoples it might fear in Canaan are the same kind of population its neighbors had already successfully displaced.

234 — A ninth-century monk copies out a lost Greek Enoch

Matthew Black, ed., with Albert-Marie Denis, Apocalypsis Henochi Graece, Pseudepigrapha Veteris Testamenti Graece 3 (Leiden: Brill, 1970), the critical edition collecting the surviving Greek witnesses to 1 Enoch, including the excerpts preserved by the Byzantine chronographer George Syncellus in his Chronography (compiled c. 800 CE). The Syncellus excerpt of 1 Enoch 7:2 describes the Watchers' human wives bearing three successive kinds of offspring — giants, who beget the Naphelim (Nephilim), who in turn beget the Elioud — a genealogical chain not preserved in the Ethiopic text that otherwise serves as 1 Enoch's fullest complete witness.

235 — The same chain, a different set of names

R. H. Charles, trans. and ed., "The Book of Jubilees," in The Apocrypha and Pseudepigrapha of the Old Testament in English, vol. 2: Pseudepigrapha (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1913), Jubilees 7:20-25. Charles's classical translation of Jubilees 7:22 renders the same monstrous succession under Ethiopic-preserved names distinct from the Greek Enoch tradition: "they begat sons the Naphidim, and they were all unlike, and they devoured one another: and the Giants slew the Naphil, and the Naphil slew the Eljo, and the Eljo mankind" — Eljo occupying the same structural position in this genealogy that Elioud occupies in the Syncellus Greek excerpt of 1 Enoch.

236 — A scholar's own title calls the term what it is

Matthew Goff, "A New Suggestion Concerning the Enigmatic Elioud of the Book of the Watchers," in Figures Who Shape Scriptures, Scriptures That Shape Figures: Essays in Honour of Benjamin G. Wright III, eds. Geza G. Xeravits and Greg Schmidt Goering (Berlin: De Gruyter, 2018), 91-104.
