Goff's own title names the term "enigmatic," and the chapter treats its precise etymology, its relationship to Jubilees' Eljo, and whether it designates a coherent third category of being at all as genuinely open questions in current scholarship rather than settled findings — the most direct evidence available that Elioud is a real but narrow and unresolved detail of Second Temple textual transmission, not a term absent from ancient sources altogether, and also not a term whose ancient meaning matches its confident modern popular elaboration.

237 — A two-thousand-year argument conducted by expansion

Annette Yoshiko Reed, Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity: The Reception of Enochic Literature (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2005), esp. ch. 1. Reed traces how the Book of the Watchers and its successors function as extended exegesis of the small set of details Genesis 6:1-4 supplies — a sin, a punishment, and almost no explanatory mechanism — arguing that later Enochic, rabbinic, and patristic literature is best read not as freestanding invention but as a continuous, centuries-long argument about what those four compressed verses meant, an argument whose sheer duration and elaboration is itself evidence for how much interpretive pressure the base text's brevity generates.

238 — Three readings, laid out, none chosen

Claus Westermann, Genesis 1-11: A Commentary, trans. John J. Scullion (Minneapolis: Augsburg Publishing House, 1984), commentary ad loc. Genesis 6:1-4. Westermann surveys the three positions scholarship has taken on the identity of the "sons of God" — divine or angelic beings drawing on the same phrase's use elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, the Sethite reading in which the phrase names the righteous line of Seth intermarrying with the line of Cain, and readings that locate the "sons" among human rulers claiming divine status — without endorsing one over the others, treating the ambiguity as a genuine feature of the Hebrew text rather than a problem later readers introduced.

239 — A heavenly court, not a family tree

E. Theodore Mullen Jr., The Divine Council in Canaanite and Early Hebrew Literature, Harvard Semitic Monographs 24 (Chico, CA: Scholars Press, 1980). Mullen traces the recurring West Semitic and Israelite motif of a divine assembly presided over by a chief deity, with subordinate divine beings reporting, deliberating, or acting on the assembly's business — the same setting bene elohim/bene ha-elohim describes explicitly in Job 1:6, 2:1, and 38:7 — and argues that Genesis 6:2's use of the identical phrase draws on this established institutional image rather than coining a new, unrelated sense of "sons."

240 — A Bronze Age king who wanted what the sons of God already have

Ronald S. Hendel, "Of Demigods and the Deluge: Toward an Interpretation of Genesis 6:1-4," Journal of Biblical Literature 106, no. 1 (1987): 13-26. Hendel argues that the Ugaritic Kirta epic — in which the human king Kirta is offered, and then denied, the immortality reserved for the divine assembly — supplies the closest real literary parallel to Genesis 6:1-4's concern with beings crossing the line between divine and mortal status, and that the flood which follows in Genesis functions, as destructions follow comparable transgressions in other ancient Near Eastern and Greek deluge traditions, as the corrective for exactly that kind of boundary violation.

241 — Where to actually read the Kirta epic

Simon B. Parker, ed., Ugaritic Narrative Poetry, Society of Biblical Literature Writings from the Ancient World 9 (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1997), the Kirta epic (KTU 1.14-16) translated by Edward L. Greenstein. This volume supplies the standard accessible English translation of the Kirta text Hendel and other comparativists draw on when reading Genesis 6:1-4 against Ugaritic material.

242 — Sons of God as royal ideology

Meredith G. Kline, "Divine Kingship and Genesis 6:1-4," Westminster Theological Journal 24, no. 2 (1962): 187-204. Kline argues that "sons of God" reflects the wider ancient Near Eastern royal ideology in which a king could be styled a son of his city's patron deity, and reads Genesis 6:1-4 as a polemic against the polygamous excess such divine-sonship claims licensed among human dynasts, rather than a report involving literal angels or a literal righteous bloodline; the reading remains a minority position relative to the divine-beings majority view but is argued on textual and comparative grounds rather than asserted without support.

243 — Two Greek words for one Hebrew phrase

Robert C. Newman, "The Ancient Exegesis of Genesis 6:2, 4," Grace Theological Journal 5, no. 1 (1984): 13-36. Newman surveys the Septuagint's split manuscript tradition at Genesis 6:2, where the majority of witnesses read huioi tou theou ("sons of God") but a minority, including Codex Alexandrinus, reads angeloi tou theou ("angels of God"), and notes that the angeloi understanding is independently attested in the first-century writings of Philo and Josephus, meaning it reflects a genuinely old exegetical tradition rather than a late scribal innovation; Newman further observes that New Testament writers, including Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4, appear to assume the angelic reading of Genesis 6 in their own use of the passage.

244 — The critical edition's own choice

John William Wevers, ed., Septuaginta: Vetus Testamentum Graecum Auctoritate Academiae Scientiarum Gottingensis editum, vol. 1: Genesis (Gottingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1974). Wevers's reconstructed critical text of the Septuagint's Genesis prints huioi tou theou as the base reading at 6:2, judging it earlier and more broadly attested across the surviving manuscript groups than the angeloi tou theou variant, which the edition's apparatus records as a secondary reading rather than the original translation.

245 — A translator's word choice as a theological signal

John William Wevers, Notes on the Greek Text of Genesis, Septuagint and Cognate Studies 35 (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1993), ad loc. Genesis 6:2. Wevers's companion volume of running textual notes discusses the huioi/angeloi fork directly, treating the translator's choice between two near-synonymous renderings of bene ha-elohim as a case where a Greek translation quietly resolves, in one direction or the other, an ambiguity the underlying Hebrew leaves open.

246 — Does verse 4 name one group or two

Robin Routledge, "The Nephilim: A Tall Story? Who Were the Nephilim and How Did They Survive the Flood?," Tyndale Bulletin 66, no. 1 (2015): 19-40. Routledge surveys the Hebrew syntax of Genesis 6:4, concluding that the verse's claim that the Nephilim were on the earth "in those days, and also afterward," followed by the account of the sons of God's union with human women producing the gibborim, does not itself grammatically settle whether the Nephilim and the gibborim are the same beings under two labels or two related but distinct categories; both readings remain defensible from the text alone.

247 — A lifespan limit, or a countdown to the flood

Claus Westermann, Genesis 1-11: A Commentary, trans. John J. Scullion (Minneapolis: Augsburg Publishing House, 1984), commentary ad loc. Genesis 6:3. Westermann sets the two live readings of the "120 years" against each other — a divinely imposed cap on ordinary human lifespan, and a countdown to the flood itself — noting that the lifespan reading sits awkwardly against the ages the text goes on to assign Noah and the patriarchs who follow him, while the countdown reading fits the flood's own subsequent timing more comfortably; he does not treat either as definitively established by the grammar alone.

248 — A commentary compiled centuries after the Mishnah, in Roman Palestine

H. L. Strack and Gunter Stemberger, Introduction to the Talmud and Midrash, trans. Markus Bockmuehl, 2nd ed. (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 1996), section on the classical aggadic midrashim, entry on Genesis Rabbah (Bereshit Rabbah). Strack and Stemberger date Genesis Rabbah's compilation to Roman Palestine, most likely the first half of the fifth century CE, assembled over generations from earlier amoraic exegetical tradition rather than composed at a single sitting by a single author. The work proceeds verse by verse through Genesis, pausing at each verse to record whatever rabbinic comments had accumulated around it, including comments that flatly disagree with one another, preserved side by side rather than adjudicated by the compilers.

249 — A curse aimed at anyone who translates two words as angels

Genesis Rabbah 26:5, in Midrash Rabbah: Genesis, trans. H. Freedman, in Midrash Rabbah, ed. H. Freedman and Maurice Simon, vol. 1 (London: Soncino Press, 1939). Commenting on Genesis 6:2's "the sons of God [bnei ha'elohim] saw that the daughters of man were fair," the midrash records Rabbi Simeon ben Yohai reading bnei ha'elohim as bnei dayanaya, "sons of the judges" — meaning powerful human magistrates, not divine or angelic beings — and pronouncing a curse on anyone who instead translates the phrase to mean literal angels. The curse is not a passing aside; it names, and rejects, the very reading this book's earlier chapter on Genesis's own philology reports as the majority position among modern critical scholars, for entirely different, comparative-Semitic reasons.

250 — The same running commentary keeps the reading it just cursed

Genesis Rabbah 26:5, Soncino trans. (London: Soncino Press, 1939), read alongside Annette Yoshiko Reed, Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity: The Reception of Enochic Literature (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2005), ch. 6, "The Interpenetration of Jewish and Christian Traditions in Late Antiquity: The Exegesis of Genesis and the Marginalization of Enochic Literature." Genesis Rabbah is a compilation, not a single argument, and elsewhere in its own running commentary on these verses the angelic reading of bnei ha'elohim surfaces again, unrebutted, beside catalogues of the pre-Flood generation's specific corruptions. Reed reads Rabbi Simeon ben Yohai's curse not as proof that rabbinic Judaism erased the angelic reading, but as one strong voice within a text that itself declined to delete the very reading it condemned.

251 — Why pull away from angels at all

Annette Yoshiko Reed, Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity: The Reception of Enochic Literature (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2005), ch. 6. Reed situates the rabbinic turn against the angelic reading of Genesis 6 within a wider late-antique contest over the older Enochic Book of the Watchers and its myth of angelic descent. By the second through fourth centuries CE, she argues, that myth had become heavily used in Christian and Gnostic literature to explain the origin of evil and to blur the line between the divine and human realms — exactly the blurring rabbinic authorities, insisting on a stricter separation between God's own heavenly court and any story of angels intermarrying with mortal women, had independent theological reasons to resist. Reed treats the demythologized reading as a dominant tendency within the tradition's normative legal-theological mainstream, not an enforced, uniform position silencing every rabbinic voice or genre.

252 — The strongest of mountains, in a Baraita cited to explain a word

Babylonian Talmud, tractate Yoma 67b, in The Babylonian Talmud, trans. under the editorship of Isidore Epstein (London: Soncino Press, 1935-1948), Seder Mo'ed, Yoma. Discussing the Yom Kippur ritual of Leviticus 16, in which one of two goats chosen by lot is sent "for Azazel" into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:8, 10, 26), Yoma 67b cites a Baraita explaining the name as describing the ritual's destination itself: a compound reading "az" (rugged, or strong) onto a term for a mountain or cliff, so that the goat is driven to the harshest, most precipitous drop-off point available. A closely related explanation recorded in the same passage calls the place simply the hardest of the mountains. Both readings treat Azazel as a place-name describing rough terrain, not as a person.

253 — Two names dropped into the Gemara without an explanation

Babylonian Talmud, tractate Yoma 67b, trans. Isidore Epstein (London: Soncino Press, 1935-1948); Wojciech Kosior, "'The Affair of Uzza and Azael' (b. Yoma 67b): The Creation of Demons and the Myth of the Fallen Angels in the Babylonian Talmud," Henoch: Historical and Textual Studies in Ancient and Medieval Judaism and Christianity 43, no. 2 (2021): 294-322. The same page of Yoma also records a second, minority etymology, attributed to the school of Rabbi Ishmael: that "Azazel" is so called because it atones for the deeds of Uzza and Azael. The Talmud supplies no gloss on who these two figures are or what deeds are meant; the names simply appear, doing interpretive work the text assumes its audience can already supply. Kosior's study treats this as a rare, deliberately understated surfacing of the fallen-angels myth inside an otherwise purely ritual-legal discussion.

254 — A medieval commentator, not the Talmud itself, names the angels

Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki), commentary ad loc. Babylonian Talmud, tractate Yoma 67b, s.v. "Uzza va-Azael," in the standard Vilna Shas printing of the Babylonian Talmud with the Rashi commentary in its customary inner-margin position (any standard printed edition). Rashi, writing in eleventh-century northern France, identifies the Talmud's unglossed "Uzza and Azael" as two angels of destruction who descended to earth and sinned with mortal women in the days before the Flood, explicitly pulling the passage back to the Genesis 6 material, and reads the scapegoat's atonement, on that etymology, as atoning specifically for the sin of illicit union those angels committed. The identification is Rashi's own contribution to the page, not a claim the Talmudic text itself makes in its own wording.

255 — An Aramaic expansion, not a plain translation, of uncertain final date

Michael Maher, trans., Targum Pseudo-Jonathan: Genesis, The Aramaic Bible, vol. 1B (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 1992), introduction. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan is one of the Palestinian Targums, an Aramaic rendering of the Torah expanded throughout with narrative additions well beyond a literal translation. Maher's introduction surveys the long-unsettled question of its final date: the work incorporates demonstrably very old material alongside demonstrably very late material, so most modern scholars place its final redaction somewhere in the early Islamic period, roughly the seventh to eighth centuries CE, while recognizing that individual traditions embedded within it, including its treatment of Genesis 6, may be considerably older than that final redaction. The traditional attribution of the whole work to the Tannaitic sage Jonathan ben Uzziel is rejected by the modern critical consensus Maher represents.

256 — The same demythologizing move Genesis Rabbah makes, in Aramaic

Michael Maher, trans., Targum Pseudo-Jonathan: Genesis, The Aramaic Bible, vol. 1B (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 1992), ad loc. Genesis 6:2. Where the Hebrew reads "the sons of God saw that the daughters of man were fair," Targum Pseudo-Jonathan renders the phrase "the sons of the great ones saw that the daughters of man were beautiful, that they painted their eyes and put on rouge, and walked about with naked flesh" — substituting a term for powerful, high-ranking men for the Hebrew's divine-sounding original, the same interpretive move Genesis Rabbah 26:5 makes in Hebrew. The added detail about eye paint, rouge, and exposed flesh has no equivalent anywhere in the Hebrew text; it is the targum's own narrative expansion, reading moral corruption into the daughters of men's conduct as well as the sons' desire.

257 — The same targum names actual angels two verses later

Michael Maher, trans., Targum Pseudo-Jonathan: Genesis, The Aramaic Bible, vol. 1B (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 1992), ad loc. Genesis 6:4; compare the earlier translation in J. W. Etheridge, The Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan Ben Uzziel on the Pentateuch (London: Longman, Green, Longman, Roberts, and Green, 1862; repr. New York: Ktav Publishing House, 1968). Two verses after replacing "sons of God" with "sons of the great ones," the same targum's rendering of Genesis 6:4 names two fallen angels outright as having fallen from heaven and been on the earth in those days: Shamhazai, and a second angel. The manuscript witnesses do not agree on the second name — Etheridge's nineteenth-century printed edition gives Uzziel, while the text underlying most recent scholarly citation gives Azael — but every witness agrees on naming real, individual fallen angels at 6:4, in direct tension with the same text's own avoidance of angelic language for the same beings two verses earlier.

258 — A story that reads ancient, written down in the eleventh century

Chanoch Albeck, ed., Midrash Bereshit Rabbati (Jerusalem: Mekitze Nirdamim, 1940), editor's introduction; Annette Yoshiko Reed, Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity: The Reception of Enochic Literature (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2005), ch. 7, "The Apocalyptic Roots of Merkabah Mysticism? The Reemergence of Enochic Traditions in Rabbinic Judaism." Bereshit Rabbati, the compilation preserving the fullest version of the Midrash of Shemhazai and Azael, is attributed to the school of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan of Narbonne, active in Provence in the first half of the eleventh century CE. The work was known to later medieval writers only by citation until a single manuscript surfaced in the twentieth century and was published by Chanoch Albeck in 1940. Despite its clear debt to far older material, the Midrash of Shemhazai and Azael as it survives is a medieval composition, roughly a millennium removed from the Second Temple-era Enochic literature it most closely resembles, not a freshly rediscovered ancient text.

259 — A woman who out-thinks a fallen angel and becomes a constellation

Midrash Bereshit Rabbati, ed. Chanoch Albeck (Jerusalem: Mekitze Nirdamim, 1940); summarized in Annette Yoshiko Reed, Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity: The Reception of Enochic Literature (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2005), ch. 7. In the Midrash of Shemhazai and Azael, two angels named Shemhazai and Azael obtain God's permission to descend to earth and prove human wickedness overstated. Shemhazai becomes infatuated with a woman named Istehar and propositions her; she agrees only on condition that he first teach her the Ineffable Name of God, whose correct utterance grants the power of ascent. He teaches it to her; she pronounces it and rises directly to heaven rather than yielding to him, where, the midrash reports, God fixes her among the stars as a constellation in reward for her preserved chastity.

260 — Giant sons who dream the Flood before it comes

Midrash Bereshit Rabbati, ed. Chanoch Albeck (Jerusalem: Mekitze Nirdamim, 1940); discussed in Annette Yoshiko Reed, Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity: The Reception of Enochic Literature (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2005), ch. 7. The midrash gives Shemhazai two giant sons by a human mother, named in the surviving manuscript Hiwwa and Hiyya (also transliterated Heyya and Aheyya in other discussions of the same text). Both sons experience prophetic dreams of a coming catastrophe — one dreams of a great inscribed stone tablet, submerged and then shattered; the other dreams of a garden destroyed down to a single surviving tree — dreams the midrash presents as previsions of the Flood that will drown the giants along with the rest of the corrupted pre-Flood world. Reed notes the structural resemblance between this dream pair and the giants' own dreams preserved separately in the fragmentary Qumran Book of Giants.

261 — One angel repents by hanging upside down; the other does not repent at all

Midrash Bereshit Rabbati, ed. Chanoch Albeck (Jerusalem: Mekitze Nirdamim, 1940); discussed in Annette Yoshiko Reed, Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity: The Reception of Enochic Literature (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2005), ch. 7. The midrash closes its narrative of the two fallen angels with sharply divergent fates. Shemhazai, confronted with what his transgression has caused, repents, and as an act of self-punishment suspends himself between heaven and earth, head downward, unwilling to appear again before God — the text describes him as still hanging there. Azael does not repent, and is instead appointed, within the world's ongoing operation, patron of the cosmetics, dyes, and adornments women use to make themselves attractive, a continuing occasion of the same temptation his original descent was meant to test.

262 — A medieval story that still knows an ancient one, by a route scholarship has not settled

J. T. Milik, ed., with the collaboration of Matthew Black, The Books of Enoch: Aramaic Fragments of Qumran Cave 4 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1976), on the Book of Giants fragments and their proposed later reception; Annette Yoshiko Reed, Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity: The Reception of Enochic Literature (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2005), ch. 7. The medieval Midrash of Shemhazai and Azael shares its lead angel's name (Shemhazai, close in sound to 1 Enoch's Shemihazah), a basic plot of angelic descent and giant offspring, and, in the sons' dreams, a structural echo of dream material in the ancient, fragmentary Aramaic Book of Giants recovered at Qumran. Milik argued for a fairly direct line of transmission, treating the medieval midrash as a late descendant that preserved substantial elements of the ancient Enochic dream material across the gap. Reed is considerably more cautious, judging the parallels real but too general and too heavily mediated by centuries of retelling to support a claim of direct literary dependence, and reads the medieval midrash instead as evidence that some memory of the ancient Enochic mythology persisted and was reactivated in early medieval Jewish exegetical culture, by a route scholarship has not been able to reconstruct in detail, rather than as proof of an unbroken manuscript chain.

263 — A last elaboration, in the foundational text of Kabbalah

Joseph Dan, "Uzza and Aza'el," in Encyclopaedia Judaica, 2nd ed., ed. Fred Skolnik and Michael Berenbaum, vol. 20 (Detroit: Macmillan Reference USA / Keter Publishing House, 2007). The Zohar, the foundational work of Kabbalistic literature that began circulating in Castile in the final decades of the thirteenth century under Moses de Leon, returns to the Uzza-and-Azael legend more than once and layers its own symbolic vocabulary onto it: at one point it has a pre-Flood woman named Naamah seduce "the sons of God, Uzza and Azael" (Zohar 1:19b); elsewhere it describes God casting Uzza and Azael down from their holy place for pursuing mortal women (Zohar 3:208a). Dan reads this as a late stage in a very long chain: an ancient Enochic myth, marginalized by the rabbinic legal-theological mainstream this chapter has traced, resurfacing centuries afterward in medieval Jewish mysticism with new symbolic freight attached — a large subject in its own right that this chapter can only flag, not pursue.

264 — Justin Martyr on the cause of all evils

Justin Martyr, Second Apology, chapter 5 ("On the Cause of All Evils"), in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, trans. Marcus Dods and George Reith, ed. Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885; standard text also at newadvent.org/fathers/0127.htm). Justin writes that God committed "the care of men and of all things under heaven" to angels, but that these angels "transgressed this appointment, and were captivated by love of women, and begot children who are those that are called demons." He goes on to say these fallen angels and their offspring "subdued the human race to themselves" through magical writings, terror, and blood sacrifice, and that the poets and mythologists of Greco-Roman religion, not knowing the true origin of what they describe, unwittingly narrate as the deeds of "gods" what are, on Justin's account, the deeds of the Watchers' own demonic children.

265 — Athenagoras makes the same case to a Roman emperor

Athenagoras, A Plea for the Christians (also titled Legatio pro Christianis, or Embassy for the Christians), chapters 24-25, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2, trans. B. P. Pratten (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885). Writing a formal legal defense of Christianity addressed directly to the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus, Athenagoras describes angels appointed "for the care of the elements, the heavens, and the world" who instead "outraged both the constitution of their nature and the government entrusted to them," falling into "impure love of virgins" and being "subjugated by the flesh" until they fathered giants (ch. 24). Chapter 25 identifies "the souls of the giants" as the wandering demons behind pagan oracles and idol-worship, independently reaching, within a generation of Justin Martyr, essentially the same structural argument.

266 — Tertullian defends the Book of Enoch by name

Tertullian, On the Apparel of Women (De Cultu Feminarum), Book 1, chapters 2-3, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 4, trans. S. Thelwall (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885). Chapter 2 ("The Origin of Female Ornamentation, Traced Back to the Angels Who Had Fallen") attributes the origin of metalworking, jewelry, and cosmetics to the fallen angels who "disclosed" these arts to the women they courted. Chapter 3 ("Concerning the Genuineness of the Prophecy of Enoch") mounts a dedicated defense of the Book of Enoch's authenticity against the objection that it is not part of the Jewish scriptural canon, arguing that Noah, Enoch's own great-grandson and the Flood's sole survivor, had every means to preserve his ancestor's writing, and noting that "Enoch possesses a testimony in the Apostle Jude" — the New Testament itself, on Tertullian's reading, having already settled the question of the book's authority.

267 — Tertullian returns to the argument twice more

Tertullian, On Idolatry (De Idololatria), chapters 4 and 9, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 3, trans. S. Thelwall (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885). Chapter 4 cites Enoch by name a second time, quoting the prophecy that "the demons, and the spirits of the angelic apostates" would corrupt the created order through idolatry, echoing 1 Enoch 99:6. Chapter 9 ("Of Astrology in Particular") attributes astrology specifically to "the deserters from God, the lovers of women" — the fallen angels once again — who "were likewise the discoverers of this curious art," though this chapter does not repeat the Enoch citation by name; the two chapters together show Tertullian returning to the Watchers material as settled background across two different arguments within the same treatise.

268 — The veil, Paul, and the angels of Genesis 6

Tertullian, On the Veiling of Virgins (De Virginibus Velandis), chapter 7 ("Of the Reasons Assigned by the Apostle for Bidding Women to be Veiled"), in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 4, trans. S. Thelwall (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885). Defending the veiling of unmarried women, Tertullian reaches for Genesis 6 to explain Paul's own instruction in 1 Corinthians 11:10 that a woman ought to have "a symbol of authority on her head, because of the angels" — explaining that it is "on account of the angels... whom we read of as having fallen from God and heaven on account of concupiscence after females" that even virgins, not only wives, require veiling. This chapter does not name Enoch outright, unlike On the Apparel of Women and On Idolatry; the argument here is built directly on Genesis and Paul. The 1 Corinthians 11:10 connection this chapter draws is examined at length in this book's later chapter on the New Testament's citations of Enochic material.

269 — Irenaeus and the forbidden arts the Watchers taught

Irenaeus of Lyons, Proof of the Apostolic Preaching (also called Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching), section 18, trans. J. Armitage Robinson (London: Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, 1920); also available in Ancient Christian Writers, vol. 16, trans. Joseph P. Smith (New York: Newman Press, 1952). Summarizing sacred history from creation forward, Irenaeus writes that angels "were united with the daughters of the race of mankind, and they bore to them sons" who, "for their exceeding greatness, were called giants," and that these angels "brought as presents to their wives teachings of wickedness" — "the virtues of roots and herbs, dyeing in colours and cosmetics, the discovery of rare substances, love-potions... and all sorcery and idolatry hateful to God." The passage reads as a condensed paraphrase of the corrupting-knowledge material 1 Enoch's own Book of the Watchers spends several chapters narrating.

270 — Irenaeus and the cause of the Flood

Irenaeus of Lyons, Against Heresies (Adversus Haereses), Book 4, chapter 36, section 4, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, trans. Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885). Arguing for the consistency of divine justice across both testaments, Irenaeus explains that God "justly brought on the deluge for the purpose of extinguishing that most infamous race of men then existent, who could not bring forth fruit to God, since the angels that sinned had commingled with them" — treating the Genesis 6 angelic transgression as settled historical background to the Flood narrative itself, not a contested reading requiring defense.

271 — How mainstream the angelic reading actually was

Annette Yoshiko Reed, Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity: The Reception of Enochic Literature (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2005), chapters treating patristic reception of the Watchers narrative. Reed documents that the angelic reading of Genesis 6:1-4 was, through roughly the second and much of the third century, the assumed position of Christian writers who addressed the passage at all, rather than one competing option among several defended against active resistance — a pattern this chapter traces through Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, Tertullian, and Irenaeus, four of the era's most substantial Christian authors, none of whom present the angelic reading as needing special defense against an internal Christian alternative.

272 — A parallel study of the same reception history

Archie T. Wright, The Origin of Evil Spirits: The Reception of Genesis 6:1-4 in Early Jewish Literature, Wissenschaftliche Untersuchungen zum Neuen Testament 198 (Tubingen: Mohr Siebeck, 2005; repr. Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2015). Wright's study, focused primarily on early Jewish reception but extending into the early Christian material this chapter covers, corroborates Reed's account of the angelic reading's early dominance and, further on in the same volume, discusses the theological pressures — developing doctrines of angelic nature chief among them — that made the reading progressively harder for later Christian writers to sustain without qualification.

273 — Julius Africanus offers two doors out of the angel reading

Julius Africanus, Chronographiae, fragment preserved in Georgius Syncellus, Ecloga Chronographica, ed. Alden A. Mosshammer (Leipzig: Teubner, 1984), p. 19; English text in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 6, "The Extant Fragments of the Five Books of the Chronography of Julius Africanus," trans. Rev. S. D. F. Salmond (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886). Africanus writes: "When men multiplied on the earth, the angels of heaven came together with the daughters of men. In some copies I found 'the sons of God.'" He states his own preference plainly — "the descendants of Seth are called the sons of God on account of the righteous men and patriarchs who have sprung from him... but the descendants of Cain are named the seed of men, as having nothing divine in them" — while also offering readers who wish to retain the word "angels" a fallback reading of the term as human sorcerers and astrologers "who taught the women the motions of the stars." See discussion in Annette Yoshiko Reed, Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2005), and Archie T. Wright, The Origin of Evil Spirits (Tubingen: Mohr Siebeck, 2005), both treating Africanus as an early datapoint in the shift toward the Sethite reading.

274 — Augustine frames the fall as a righteous lineage marrying down

Augustine, City of God (De Civitate Dei), Book 15, chapter 22, trans. Marcus Dods, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1887). Augustine argues that the "sons of God" of Genesis 6 were human beings distinguished from the rest of humanity only by grace — a righteous lineage who possessed "the good that is great and proper to the good" — and that their fall consisted in abandoning that good for "a paltry good," the mere physical beauty of women belonging to the earthly, ungodly city. This chapter sets up, without yet fully deciding, the identification completed in the following chapter: the righteous "sons of God" as the line of Seth, the "daughters of men" as the line of Cain.

275 — Augustine decides a question he had left open before

Augustine, City of God, Book 15, chapter 23, titled in the standard English translation "Whether We are to Believe that Angels, Who are of a Spiritual Substance, Fell in Love with the Beauty of Women, and Sought Them in Marriage, and that from This Connection Giants Were Born," trans. Marcus Dods, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1887; also Christian Classics Ethereal Library, ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf102.iv.XV.23.html). Augustine notes he had touched the question once before without resolving it — "In the third book of this work we made a passing reference to this question, but did not decide whether angels, inasmuch as they are spirits, could have bodily intercourse with women" (referring back to City of God 3.5). He does not rule out angelic embodiment on metaphysical grounds alone, citing the angels who appear to Abraham and Lot in Genesis 18-19 "in such bodies as could not only be seen, but also touched" as scriptural precedent for spirits taking tangible form. The question is instead settled for him on textual grounds: Scripture, he concludes, "unambiguously declares" that the transgressors were men, not heavenly angels — the sons of Seth, "sunk into this community when they forsook righteousness," taking wives from among the daughters of Cain.

276 — Why the reading changed: three converging pressures

Synthesis drawn from Annette Yoshiko Reed, Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2005), and Archie T. Wright, The Origin of Evil Spirits (Tubingen: Mohr Siebeck, 2005; repr. Fortress Press, 2015). Both studies point to several currents converging rather than a single decisive cause: 1 Enoch's own declining standing toward (and then largely away from) canonical status in the mainstream church, discussed in this book's earlier chapter on the text's transmission history; a hardening orthodox doctrine of angelic nature that increasingly insisted on angels as purely incorporeal spirits, making the older reading progressively harder to hold without the kind of qualification Augustine spends a full chapter negotiating; and the proximity of Enochic angelology — named Watchers, ranked spirit-hierarchies — to the elaborate angel- and aeon-systems of the Gnostic teachers the mainstream church spent the second and third centuries refuting, which made the Watchers' vocabulary harder to deploy without inviting an unwelcome comparison. Wright further notes a broader patristic tendency to relocate the theological account of the first sin among angels away from lust and appetite (the framework Justin, Athenagoras, and Tertullian all assumed) and toward will and pride instead, the same reframing visible in how later Christian tradition would come to describe Satan's own fall as self-exaltation rather than desire.

277 — A Catholic study note quietly updates the answer

New American Bible, Revised Edition (Washington, DC: United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, 2011), Genesis 6:2 and accompanying study note, official text at bible.usccb.org/bible/genesis/6. The NABRE, the translation used in the U.S. Catholic lectionary, renders the verse "sons of God" and glosses the phrase in its study note as referring to "other heavenly beings," not to any human lineage — reflecting the modern critical-scholarly consensus, discussed in this book's chapter on the passage's original Hebrew wording, that "sons of God" most plausibly denoted divine or angelic beings in its ancient Near Eastern context, closer to the reading Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, Tertullian, and Irenaeus had all assumed than to Augustine's Sethite alternative.

278 — An evangelical bestseller revives the older reading

Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm: Recovering the Supernatural Worldview of the Bible (Bellingham, WA: Lexham Press, 2015), chapters on Genesis 6:1-4 and the divine council. Heiser, a Hebrew Bible scholar writing for a popular evangelical Protestant audience, argues at length for reading "sons of God" throughout the Hebrew Bible, Genesis 6:1-4 prominent among the passages, as denoting real divine-council beings rather than any human lineage, restoring what he calls the Bible's own "supernatural worldview." The book's substantial popular readership shows the pre-Augustinian, angelic reading re-entering mainstream evangelical conversation from a direction largely independent of academic biblical criticism.

279 — A canon that never had to change its mind

Roger W. Cowley, "The Biblical Canon of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church Today," Ostkirchliche Studien 23 (1974): 318-323, the standard modern academic reference distinguishing the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's "narrower" canon (46 Old Testament books plus 35 New Testament books, 81 in total) from a still broader canon some communities within the church also recognize. 1 Enoch has stood among the Old Testament books of this canon since long before Augustine wrote City of God; a church that never stopped treating 1 Enoch as scripture had, correspondingly, no theological pressure pushing it toward the Sethite alternative other traditions eventually adopted.

280 — What a modern Latter-day Saint president taught instead

Joseph Fielding Smith, Doctrines of Salvation: Sermons and Writings of Joseph Fielding Smith, comp. Bruce R. McConkie, vol. 1 (Salt Lake City: Bookcraft, 1954), discussion of Genesis 6:1-4 and the Nephilim. Smith, president of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints from 1970 until his death in 1972, rejected the angelic-intermarriage reading and taught instead that the "sons of God" were covenant-keeping, priesthood-holding men who married outside the covenant, their offspring called Nephilim ("fallen ones") in the sense of a lineage that had abandoned its covenant standing, not a literal angelic-human hybrid race. This is presented here as Smith's own attributed teaching in a compiled volume of sermons and writings, not as a separately canonized statement of Latter-day Saint scripture; readers wanting the primary text should consult the original three-volume Doctrines of Salvation directly.

281 — A modern restatement of the second-century argument

Insight on the Scriptures, vol. 2 (Brooklyn / New York: Watchtower Bible and Tract Society of New York, 1988), s.v. "Nephilim," pp. 491-493; see also the summary at jw.org/en/bible-teachings/questions/nephilim-giants/. This Jehovah's Witnesses reference work identifies the "sons of the true God" of Genesis 6:2 as angels who "materialized" physical, tangible bodies in order to "cohabit with women," fathering the Nephilim as literal angelic-human hybrids before the Flood — the same basic mechanism Justin Martyr and Athenagoras had described some eighteen centuries earlier, arrived at through this tradition's own distinct reading of scripture rather than through continuity with patristic tradition as such.

282 — This chapter's translation, stated once

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version (Wheaton, IL: Crossway, 2001). All New Testament quotations in this chapter — Jude 1:6, Jude 1:14-15, 2 Peter 2:4, 1 Peter 3:19-20, and 1 Corinthians 11:10 — follow this translation's exact wording; the verse reference given inline (e.g., "Jude 1:6") stands in place of a separate citation at each quotation.

283 — A prophecy in the past tense

Daniel B. Wallace, Greek Grammar Beyond the Basics: An Exegetical Syntax of the New Testament (Grand Rapids: Zondervan, 1996), s.v. the proleptic (or futuristic) aorist. The Greek verb underlying the ESV's "the Lord comes" in Jude 1:14 is elthen, a simple aorist that ordinarily marks a completed past action ("came"), not a present or future one. Grammarians class this use as a proleptic aorist: a future event treated as so certain that it is described in the grammatical form normally reserved for something already accomplished. English translations split on how to render that single Greek form — the ESV chooses a present tense, "comes," to capture the sense of imminent certainty, while some older translations render the identical Greek verb literally as "came." Both are legitimate translation choices describing one underlying Greek wording, not evidence of two different underlying texts.

284 — Not a minority reading: the scholarly consensus on Jude 6

Richard Bauckham, Jude, 2 Peter, Word Biblical Commentary 50 (Waco, TX: Word Books, 1983), commentary ad loc. Jude 6. Bauckham treats the identification of Jude 1:6's disobedient angels with the Watchers of 1 Enoch's Book of the Watchers as effectively unanimous among modern critical commentators, not a contested minority position: the specific vocabulary of angels who abandoned an assigned station ("did not stay within their own position of authority"), left a proper home ("left their proper dwelling"), and are held bound in darkness pending a still-future judgment maps too closely onto 1 Enoch 10's sentencing of Azazel (10:4-6) and of Shemihazah and his companions (10:12-13) to be coincidental. This book treats the connection as established background; the genuinely open question, addressed below, is what Jude and 2 Peter's shared dependence on this material implies about their view of 1 Enoch's own authority.

285 — Which letter borrowed from which

Richard Bauckham, Jude, 2 Peter, Word Biblical Commentary 50 (Waco, TX: Word Books, 1983), Introduction, section on the literary relationship of Jude and 2 Peter, and commentary ad loc. 2 Peter 2:4; Gene L. Green, Jude and 2 Peter, Baker Exegetical Commentary on the New Testament (Grand Rapids: Baker Academic, 2008), Introduction, section on 2 Peter's relationship to Jude. Both commentators find 2 Peter 2:4's angels "cast... into hell" and "committed... to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment" too close to Jude 1:6 in wording, sequence, and surrounding material to be independent compositions, and both judge the majority scholarly position — that 2 Peter used Jude as a written source, rather than the reverse or a shared lost source behind both — the better-supported explanation, while noting it is not unanimous.

286 — What 2 Peter leaves out, and one proposal for why

Gene L. Green, Jude and 2 Peter, Baker Exegetical Commentary on the New Testament (Grand Rapids: Baker Academic, 2008), commentary ad loc. 2 Peter 2:4, discussing the parallel to Jude 1:14-15; Richard Bauckham, Jude, 2 Peter, Word Biblical Commentary 50 (Waco, TX: Word Books, 1983), commentary ad loc. 2 Peter 2:4. Where Jude quotes 1 Enoch 1:9 outright and names Enoch as the speaker (Jude 1:14-15), 2 Peter's parallel passage draws on the same binding-of-the-angels material without any comparable direct quotation or naming of Enoch or his book. Some commentators propose that 2 Peter's author, writing later and to a context with a firmer, developing sense of which books counted as scripture, deliberately avoided repeating Jude's explicit, named citation of a non-canonical text; this is offered in the literature as a plausible explanation for the omission, not a settled one, since 2 Peter also compresses and reworks a great deal of Jude's material for reasons that have nothing to do with canon or Enoch specifically.

287 — Two readings, no consensus

For the fallen-angels reading: William J. Dalton, Christ's Proclamation to the Spirits: A Study of 1 Peter 3:18-4:6, Analecta Biblica 23, 2nd rev. ed. (Rome: Pontifical Biblical Institute, 1989), identifying the "spirits in prison" of 1 Peter 3:19 with the disobedient Watchers of the Enochic tradition, imprisoned since the days of Noah per 1 Enoch 10 and 1 Enoch 21. For the human-souls reading: Wayne A. Grudem, 1 Peter, Tyndale New Testament Commentaries (Grand Rapids: Eerdmans; Leicester: Inter-Varsity Press, 1988), including a lengthy appendix defending the position that the "spirits" are the disobedient human generation that died in Noah's flood, addressed by Christ's Spirit preaching through Noah rather than by Christ himself descending to imprisoned angels after the crucifixion. Both readings remain actively defended in current scholarly literature; this book takes no position on which is correct.

288 — A notoriously difficult verse, several live readings

Tertullian, On the Apparel of Women, Book 1, ch. 3, and On the Veiling of Virgins, ch. 7 (Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 4), reading 1 Corinthians 11:10's "because of the angels" against Genesis 6:1-4's account of angels who "fell from God and heaven on account of concupiscence after females" — the earliest datable connection between this verse and the Watchers tradition. Joseph A. Fitzmyer, "A Feature of Qumran Angelology and the Angels of 1 Cor 11:10," New Testament Studies 4 (1957-58): 48-58, proposes instead that Paul has in view holy angels present at worship, per Qumran texts describing angels attending the sect's assemblies (1QS 2:3-11; 1QM 7:4-6) and being offended by any breach of proper order, not fallen angels drawn by lust. Loren T. Stuckenbruck, "Why Should Women Cover Their Heads Because of the Angels? (1 Corinthians 11:10)," Stone-Campbell Journal 4 (2001): 205-234, engages the Genesis 6/Watchers background directly as one live possibility among the options he surveys, without treating it as settled either way. Anthony C. Thiselton, The First Epistle to the Corinthians, New International Greek Testament Commentary (Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 2000), catalogs this verse among the commentary tradition's most contested cruxes, with readings ranging from a woman's own delegated authority to angels as witnesses of cosmic order to, as a minority view rather than the position most modern commentators adopt, angels drawn to lust after uncovered women per the Watchers tradition.

289 — Quoted as prophecy, but not necessarily canon

Michael Green, 2 Peter and Jude: An Introduction and Commentary, Tyndale New Testament Commentaries, rev. ed. (Leicester: Inter-Varsity Press; Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1987), commentary ad loc. Jude 14-15, concluding that "we have no means of knowing whether Jude regarded these books as canonical," only that he judged this particular oracle true and worth quoting as prophecy — Jude's introductory formula is "prophesied, saying" (Jude 1:14), not the "it is written" formula New Testament authors typically reserve for citations of recognized scripture. Tertullian, On the Apparel of Women, Book 1, ch. 3 (Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 4), draws the opposite conclusion more forcefully a century and a half later: he calls 1 Enoch "Scripture" outright and argues that Jude's quotation of it is itself apostolic testimony to its authenticity, answering objectors who noted 1 Enoch was "not admitted into the Jewish canon." Whether Jude himself intended any such canonical claim, or merely judged one particular Enochic oracle to have proven true, is not something the letter's own wording settles.

290 — One verse carries the whole story

The Study Quran, ed. Seyyed Hossein Nasr, Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E.B. Lumbard, and Mohammed Rustom (New York: HarperOne, 2015), commentary and translation ad loc. Quran 2:102. This modern scholarly translation and commentary renders the verse: "Solomon did not disbelieve, but the satans disbelieved, teaching people sorcery and that which was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut. But they would not teach anyone until they had said, 'We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve.'" The verse continues describing what those who learned this could do with it — most notably, cause estrangement between a man and his wife — while insisting the knowledge could harm no one except by God's own leave, and that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter. The entire Watchers-adjacent narrative this chapter examines survives, in the Quran itself, as a single compressed verse, not the sprawling multi-chapter account 1 Enoch devotes to a structurally similar story.

291 — A second modern rendering, same substance

M.A.S. Abdel Haleem, trans., The Quran: A New Translation, Oxford World's Classics (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2004; rev. ed. 2010), Surah al-Baqarah 2:102. Abdel Haleem's widely used modern translation agrees with The Study Quran on every substantive point this chapter relies on: Solomon's innocence of the sorcery charge leveled against him, the devils' own disbelief in teaching magic, the transmission of what was sent down to the two angels, Harut and Marut, at Babylon, and the angels' built-in warning that they exist only as a trial. Two independent modern scholarly translations converging on the same reading of the verse's plain sense gives this chapter's baseline description of 2:102 a secure footing before any of the exegetical disputes below are introduced.

292 — The premise the rest of this chapter argues against

M.A.S. Abdel Haleem, trans., The Quran: A New Translation, Oxford World's Classics (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2004; rev. ed. 2010), Surah at-Tahrim 66:6. Abdel Haleem renders the relevant clause: "angels who never disobey God's commands to them, but do as they are ordered." This is the single verse mainstream Sunni theology treats as establishing, as a matter of Quranic text rather than later inference, that angels are constitutionally incapable of disobedience — not merely angels who happen not to sin, but beings whose nature forecloses the possibility.

293 — A doctrine with a name: ismat al-malaika

Stephen R. Burge, Angels in Islam: Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti's al-Habaik fi Akhbar al-Malaik, Culture and Civilization in the Middle East (London: Routledge, 2012), chapters on angelic nature and theological controversy. Burge's study, the first monograph-length treatment in English of Islamic angelology as a distinct subject, documents the mainstream doctrine of ismat al-malaika, the impeccability or infallibility of angels, grounded in Quran 66:6 and treated across the classical tradition as settled dogma rather than a live debate. Burge identifies the Harut and Marut passage as one of a small number of genuine theological controversies this doctrine generates, precisely because the account, read plainly, appears to describe two named angels doing exactly what impeccable angels cannot do.

294 — The reference article that maps the whole dispute

Georges Vajda, "Harut wa-Marut," in Encyclopaedia of Islam, 2nd ed., vol. 3 (Leiden: E.J. Brill, 1971), 236-237. Vajda's entry in Islamic studies' standard reference encyclopedia surveys the full range of classical positions on Harut and Marut's identity and catalogs the manuscript and recitation evidence behind the dispute over whether the Quran's text names "the two angels" (malakayn) or "the two kings" (malikayn), a difference of a single short vowel in the Arabic, a fatha against a kasra, with no bearing on the consonantal skeleton of the written text. Vajda's article remains the standard scholarly starting point for tracing how many distinct, textually defensible readings this one phrase has generated.

295 — Ibn Kathir weighs the angel reading and does not reject it

Ibn Kathir, Tafsir Ibn Kathir (Abridged), trans. and ed. Safiur-Rahman al-Mubarakpuri et al., 10 vols. (Riyadh: Darussalam, 2000), commentary ad loc. Quran 2:102. Ibn Kathir reports, without dismissing it, the position he attributes to the Companion Ibn Abbas and to Ibn Mas'ud: that Harut and Marut genuinely were angels sent down to earth, and that their instruction in magic, itself a real event and not a metaphor, is reconciled with angelic impeccability the same way commentators reconcile Iblis's own fall: God's foreknowledge of what a created being will do is not the same claim as compelling it to do so. On this reading, the passage describes an actual, if narrow and divinely permitted, breach in the pattern Quran 66:6 otherwise describes as universal.

296 — The legend the Quran itself does not tell

John C. Reeves, "Some Parascriptural Dimensions of the 'Tale of Harut wa-Marut,'" Journal of the American Oriental Society 135, no. 4 (2015): 817-842. Reeves traces the extensive extra-Quranic narrative classical exegetes built onto the bare fact of 2:102: angels in heaven, appalled at human wickedness, boast of their own superior obedience; God challenges two of them to descend and face the same temptations; on earth they are drawn in by a woman (in some tellings identified with the planet Venus), drink wine, commit adultery and murder to conceal it, and find themselves barred from returning to heaven, at which point they are offered a choice between punishment in this world or judgment deferred to the next and take the earthly sentence. Reeves situates this fully developed legend as an interpretive accretion built up over centuries around the Quranic verse's few compressed lines, not a text the Quran itself narrates, but a story later generations of readers felt the verse demanded.

297 — Tabari's flat rejection of the angel reading

Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari, Jami' al-Bayan 'an Ta'wil Ay al-Quran, commentary ad loc. Quran 2:102, discussed in Georges Vajda, "Harut wa-Marut," Encyclopaedia of Islam, 2nd ed., vol. 3 (Leiden: E.J. Brill, 1971), 236-237. Where Ibn Kathir reports the angel reading without rejecting it, al-Tabari, writing more than a century earlier and compiling the single most influential early tafsir in the Sunni tradition, takes the opposite position outright: Harut and Marut were, in his judgment, two ordinary men, not angels, not Gabriel, not Michael, and the devils taught the people of Babylon their magic through these two men's hands rather than through any angelic intermediary at all. The disagreement is not a modern innovation; it runs directly through the two most cited tafsir works in the Sunni canon.

298 — A one-letter vowel and an entirely different verse

The Study Quran, ed. Seyyed Hossein Nasr et al. (New York: HarperOne, 2015), commentary ad loc. Quran 2:102. The Study Quran's commentary lays out the recitation variant behind the human-reading tradition in full: while the standard reading gives al-malakayn, "the two angels," a variant reading transmitted from the Companion Ibn Abbas and from later authorities including al-Hasan al-Basri, Abu'l-Aswad, and al-Dahhak gives al-malikayn, "the two kings," the identical consonantal text, differently voweled. Ibn Abbas is further reported to have glossed the two figures outright as "two men who practiced sorcery in Babylon." The grammatical fact underlying this whole reading is genuinely present in the text's transmission history, not an invention of modern apologetics grafted on afterward.

299 — The reading that became the modern default

Stephen R. Burge, "The Demystification of Magic in the Tafsir al-Manar: An Analysis of the Exegetical and Homiletic Devices Used in the Discussion 'Mabhath al-sihr wa-Harut wa-Marut,'" Religions 12, no. 9 (2021): article 734, https://doi.org/10.3390/rel12090734. Burge's study of Muhammad Abduh and Rashid Rida's Tafsir al-Manar, the most influential Sunni reformist commentary of the early twentieth century, shows the two scholars deploying the malikayn variant deliberately, not as one option among several but as the anchor of a sustained argument that magic itself is illusion and psychological trickery rather than a real supernatural force, that Solomon was never plausibly linked to sorcery, and that no angel of God was ever sent to teach it. Burge documents this as a considered rationalist program, using lexicography and the recitation variant together, that pushed the human-kings reading from a minority classical position toward something close to the default assumption in later reformist and modernist tafsir.

300 — A third door: angels who never actually fall

Ibn Kathir, Tafsir Ibn Kathir (Abridged), trans. and ed. Safiur-Rahman al-Mubarakpuri et al., 10 vols. (Riyadh: Darussalam, 2000), commentary ad loc. Quran 2:102, reporting the positions of al-Suddi and Mujahid ibn Jabr. A third classical position, distinct from both the fallen-angel reading and the human-kings reading, holds that Harut and Marut were angels precisely as the standard text says, sent down for the stated purpose of being a fitna, a trial or test, and that they carried out that commission exactly as instructed, without ever disobeying God at any point in the process. On this reading nothing about the episode requires angelic rebellion at all; the angels remain fully obedient throughout, and the entire moral weight of the passage falls on the humans who choose to learn and use what the angels, faithfully executing God's own test, were sent to offer.

301 — Three creations, three substances, three natures

Sahih Muslim, Kitab al-Zuhd wa-l-Raqaiq (Book of Zuhd and Softening of Hearts), hadith no. 2996, narrated from Aisha: "The angels were created from light, the jinn were created from a smokeless flame of fire, and Adam was created from that which has been described to you (clay)." Compare Quran 15:27 ("the jinn We created before from the fire of a scorching wind") and Quran 55:15 ("He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire"). Islamic cosmology places jinn in a wholly separate ontological category from angels: a third order of creation, morally accountable and capable of both belief and disbelief in a way angels, bound per Quran 66:6 to permanent obedience, are not.

302 — Where illicit unions with humans actually sit in Islamic tradition

Amira El-Zein, Islam, Arabs, and the Intelligent World of the Jinn (Syracuse, NY: Syracuse University Press, 2009), chapters on jinn cosmology and folk belief. El-Zein documents that Islamic jurisprudence and theology generally prohibit marriage between jinn and humans, yet popular folk tradition across many Muslim societies persistently describes such unions occurring anyway, typically framed as producing hybrid offspring credited with unusual powers. The figures who occupy the "illicit union with a human" role that this book's earlier chapters trace through the Watchers and their parallels belong, in Islamic tradition specifically, to jinn folklore, a body of popular belief running alongside, not inside, the Quranic text, not to Harut and Marut, whose own story as told in 2:102 involves no procreation, no offspring, and no giants at all.

303 — Why Babylon, specifically

Francesca Rochberg, The Heavenly Writing: Divination, Horoscopy, and Astronomy in Mesopotamian Culture (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2004), chapters on celestial divination's long institutional history. Rochberg documents that Babylon, across more than a millennium of cuneiform scholarly tradition, functioned as the ancient Near East's preeminent center for celestial divination and astrology, staffed by a professional class of scribal specialists whose methods were later transmitted to Greek and, eventually, wider Mediterranean astrological practice. The Quran's own choice of Babylon as the site where forbidden magical instruction reaches humanity sits on top of an already many-centuries-old cultural association between that specific city and esoteric, divinatory knowledge, a real historical resonance the text does not need to spell out for its original audience to recognize.

304 — Hesiod's own list of gods who slept with mortals

Glenn W. Most, ed. and trans., Hesiod, Vol. I: Theogony, Works and Days, Testimonia, Loeb Classical Library 57N (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2006), Theogony 940-944, 965-1020. Most's edition gives the Theogony's own closing genealogical catalogue, where the poem records, among many divine-mortal pairings, Zeus's union with Semele producing "much-cheering Dionysus" (940-942) and his union with Alcmene producing "the strength of Heracles" (943-944); the poem then closes with a companion catalogue running the pattern in the other direction, goddesses who slept with mortal men, including Demeter with Iasion (parents of Plutus) and Aphrodite with the Trojan prince Anchises (parents of Aeneas). Theogony is the closest thing archaic Greek epic has to a single register of these unions, though it names only a fraction of the pairings later tradition would attribute to Zeus alone.

305 — A fourth race, wedged between bronze and iron

Glenn W. Most, ed. and trans., Hesiod, Vol. I: Theogony, Works and Days, Testimonia, Loeb Classical Library 57N (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2006), Works and Days 156-173. Most's translation gives Hesiod's Five Races schema its clearest statement: after the bronze race destroys itself, Zeus creates a further race, "who are called demigods, the generation before our own upon the boundless earth" (156-160), a race explicitly set apart from the otherwise unbroken metallic sequence of gold, silver, bronze, and iron that frames it on both sides. Hesiod states plainly that "evil war and dread battle destroyed" this race, "some under seven-gated Thebes in the land of Cadmus while they fought for the sake of Oedipus' sheep, others brought in boats over the great gulf of the sea to Troy for the sake of fair-haired Helen" (161-165), before reporting that a portion of survivors was granted a home at the ends of the earth, the Isles of the Blessed, under the rule of Cronus (170-173).

306 — The god who borrowed a husband's face

[Hesiod], Shield of Heracles 1-56, in Glenn W. Most, ed. and trans., Hesiod, Vol. II: The Shield, Catalogue of Women, Other Fragments, Loeb Classical Library 503 (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2007); see also Timothy Gantz, Early Greek Myth: A Guide to Literary and Artistic Sources (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1993), 374-380. The Shield's proem, drawn from the same Hesiodic-school tradition that produced the Catalogue of Women, narrates Zeus visiting Alcmene at Thebes in the exact likeness of her husband Amphitryon on the single night before Amphitryon himself returns home from campaign; Alcmene conceives twin sons in immediate succession, unequal in parentage: Heracles by Zeus, Iphicles by Amphitryon. Gantz notes that later sources add a further embellishment absent from the Shield itself, that Zeus stretched the night to three times its ordinary length, and traces the story's stable core across the surviving literary tradition despite that later accretion.

307 — A shower of gold through a bronze roof

Pseudo-Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.4.1, trans. Robin Hard, The Library of Greek Mythology, Oxford World's Classics (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1997); Pindar, Pythian 12, in William H. Race, trans., Pindar: Olympian Odes, Pythian Odes, Loeb Classical Library 56 (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1997); compiled with full source apparatus in Timothy Gantz, Early Greek Myth (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1993), 300-311. King Acrisius of Argos, warned by an oracle that a son of his daughter Danae would kill him, locks her in an underground bronze chamber; Zeus reaches her anyway, entering as a shower of gold that pours through the roof, and she bears Perseus. Pindar's ode, among the earliest surviving literary references to Perseus, already assumes the story's broad outline without narrating the conception scene directly; the fuller connected narrative survives complete only in the later mythographic tradition Gantz compiles.

308 — One night, two fathers, two eggs

Pseudo-Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.10.7, trans. Robin Hard, The Library of Greek Mythology (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1997); compiled with the full range of literary and artistic sources in Timothy Gantz, Early Greek Myth (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1993), 318-323. Zeus visits Leda, wife of the Spartan king Tyndareus, in the form of a swan; the Bibliotheca's version has Leda lying with both Zeus and Tyndareus the same night and afterward bearing two eggs, from which hatch two of her four children as Zeus's offspring, Helen and Polydeuces, and two as Tyndareus's, Clytemnestra and Castor. Gantz notes the tradition is not fully stable across its sources on which children belong to which egg or father, but the split it settles into most often, a mortal Castor paired with an immortal Polydeuces, is what later motivates the story of Castor's death in battle and the brothers' shared, alternating immortality.

309 — A prequel to the Iliad that survives only in summary

M. L. West, ed. and trans., Greek Epic Fragments: From the Seventh to the Fifth Centuries BC, Loeb Classical Library 497 (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2003), 65-71. The Cypria was an epic poem of the so-called Trojan Cycle, covering events from the origins of the Trojan War through the action immediately preceding the Iliad; no continuous text of it survives. Ancient testimony disagreed even on its author, crediting it variously to Stasinus of Cyprus, Hegesias of Salamis, or simply "Homer," a claim Herodotus himself reports doubting. What survives is a prose summary by the later epitomizer Proclus, preserved in manuscripts of the Iliad, plus roughly forty quoted fragments embedded in later grammarians, lexicographers, and scholiasts, collected and re-edited with full source apparatus by West.

310 — Zeus and Themis open the poem with a population problem

Proclus, Chrestomathy, summary of the Cypria, in M. L. West, ed. and trans., Greek Epic Fragments, Loeb Classical Library 497 (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2003), 68-71. Proclus's summary opens the Cypria with Zeus, in consultation with the goddess Themis, planning the Trojan War as a means of relieving the earth of the burden of an overgrown human population; the summary then moves directly into the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, the strife the goddess Eris introduces there among the goddesses, and Paris's judgment among Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite, the chain of causation that produces the war Proclus says Zeus and Themis had already resolved on as their intended outcome.

311 — The poem's own opening lines, quoted rather than summarized

Cypria fr. 1 West, quoted in a scholion on Homer, Iliad 1.5, in M. L. West, ed. and trans., Greek Epic Fragments, Loeb Classical Library 497 (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2003), 66-67. Unlike Proclus's later prose paraphrase, this fragment preserves what is very likely close to the poem's own hexameter language, quoted by an ancient commentator explaining what Homer means by "the plan of Zeus" in the Iliad's own opening lines. West's translation renders it: "There was a time when the countless races of men roaming over the land were weighing down the deep-breasted earth's expanse. Zeus took pity when he saw it, and in his complex mind he resolved to relieve the all-nurturing earth of mankind's weight by fanning the great conflict of the Trojan War, to void the burden through death. So the warriors at Troy kept being killed, and Zeus' plan was being fulfilled." West treats the fragment as very likely the Cypria's own proem, directly answering the unexplained phrase that opens the Iliad.

312 — Thunderbolt, flood, or war: Zeus weighs his options

Elton T. E. Barker, "Momos Advises Zeus: Changing Representations of 'Cypria' Fragment 1," in Ettore Cingano and Lucio Milano, eds., Papers on Ancient Literatures: Greece, Rome and the Near East (Padua: S.A.R.G.O.N. Editrice e Libreria, 2008), 33-73; Menelaos Christopoulos, "Casus belli: Causes of the Trojan War in the Epic Cycle," Classics@ 6, ed. Efimia D. Karakantza (Washington, DC: Center for Hellenic Studies, 2011); primary text in M. L. West, ed. and trans., Greek Epic Fragments, Loeb Classical Library 497 (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2003), 66-69. The fuller scholion surrounding fragment 1 supplies detail Proclus's bare summary omits: the earth, overburdened and unable to bear mankind's impiety any longer, begged Zeus for relief; Zeus, capable of destroying the human population outright by thunderbolt or by flood, weighed doing exactly that before his adviser Momos, personification of blame and mockery, proposed instead engineering a war through a marriage (Peleus to Thetis) and a beautiful daughter (Helen), a plan judged to relieve the earth's burden by more selective, less total means. Barker's study traces how this fragment's wording and framing shifted across the different ancient sources that quote it, cautioning against reading any single surviving version as a stable, unmediated window onto the Cypria's original text.

313 — How much of this pattern did Greece inherit, and from where

M. L. West, The East Face of Helicon: West Asiatic Elements in Greek Poetry and Myth (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1997), chapters treating Hesiod's Theogony and Works and Days. West documents extensive, well-evidenced Near Eastern borrowing behind other parts of Hesiod's poetry, most securely the Theogony's succession myth of Ouranos, Kronos, and Zeus, closely paralleled in the Hurro-Hittite Kumarbi cycle and the Babylonian Enuma Elish. For the Five Races schema specifically, West finds the case for direct Near Eastern borrowing weaker and more mixed: he identifies partial parallels in Zoroastrian, Mesopotamian, and biblical (Daniel 2) traditions, but also elements matched only in the Vedic tradition's four ages, or yugas, leading him to treat Hesiod's schema as an amalgam that may preserve a shared Indo-European inheritance running through the Greek and Indic branches alongside, rather than as a single direct import from one identifiable Near Eastern source. West's own caution here argues against extending equal confidence to any claim of direct contact between the Cypria's overpopulation motif specifically and the Enochic giants-and-flood tradition; the two may share a structural logic without either being the other's source.

314 — Worshipped at shrines, not drowned in judgment

Carla M. Antonaccio, An Archaeology of Ancestors: Tomb Cult and Hero Cult in Early Greece (Lanham, MD: Rowman & Littlefield Publishers, 1995), chapters 1-2; Gregory Nagy, The Best of the Achaeans: Concepts of the Hero in Archaic Greek Poetry (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1979). Antonaccio's archaeological survey documents cult activity, tomb offerings, and shrines dedicated across the Greek world to figures the tradition regarded as products of divine-mortal unions, Heracles chief among them, with a major cult center at Thebes; Nagy's study of the Homeric vocabulary of heroism situates that reverence within a broader poetic and religious system that made "hero" a title of the highest honor rather than a mark of monstrosity. Nothing in the surviving Greek material treats the demigod generation as a category requiring divine punishment or eradication in the way 1 Enoch treats its giants; where the Greek tradition ends the age, it ends it through a war Zeus engineers to relieve a population problem, not through a verdict against the demigods' own nature.

315 — A Babylonian priest writes Babylon's history in Greek

Gerald P. Verbrugghe and John M. Wickersham, Berossos and Manetho, Introduced and Translated: Native Traditions in Ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt (Ann Arbor: University of Michigan Press, 1996). Berossus was a priest of the Babylonian god Bel-Marduk who composed a three-book history of Babylon, the Babyloniaca, in Greek for the Seleucid court around 290-278 BCE. The work itself does not survive; it is known only through fragments and paraphrases quoted by the first-century BCE historian Alexander Polyhistor, whose own history is likewise lost but was in turn excerpted by the Christian chronicler Eusebius of Caesarea in the fourth century CE and, later still, by the Byzantine chronicler George Syncellus around 800 CE. Verbrugghe and Wickersham's 1996 volume assembles and translates the surviving fragments with full critical apparatus and is the standard modern access point to a text that exists, in the strict sense, only as quotations of quotations of quotations.

316 — The primary account, quoted directly: what Oannes was and what he taught

Berossus's account of Oannes, translated from the Greek excerpts preserved in Eusebius and George Syncellus by the antiquarian Isaac Preston Cory, Ancient Fragments of the Phoenician, Chaldaean, Egyptian, Tyrian, Carthaginian, Indian, Persian, and Other Writers, 2nd ed. (London: William Pickering, 1832). Of the being's form: "the whole body of the animal was like that of a fish; and had under a fish's head another head, and also feet below, similar to those of a man, subjoined to the fish's tail," with a voice and language "articulate and human." Of his teaching: "This Being, in the day-time, used to converse with men; but took no food at that season; and he gave them an insight into letters, and sciences, and every kind of art. He taught them to construct houses, to build temples, to compile laws, and explained to them the principles of geometrical knowledge. He made them distinguish the seeds of the earth, and shewed them how to collect the fruits; in short, he instructed them in every thing which could tend to soften manners and humanize their lives." Cross-checked against Gerald P. Verbrugghe and John M. Wickersham's modern critical translation (Berossos and Manetho, University of Michigan Press, 1996), which corroborates the substance of Cory's older rendering while supplying updated source-critical apparatus unavailable in 1832.

317 — A teacher who never stays on land after dark

The same Berossus fragment, as translated in Isaac Preston Cory, Ancient Fragments of the Phoenician, Chaldaean, Egyptian, Tyrian, Carthaginian, Indian, Persian, and Other Writers, 2nd ed. (London: William Pickering, 1832). Oannes's teaching was bounded to daylight hours only: "when the sun had set, this Being Oannes, retired again into the sea, and passed the night in the deep; for he was amphibious." Berossus adds that similar beings appeared in later antediluvian reigns after Oannes; read alongside the cuneiform Uruk List of Kings and Sages, the tradition counts a total of seven such culture-bringing sages across the antediluvian period, of which Oannes is the first and most fully described.

318 — The cuneiform record independent of Berossus's Greek report

Alan Lenzi, "The Uruk List of Kings and Sages and Late Mesopotamian Scholarship," Journal of Ancient Near Eastern Religions 8, no. 2 (2008): 137-169. Lenzi analyzes a Seleucid-era cuneiform tablet excavated at Uruk in the 1959-60 season and first published by Jan van Dijk in 1962. The tablet pairs each of seven antediluvian kings with a corresponding apkallu-sage, Oannes (cuneiform Uanna) among them, then continues the list into the post-flood period, pairing later historical kings with human ummanu-scholars rather than sage-beings. Lenzi reads the tablet as evidence that Seleucid-period Mesopotamian scribes traced their own professional lineage directly back to these seven pre-flood culture-bringers in their own native written record, independent of and earlier than Berossus's later Greek-language summary composed for a Seleucid royal audience.

319 — Seven names, and a later, larger roster

Erica Reiner, "The Etiological Myth of the 'Seven Sages,'" Orientalia 30, no. 1 (1961): 1-6, first published the clearest cuneiform witness to the seven apkallu by name and epithet, an incantation text generally associated with the ritual series Bit Meseri, "protected house": Uanna, who "completed the plans of heaven and earth"; Uannedugga, "endowed with comprehensive intelligence"; Enmedugga; Enmegalamma; Enmebulugga; An-Enlilda, remembered as "the conjurer of the city of Eridu"; and Utuabzu, the only one credited with ascending to heaven. Helge S. Kvanvig, Roots of Apocalyptic: The Mesopotamian Background of the Enoch Figure and of the Son of Man, Wissenschaftliche Monographien zum Alten und Neuen Testament 61 (Neukirchen-Vluyn: Neukirchener Verlag, 1988), discusses this list at length and notes that Mesopotamian scribal tradition did not stop at seven: a further set of four post-diluvian figures, described as only two-thirds apkallu rather than full sages, continue the lineage after the flood, serving historical-era kings in essentially the same advisory capacity but at a lesser, part-human rank. Seven is the tradition's stable core; the roster's later expansion is the tradition's own solution to a story that had to keep explaining scribal wisdom long after its flood was supposed to have ended it.

320 — What the apkallu looked like, and what they were used for

F. A. M. Wiggermann, Mesopotamian Protective Spirits: The Ritual Texts, Cuneiform Monographs 1 (Groningen: STYX Publications, 1992). Wiggermann's study of first-millennium BCE Mesopotamian ritual and apotropaic texts identifies the apkallu's most common surviving artistic form as a bearded human figure wearing the skin of a carp draped over the body like a cloak, the fish's head resting atop the man's own; a second common type shows the apkallu as winged, bird-headed figures. Both types are regularly shown holding a small bucket (banduddu) in one hand and a cone-shaped object (mullilu), usually identified as a stylized pine or date-palm inflorescence, in the other, an implement pair Wiggermann connects to purification rites, aspersion, and the sanctifying of temples, kings, and sacred trees. Clay figurines of both apkallu types were manufactured according to prescribed ritual instructions and buried beneath the floors of ordinary houses as apotropaic foundation deposits, meant to keep evil from entering the home.

321 — A shared word: "watchers" applied to the apkallu themselves

Amar Annus, "On the Origin of Watchers: A Comparative Study of the Antediluvian Wisdom in Mesopotamian and Jewish Traditions," Journal for the Study of the Pseudepigrapha 19, no. 4 (2010): 277-320. Annus's central philological observation is that Akkadian sources apply the term massaru, "watcher" or "guardian," to the apkallu themselves, the same root later rendered into Aramaic and then Greek and Ethiopic as the designation "Watchers" for Enoch's fallen angels.
