A giant of the Book of Giants, identified as the son of the Watcher Baraqel rather than Shemihazah, distinguishing his parentage from Ohyah and Hahyah's. Mahaway alone undertakes the flight to Enoch to seek interpretation of the giants' shared dream-visions, described in the fragments as mounting into the air "like strong winds" and flying "with his hands like eagles" across a wilderness named Desolation [176] [177].

MALLEUS MALEFICARUM

A 1487 witch-hunting manual compiled principally by the Dominican inquisitor Heinrich Kramer, arguing at length, in Part 1, Question 3, for the reality of demonic sexual contact with humans, and building its case for the danger and prosecutability of witchcraft directly on Thomas Aquinas's incubus/succubus mechanism [357] [358].

MANI

Persian religious teacher (216-274 CE), founder of Manichaeism, raised within an Elchasaite Jewish-Christian baptizing sect according to the Cologne Mani Codex before founding his own religion. Reworked a version of the Jewish Book of Giants into one of his own religion's seven canonical scriptures [184] [185].

MANICHAEISM

The religion founded by the third-century Persian prophet Mani, which counted a reworked Book of Giants among its seven canonical scriptures. Manichaean missionaries carried the religion, and this text, east along the Silk Road; fragments of its Book of Giants survive in Middle Persian, Parthian, Sogdian, and Old Uyghur, recovered from ruined temple libraries at Turfan in Central Asia by early twentieth-century German expeditions [185] [188] [187].

MANUSMRITI

The central Hindu dharma text on law and social duty, whose third chapter (3.20-3.34) catalogs eight recognized forms of marriage, including the Gandharva and Rakshasa forms this chapter distinguishes carefully from one another [345] [351].

MARGARET CLUNIES ROSS

Scholar of Old Norse literature whose Prolonged Echoes: Old Norse Myths in Medieval Northern Society (1994) argues that Snorri Sturluson's pedagogical, systematizing aims in the Prose Edda complicate any simple reading of it as a direct transcription of pre-Christian belief [339].

MARUT

The second of the two figures named alongside Harut in Quran 2:102, inseparable from Harut in every reading the classical and modern tafsir tradition offers. No independent tradition distinguishes Marut's fate, character, or identity from Harut's; the two are treated as a single interpretive unit throughout the exegetical literature this chapter surveys [290] [294].

MASTEMA

The chief of the evil spirits in the Book of Jubilees, named at Jubilees 10:8 as the offspring of the drowned Watchers who petitions God, after the flood, to leave a portion of the surviving spirits free rather than have all of them bound. God grants the request as a precise fraction: nine-tenths bound and cast down, one-tenth left free under Mastema's own command, to continue leading humanity astray until the final judgment [219]. His name derives from a Hebrew root meaning hostility or accusation, functioning almost as a title — the Hostile One, the Accuser — and Jubilees has him act in a role its later chapters treat as functionally continuous with the more familiar ha-satan of Job and Zechariah, though the text never states that identification outright [220].

MAUGANTIUS

The wise counselor in Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae who, hearing the testimony of Merlin's mother, supplies the technical identification of her visitor as an incubus daemon, citing the Roman writer Apuleius's De Deo Socratis on spirits inhabiting the region between the moon and the earth [360].

MENAKA

An Apsara sent by Indra to seduce the sage Vishvamitra and break his advancing tapas, as told in the Mahabharata's Adi Parva. Their union produces a daughter, whom Menaka leaves in the forest before returning to the world of the gods; the sage Kanva finds and raises the child as Shakuntala [342].

MEREDITH G. KLINE

Old Testament scholar who argued in a 1962 Westminster Theological Journal article that Genesis 6:1-4's "sons of God" are best read as human dynastic rulers claiming divine sonship, a minority position among modern critical readings of the passage [242].

MERLIN

The prophet-wizard of Arthurian legend, first given extended treatment in Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae as a composite of the older Welsh prophet-figure Myrddin Wyllt and the war leader Ambrosius Aurelianus. Geoffrey leaves his paternity as an ambiguous spirit-visitor testimony, technically glossed as an incubus daemon by the secondary character Maugantius [360]; Robert de Boron's later Merlin makes the incubus paternity explicit and central to a foiled devils' Antichrist plot resolved by baptism at birth, the traditional source of Merlin's prophetic gift [363] [364].

METATRON

The exalted angel Rabbi Ishmael meets in the seventh heavenly palace in 3 Enoch, identified there as "Prince of the Divine Presence" and second only to God in the celestial hierarchy. Metatron reveals himself to be the transformed patriarch Enoch (3 Enoch 4), his body enlarged "to match the world in length and breadth" and given thirty-six or seventy-two wings (manuscripts vary) and hundreds of eyes (3 Enoch 9), and is called by God "the Lesser YHWH" (3 Enoch 12). A Talmudic tradition (b. Hagigah 15a) narrates Metatron being punished with sixty lashes of fire after the sage Elisha ben Abuyah saw him seated and concluded there were "two powers in heaven" [165] [167] [168].

METHUSELAH

Antediluvian patriarch, son of Enoch and father of Lamech (Genesis 5:21-27). In 1 Enoch 106-107 he carries his son Lamech's fear about the newborn Noah to his own father Enoch at "the ends of the earth," and returns with Enoch's reassurance and the child's name.

MICHAEL (ARCHANGEL)

One of the four archangels who look down from heaven, see the bloodshed the Watchers' giants have caused, and bring the resulting complaint before God (9:1). In the judgment that follows, Michael is assigned to bind Shemihazah and the other Watchers who took human wives, imprisoning them for seventy generations until the final judgment (10:11-14) [28].

MICHAEL D. COE

American Maya archaeologist whose 1989 study "The Hero Twins: Myth and Image" identified recurring Hero Twins scenes on painted Late Classic Maya ceramics centuries predating the Ximenez manuscript, evidence independent of the colonial-era text for the deep antiquity of the underlying mythic complex [421] [422].

MICHAEL GREEN

New Testament scholar, author of 2 Peter and Jude: An Introduction and Commentary (Tyndale New Testament Commentaries, rev. ed. 1987), cited in this chapter on the unresolved question of whether Jude regarded 1 Enoch as canonical scripture [289].

MIDRASH OF SHEMHAZAI AND AZAEL

A medieval Hebrew narrative midrash preserved within Bereshit Rabbati, attributed to the school of Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan of Narbonne (Provence, first half of the eleventh century CE), known to later medieval writers only through citation until a single surviving manuscript was published by Chanoch Albeck in 1940 [258]. It gives the fullest rabbinic-tradition narrative of the two fallen angels: their descent, Shemhazai's infatuation with Istehar [259], the birth of his giant sons Hiwwa and Hiyya and their destruction-dreams [260], and the angels' divergent fates, Shemhazai's repentance against Azael's refusal [261]. Scholars including J. T. Milik and Annette Yoshiko Reed dispute how directly this medieval text relates to the ancient Enochic material it resembles [262].

MILIK'S LATE-DATING ARGUMENT

J. T. Milik's 1976 argument, built on the total absence of Parables material among the Qumran Aramaic Enoch fragments, that the Parables were a late, third-century-CE Christian or Jewish-Christian composition rather than a Second Temple Jewish text [87]. Substantially revised by subsequent scholarship, which has largely relocated the Parables to the late first century BCE or early-to-mid first century CE, though the revision is not unanimous [88] [89] [90] [91].

MOMOS

Greek god personifying blame, censure, and mockery, cast in the fuller scholion on the Cypria's opening fragment as the adviser who talks Zeus out of destroying humanity outright by thunderbolt or flood and proposes the more selective alternative of engineering the Trojan War through Helen's birth [312].

MOUNT HERMON

The real, identifiable peak where the two hundred Watchers descend and swear their mutual oath "in the days of Jared" (1 Enoch 6:6) — the southernmost and highest summit of the Anti-Lebanon range, today divided among Israel, Lebanon, and Syria, and the source of the Jordan River's headwaters [18]. Long before 1 Enoch, the mountain marked Israel's northern boundary in Deuteronomy 3:8-9 and carried the compound name Baal-Hermon in Judges 3:3 and 1 Chronicles 5:23, evidence of an established Canaanite cult on its slopes [19]. 1 Enoch explains the name itself as an etymological record of the Watchers' oath, playing on the Hebrew-Aramaic root hrm, "to curse" or "devote to destruction" [16]. A Greek inscription recovered from a summit sanctuary at Qasr Antar in 1869, translated by George Nickelsburg, shows the mountain was still associated with oath-taking well into the Hellenistic period, independent of 1 Enoch itself [20].

MUHAMMAD ABDUH

Egyptian reformist scholar (d. 1905) whose Quranic commentary, completed and extended by his student Rashid Rida as Tafsir al-Manar, argued for a rationalist reading of Quran 2:102 that treats magic as illusion rather than genuine supernatural power and denies that any angel was ever sent to teach it, favoring the human-kings reading of Harut and Marut over the fallen-angel tradition [299].

MUJAHID IBN JABR

Early Meccan authority on tafsir, a student of Ibn Abbas, cited by Ibn Kathir alongside al-Suddi as a source for the reading that treats Harut and Marut as angels who remained fully obedient throughout their mission, with the entire moral weight of the episode falling on the humans who chose to learn from them [300].

NEPHILIM

The rarest and most contested term in this vocabulary, appearing only at Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33. Long popularly derived from the Hebrew root נפל (naphal, "to fall"), yielding "fallen ones," but standard lexicography (BDB, HALOT) treats that derivation as plausible rather than proven, glossing the word simply as "giants" or "monster" without committing to an etymology [224] [225]. See Chapter 7 for the fuller post-Flood survivor puzzle.

NJORD

A god of the Vanir, folded into the Aesir's household after an earlier peace settlement between the two groups, later married to the giantess Skadi as compensation for her father Thjazi's death — a match that fails over the couple's incompatible preferred homes [333] [334].

OANNES

The first and most fully described of the Mesopotamian apkallu, per the Babyloniaca of the Hellenistic Babylonian priest Berossus, preserved only in later quotation. Described as part-fish and part-man, articulate and human in voice, Oannes emerges from the sea each day to instruct the antediluvian kings in writing, the sciences, construction, temple-building, law, geometry, and agriculture, before returning each night to the deep, "for he was amphibious," and taking no food on land [316] [317]. Berossus presents his teaching as a benefaction to be honored, the polarity 1 Enoch's Watchers narrative is argued to invert most sharply. Independent cuneiform evidence, the Uruk List of Kings and Sages, pairs a sage named Uanna, generally identified with Oannes, alongside the first antediluvian king, confirming the figure predates and underlies Berossus's later Greek report [318].

ODIN

Chief of the Aesir, son of the god Bor and the giantess Bestla. Odin later fathers Thor by the giantess Jord and is credited elsewhere in the tradition with further unions among the giantesses; his own parentage establishes, at the head of the pantheon, the pattern of god-giant intermarriage this chapter traces [329] [332].

OG OF BASHAN

King of Bashan, described as "the remnant of the Rephaim" and the last survivor of that giant clan in Israelite memory (Deuteronomy 3:11). His iron bed, nine cubits long and four cubits wide by the common cubit, is described as a still-visible object in Rabbah of the Ammonites at the time Deuteronomy was composed. Scholarly debate over the bed's true nature, royal furniture, funerary sarcophagus, or dark basalt slab, remains unresolved [52] [51].

OHYAH AND HAHYAH

Two giants of the Book of Giants, identified in the fragments as sons of Shemihazah, given extended dialogue, competing dream-visions, and distinguishable personalities across several manuscripts — quarrelsome and self-assured at first, increasingly frightened as the visions of coming judgment accumulate. Ohyah is associated in the fragments with a vision of a great tree uprooted except for three surviving roots [175] [180].

ON IDOLATRY (DE IDOLOLATRIA)

Tertullian's treatise cataloguing pagan practices Christians must avoid; chapter 9 attributes astrology to the fallen angels, and chapter 4 cites 1 Enoch by name as prophesying the corrupting spread of idolatry through "the spirits of the angelic apostates" [267].

ON THE APPAREL OF WOMEN (DE CULTU FEMINARUM)

Tertullian's treatise against ostentatious female dress, tracing cosmetics and jewelry to teachings the fallen angels gave their human wives (Book 1, chapter 2) and mounting a dedicated defense of the Book of Enoch's scriptural authenticity, citing its quotation in the Epistle of Jude (Book 1, chapter 3) [266].

ON THE VEILING OF VIRGINS (DE VIRGINIBUS VELANDIS)

Tertullian's treatise defending the veiling of unmarried women; chapter 7 connects Genesis 6's transgressing angels directly to Paul's instruction in 1 Corinthians 11:10 that a woman should have "a symbol of authority on her head, because of the angels" — a connection this book's chapter on the New Testament's use of Enochic material returns to directly [268].

ONE HUNAHPU

Son of the primordial diviner pair Xpiyacoc and Xmucane and, with his brother Seven Hunahpu, a passionate ballplayer whose games near the entrance to Xibalba draw the Lords of Death's anger. Summoned to the underworld and put to death there, his severed head is hung in a barren tree that instantly fruits into gourds around it [411] [412]. His head later speaks to and impregnates Xquic by spitting into her hand, without intercourse, making him father of the Hero Twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque [414].

OXFORD (BODLEIAN LIBRARY)

The Oxford library that received two of the four complete Ge'ez manuscripts of 1 Enoch James Bruce brought to Europe in 1773 (one presented directly, one retained by Bruce and deposited later). Richard Laurence produced the first complete English translation of 1 Enoch from one of these manuscripts in 1821 [391].

PARIS (BIBLIOTHEQUE NATIONALE DE FRANCE)

The Paris institution, formerly the Royal Library, that received one of the four complete Ge'ez manuscripts of 1 Enoch James Bruce brought to Europe in 1773, per Ariel Hessayon's archival research into Bruce's papers and correspondence [391].

PEARL OF GREAT PRICE

One of the four "standard works" of scripture recognized by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, alongside the Bible, the Book of Mormon, and the Doctrine and Covenants. Compiled from several of Joseph Smith's writings, first as an 1851 British Mission pamphlet, canonized by a sustaining vote of general conference on October 10, 1880, and standardized into its current chapter-and-verse form under Elder James E. Talmage in 1902. Contains the Book of Moses. Recognized as scripture only within the Latter-day Saint tradition, a structural parallel to 1 Enoch's own status as canonical scripture solely within Ethiopian Orthodoxy [400] [402].

PERSEUS

Son of Zeus and the mortal woman Danae, conceived when Zeus entered Danae's bronze prison chamber as a shower of gold, defeating the precaution her father Acrisius had built specifically to prevent any such union after an oracle warned him a son of Danae's would kill him [307].

POPOL VUH

K'iche' Maya mythological-historical narrative recounting the creation of the world, the exploits of the Hero Twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque, and the genealogy of the K'iche' ruling lineages. First set down in alphabetic Quiche script around 1554-1558; that original manuscript is lost, and the text survives only through an early eighteenth-century copy and Spanish translation by the Dominican friar Francisco Ximenez, held today at the Newberry Library in Chicago [409]. Cited in this chapter from the standard modern translations of Dennis Tedlock and Allen J. Christenson [410].

PROOF OF THE APOSTOLIC PREACHING

Irenaeus of Lyons's shorter summary of Christian sacred history; section 18 gives the fullest patristic-era paraphrase of the forbidden arts — cosmetics, metallurgy, sorcery, astrology — the Watchers are accused of teaching humanity [269].

QASR ANTAR STELE

A Greek-inscribed limestone pillar recovered in 1869 by the British surveyor Charles Warren from the ruined sanctuary of Qasr Antar, near Mount Hermon's summit, and now held by the British Museum (museum number G,1903.0422.1). Its inscription — "According to the command of the greatest and Holy God, those who take an oath (proceed) from here" — is read by Nickelsburg as independent, centuries-later evidence that people were still swearing oaths at a sanctuary on this mountain's summit well into the Hellenistic period, distinct from, but suggestive alongside, 1 Enoch 6's account of the Watchers' own oath at the same mountain [20]. It is the only object in this book's object survey that is stone rather than manuscript.

QASR IBRIM COPTIC FRAGMENTS

Four Coptic parchment leaves, dated to the eighth through tenth centuries CE, recovered from the Nubian site of Qasr Ibrim (now an island in Lake Nasser) during the Egypt Exploration Society's 1963 rescue excavation ahead of the Aswan High Dam's floodwaters. Identified by Joost Hagen in 2009 as a translation of 2 Enoch chapters 36-42, matching the shorter recension, they are the only attestation of 2 Enoch in a language besides Slavonic [149].

QUMRAN (KHIRBET QUMRAN)

The archaeological site on a marl plateau above Wadi Qumran, roughly 1.5 km from the Dead Sea's northwestern shore and 10 km south of Jericho (approx. 31 deg 44 min N, 35 deg 28 min E), excavated by Roland de Vaux between 1951 and 1956. Cave 4 at this site produced the Aramaic 1 Enoch fragments (Milik and Black, 1976) and Book of Giants fragments (Stuckenbruck, 1997) this book draws on in its ninth and seventeenth chapters [387].

QUMRAN ARAMAIC ENOCH MANUSCRIPTS

Eleven Aramaic manuscript copies of Enochic material recovered from Qumran Cave 4 and published by Jozef T. Milik in 1976: seven copies of the Book of the Watchers, the Book of Dreams, and the Epistle of Enoch, plus four copies of the separate Astronomical Book. Paleographically dated from roughly 200-150 BCE onward; none contains any portion of the Book of Parables, chapters 37-71 [67] [69].

R.H. CHARLES

Biblical scholar whose 1906 critical edition of the Ethiopic text and 1912 revised English translation and commentary of 1 Enoch remained the standard scholarly reference for most of the twentieth century, until superseded by editions incorporating the Qumran Aramaic fragments [80].

RABBI ISHMAEL

A historical second-century Tanna (rabbinic sage of the Mishnaic period) cast, centuries after his own lifetime, as the first-person narrator and human protagonist of 3 Enoch's heavenly ascent, in which he questions the angel Metatron in the seventh heavenly palace [161].

RABBI SIMEON BEN YOHAI

Second-century tannaitic sage credited elsewhere in rabbinic literature with extensive halakhic and mystical teaching. Genesis Rabbah 26:5 records him reading Genesis 6:2's "sons of God" (bnei ha'elohim) as bnei dayanaya, "sons of the judges" — powerful human magistrates, not angels — and cursing anyone who translates the phrase to mean literal angels [249]. His reading anchors rabbinic Judaism's normative-mainstream turn away from the angelic interpretation of the Watchers material, though the same compiled text preserving his curse also preserves the angelic reading elsewhere, unrebutted [250] [251].

RAELISM (RAELIAN MOVEMENT)

New religious movement founded in 1974 by Claude Vorilhon ("Rael"), teaching that humanity was created through genetic engineering by an extraterrestrial species the movement calls the Elohim, reinterpreting the Hebrew word elsewhere translated "God" or "gods" as literally meaning "those who came from the sky" [377]. Studied academically as a new religious movement by the sociologist Susan Palmer, whose fieldwork is the standard scholarly treatment of the group [376]; its theology stands outside mainstream biblical scholarship's understanding of Elohim and the "sons of God" of Genesis 6:1-4 [378].

RAGUEL

One of the seven named angels of 1 Enoch 20, described as the angel who exacts vengeance on the world of the luminaries (20:4) — an office found nowhere in the earlier, four-angel roster of chapter 9 [56] [58].

RAKSHASA

A general class of demonic beings in Hindu cosmology, attested with several separate and competing origin accounts (from Brahma's breath or foot, or descent from the sage Pulastya or the goddess Nirriti), and named as a distinct, non-consensual form of marriage (abduction) in the Manusmriti's list of eight. No source located for this chapter connects Rakshasas generally to the Apsara-sage seduction pattern traced here; the two categories are kept genuinely distinct in the classical sources [351].

RAMBHA

An Apsara sent by Indra to seduce the sage Vishvamitra during a later period of tapas described in the Ramayana's Balakanda. Unlike Menaka in the earlier Mahabharata episode, Rambha is refused; Vishvamitra curses her to become a stone for ten thousand years, an act of anger the narrative treats as itself costing him the tapas he had accumulated [350].

RAPHAEL (ARCHANGEL)

One of the four archangels who bring the complaint of chapter 9; assigned in the judgment of chapter 10 to bind Azazel hand and foot in the desert at Dudael and cover him with darkness until the day of judgment (10:4-8) [28]. Later in the Book of Watchers, Raphael also identifies the still-crying spirit of Abel to Enoch during his tour of the places where the dead are kept (22:5-7) [24].

RASHI

Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040-1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on both the Hebrew Bible and the Babylonian Talmud. His commentary on tractate Yoma 67b identifies the otherwise-unglossed "Uzza and Azael" of that Talmudic passage as two angels of destruction who descended to earth and sinned with mortal women before the Flood, explicitly connecting the Talmud's brief aside back to the Genesis 6 material — an identification his own commentary supplies, not one present in the Talmud's own wording [254].

RASHID RIDA

Syrian-Egyptian scholar and student of Muhammad Abduh who completed and published Tafsir al-Manar after Abduh's death, including its extended discussion of magic and Harut and Marut ("Mabhath al-sihr wa-Harut wa-Marut"), which became one of the most influential vehicles for the modern reformist reading that treats Harut and Marut as human kings rather than fallen angels [299].

REMIEL

One of the seven named angels of 1 Enoch 20, set over those who rise (20:8), an office generally read as concerned with resurrection. Remiel is the name least securely attested across the manuscript tradition: present in the Greek witness, absent from part of the Ethiopic tradition [57].

REPHAIM

A biblical term with two distinct senses: an aboriginal category of formerly widespread, unusually tall pre-Israelite peoples in Transjordan and Canaan, displaced by Israel's neighbors and named alongside local variants such as the Emim (Moabite usage) and Zamzummim (Ammonite usage), and repeatedly measured against the Anakim (Genesis 14:5; Deuteronomy 2:10-11, 2:20, 2:20-21, 3:11) [50]; and, separately, elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, the shades of the dead in the underworld (Isaiah 14:9, 26:14; Proverbs 2:18, 9:18; Psalm 88:10-11) [51]. The Ugaritic cognate rapiuma — deified royal ancestors who feast with the god El despite belonging to the realm of the dead — is the strongest evidence the two senses share deep, if textually unconfirmed, common roots; scholarship debates which sense is historically prior [229] [230].

RICHARD LAURENCE

Regius Professor of Hebrew at Oxford who in 1821 published The Book of Enoch the Prophet, translated from one of James Bruce's Bodleian manuscripts — the first complete English translation of 1 Enoch to appear in print [79].

ROBERT C. NEWMAN

Scholar whose 1984 Grace Theological Journal article surveys the ancient exegesis of Genesis 6:2 and 6:4, documenting the Septuagint's huioi/angeloi manuscript split and its roots in first-century Jewish exegesis attested by Philo and Josephus [243].

ROBERT DE BORON

French poet (fl. c. 1191-1202) whose verse romance Merlin rebuilds Geoffrey of Monmouth's ambiguous spirit-father scene into fully explicit Christian doctrine: a devils'-council conspiracy to father an Antichrist-like figure through an incubus, foiled by the infant's immediate baptism [362] [363].

ROBIN ROUTLEDGE

Biblical scholar whose 2015 Tyndale Bulletin article examines the Hebrew syntax of Genesis 6:4, concluding that the text does not itself settle whether the Nephilim and the gibborim it names are the same beings under two labels or two related but distinct categories [246].

ROME (VATICAN LIBRARY)

The Rome institution holding a fourth Ge'ez manuscript of 1 Enoch, shelf-mark Vat. et. 71, given by James Bruce to a cardinal's library during a stop in Rome on his 1773 return journey from Ethiopia, after meeting Pope Clement XIV. The manuscript's provenance went unresolved until Ariel Hessayon's archival research identified it [391].

RONALD S. HENDEL

Biblical scholar whose 1987 Journal of Biblical Literature article argues for reading Genesis 6:1-4's "sons of God" as divine beings by comparison with the Ugaritic Kirta epic, proposing that the passage concerns a violated boundary between divine and mortal status rather than illicit sex as such [240].

RONALD STORY

Editor of The Space-Gods Revealed: A Close Look at the Theories of Erich Von Daniken (1976), a foreword by Carl Sagan and contributions from working scientists that answered von Daniken's Chariots of the Gods? claim by claim, site by site, and documented von Daniken's 1970 Swiss conviction for embezzlement, fraud, and forgery [367].

SARIEL (SARAQAEL)

One of the seven named angels of 1 Enoch 20, given authority over the spirits who sin against the spirit (20:6). Appears in the earlier, four-angel roster of chapter 9 under this same name in some manuscript witnesses, where other witnesses read Uriel instead [58].

SARIEL / URIEL

The third of the four archangels named in 1 Enoch 9:1, commissioned in this chapter to warn Noah of the coming flood and instruct him how to survive it (10:1-3), the same figure whose name is given as Sariel in the oldest Aramaic evidence and the Qumran War Scroll's own four-angel roster, and as Uriel in the complete Ethiopic manuscripts, the later Ethiopic manuscript tradition, the fragmentary Greek Akhmim manuscript, and R. H. Charles's public-domain translation — the identical manuscript fork already present in the four-archangel list of the preceding chapter [30] [21] [28].

SATANAIL

The named prince or leader of the Grigori in 2 Enoch (18:3), who "with their prince Satanail rejected the Lord of light." Unlike 1 Enoch's Book of the Watchers, which names group leaders such as Shemihazah and Asael but no single overarching commander, 2 Enoch consolidates leadership of the fallen host into one named figure whose title is recognizable as an early form of "Satan" — a development Andrei Orlov treats as significant for the later history of Jewish and Christian demonology [156].

SCAPEGOAT (YOM KIPPUR)

The ritual described in Leviticus 16:8-10, 26, in which one of two goats, having had the community's confessed sins symbolically placed upon it, is sent "for Azazel" into the wilderness on the Day of Atonement. Scholars including Lester L. Grabbe, Daniel Stokl Ben Ezra, and Andrei A. Orlov have argued this ritual and this chapter's treatment of Azazel share a genuine intertextual connection: a common name, punishment or expulsion specifically into the desert, and the concentration of collective wrongdoing onto a single bearer before his removal from human company (10:4-8) [31] [32] [33].

SEPTUAGINT (LXX) GENESIS 6:2 VARIANT

The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, whose manuscript tradition at Genesis 6:2 splits between huioi tou theou ("sons of God"), the majority reading, and angeloi tou theou ("angels of God"), a minority reading including Codex Alexandrinus and independently reflected in the first-century writings of Philo and Josephus [243]. The modern critical edition of the Septuagint prints huioi as the base text [244], while its editor's companion volume of textual notes discusses the fork directly [245].

SETHITE INTERPRETATION

A reading of Genesis 6:1-4 in which "sons of God" names not divine beings but the righteous human line descended from Seth, intermarrying with the corrupt line of Cain (the "daughters of men") — a moral-genealogical rather than supernatural account of the chapter's sin. Introduced here as a live philological option surveyed alongside the divine-beings and dynastic-ruler readings [238]. First proposed, in surviving Christian sources, by Julius Africanus in the early third century, and cemented as the dominant Western Christian position two centuries later by Augustine of Hippo's City of God; its long history in patristic exegesis is this book's business in a later chapter on the church fathers [273] [274] [275].

SEVEN HUNAHPU

Brother of One Hunahpu, killed alongside him after the two are summoned to Xibalba following the Lords of Death's irritation at their ballgame; unlike his brother, he is killed outright and buried rather than beheaded and displayed [411].

SEVENTY GENERATIONS

The term of Shemihazah's binding "in the valleys of the earth" set by Michael's commission (10:12), a schematic rather than literal number in the judgment of scholars of Second Temple apocalypticism, part of a broader pattern in which the number seventy recurs across Enochic literature (compare the "seventy shepherds" of the later Animal Apocalypse, 1 Enoch 89:59-90:19) and in Daniel 9:24-27's reinterpretation of Jeremiah's prophesied seventy-year exile (Jeremiah 25:11-12; 29:10), signaling a bounded, divinely counted period of restraint rather than an open-ended one [38].

SEVENTY SHEPHERDS

Seventy angelic figures the Lord of the sheep appoints, following the Babylonian conquest and exile, each given a fixed and limited period to pasture (rule over and expose to danger) the flock of Israel, with a hidden scribe secretly recording their individual excesses for later judgment (1 Enoch 89:59-90:5). The text groups them into four blocks, widely though not universally correlated with the Babylonian, Persian, Ptolemaic, and Seleucid periods of foreign rule [114]. Their eventual judgment, alongside the fallen stars and failed sheep, comes at 90:20-27 [119].

SHAKUNTALA

The daughter of the sage Vishvamitra and the Apsara Menaka, abandoned in the forest at birth and raised by the sage Kanva, who names her for the sakunta birds that sheltered her. She later marries King Dushyanta by Gandharva rite and becomes, in tradition, mother to Bharata. Her story is told first, and controllingly, in the Mahabharata's Adi Parva, and later dramatized with significant additions by Kalidasa in Abhijnanashakuntalam [343] [344].

SHEMIHAZAH

Leader of the two hundred Watchers who descend on Mount Hermon (1 Enoch 6:3-6); spelled Semihazah, Semyaza, Shemyaza, Samyaza, and Shemhazai across various manuscripts and secondary literature, and given as Shemihazah in the Dead Sea Aramaic fragments, the form generally preferred in critical editions [11]. He proposes the plan to take human wives but fears bearing sole guilt for it, a fear the other Watchers answer by binding all two hundred together in a mutual oath rather than leaving the decision to him alone (6:3-5). Named at the head of the rebel band in the Book of the Watchers' own list of ringleaders, he also appears in the Book of Giants as the father of the giants Ohyah and Hahyah [175].

SHEMIHAZAH (SEMJAZA)

Leader of the two hundred Watchers who descend and bind themselves by oath to take human wives, introduced in earlier chapters of this survey. Named first among those credited with teaching forbidden arts in 1 Enoch 8:3, where he is said to have taught "enchantments, and root-cuttings" — one of eight specialties distributed among named Watchers in that verse, alongside astrology, constellations, and the reading of clouds, earth-signs, sun-signs, and the moon's course [205]. In this chapter the Lord commissions Michael to bind Shemihazah and his companions "for seventy generations in the valleys of the earth," after their giant sons have destroyed one another in battle, until "the judgement that is for ever and ever is consummated," when they will be led to "the abyss of fire" (10:11-13). R. H. Charles's public-domain translation, quoted directly in this chapter, spells the name "Semjaza" [38].

SHEMIHAZAH STORY AND ASAEL STORY

The two originally separate literary strands that source critics, following Paul D. Hanson's 1977 study, identify as interwoven across 1 Enoch chapters 6-11: a "Shemihazah story" centered on the watchers' illicit marriages and the birth of giants, and an "Asael story" centered on a single rebel angel's revelation of forbidden metallurgical, cosmetic, and divinatory knowledge [195]. 1 Enoch 7's brief mention of sorcery, charms, and root-cutting (7:1) is the compressed first appearance of material the Asael strand develops at length in chapter 8.

SHEOL (1 ENOCH 22)

The great, hard mountain Enoch is shown containing several deep, hollow compartments where the spirits of the dead assemble to await a still-future judgment (22:1-4), guided by the angel Raphael. The compartments are differentiated by category: a bright, spring-fed place for the righteous (22:9), a place for sinners not yet punished in life (22:10-11), a place for sinners already suffering active torment, and a place holding the specific case of Abel's murdered spirit, still pleading against Cain (22:7). Scholarship treats this vision as a documented step in the development of differentiated Jewish and Christian afterlife belief, and notes its likely bearing on Luke 16:19-31 and 1 Peter 3:19, treated fully in a later chapter of this book [60] [61] [62] [63].

SHEOL (IN THE EPISTLE OF ENOCH)

The place of the dead to which the souls of the righteous descend "with grief" at death (102:5), before the Epistle's closing chapters promise them vindication: their spirits "will not perish," and they "will shine like the luminaries of heaven" (103:4; 104:2). The Epistle is more explicit about the survival and transformation of the spirit than about any bodily resurrection, one of several distinct positions taken on the fate of the dead across Second Temple Jewish literature [131].

SHRINE OF THE BOOK

A purpose-built wing of the Israel Museum in Jerusalem, dedicated in 1965 to house the Dead Sea Scrolls. It holds all seven of the original scrolls recovered from Qumran Cave 1 in 1947 as a single permanent collection, including the Genesis Apocryphon (1Q20), alongside rotating exhibitions of further fragments drawn from the wider Qumran corpus [394].

SIRACH (ECCLESIASTICUS)

A Second Temple Jewish wisdom book, also called Ecclesiasticus, written by Ben Sira in Hebrew around the early second century BCE. Its Praise of the Ancestors (chapters 44-50), a roll call of Israel's revered forebears, mentions Enoch twice: at 44:16, calling him "taken up" and "an example of repentance to all generations," and again at 49:14, underscoring how singular his case is — an endorsement of Enoch's exceptional status independent of the Enochic corpus itself [381].

SKADI

A giantess, daughter of the giant Thjazi, who arms herself and comes to Asgard to avenge her father's death at the Aesir's hands. Given Njord as a husband under a bargain letting her choose by the feet alone, she later returns without him to her father's mountain hall, Thrymheim, when the marriage fails [333] [334] [335].

SNORRI STURLUSON

Icelandic chieftain, poet, and historian (1179-1241) who compiled the Prose Edda roughly two centuries after Iceland's official conversion to Christianity. His pedagogical, systematizing aims — producing a handbook for skaldic poets rather than an ethnographic record — are the basis of ongoing scholarly caution about how directly his mythography preserves pre-Christian belief [339].

SPIRITS IN PRISON

The disputed phrase in 1 Peter 3:19 describing those to whom Christ "proclaimed" between his death and resurrection — read by some scholars as the imprisoned fallen Watchers of the Enochic tradition, by others as the drowned human generation of Noah's flood. A genuinely unresolved exegetical debate this book does not adjudicate [287].

SUCCUBUS

A female demon believed to have sexual intercourse with men. In Thomas Aquinas's scholastic mechanism, the succubus is the first stage of a two-part process in which the same demon assumes female form to draw semen from a man, then male form to deposit that semen in a woman as an incubus [355]. Heinrich Kramer's Malleus Maleficarum treats the succubus half of this mechanism as settled fact rather than open theological question [357].

SUSAN J. PALMER

Sociologist of religion whose Aliens Adored: Rael's UFO Religion (2004), based on more than a decade of fieldwork with unusually open access to the Raelian movement's leadership and membership, is the standard academic study of Raelism as a new religious movement [376].

TAPAS

The heat or spiritual power an ascetic accumulates through sustained austerity in Hindu cosmology, conceived as a real, escalating, and finite resource capable, if left unchecked, of growing great enough to threaten to unseat Indra from his position as king of the gods. Scholarship on the tradition's recurring seduction plots reads tapas and kama (sexual desire) as related expressions of the same underlying heat, which is why an Apsara's seduction, rather than force, is the gods' characteristic countermeasure [341].

TARGUM PSEUDO-JONATHAN

A Palestinian Aramaic expansion-translation of the Torah, incorporating traditions of varying age but most likely reaching its final form in the early Islamic period, roughly the seventh to eighth centuries CE [255]. At Genesis 6:2 it substitutes "the sons of the great ones" for the Hebrew's "sons of God," the same demythologizing move Genesis Rabbah makes in Hebrew [256] — yet two verses later, at Genesis 6:4, names two fallen angels outright as having fallen from heaven: Shamhazai, and, depending on the manuscript witness, either Uzziel or Azael [257].

TEN HEAVENS (2 ENOCH COSMOLOGY)

The layered cosmic structure Enoch ascends across 2 Enoch chapters 3 through 22, from a first heaven of atmospheric treasuries up through the fifth heaven's Grigori, the archangel-governed sixth, the star-holding eighth and ninth, and the tenth heaven, Aravoth, where God dictates the contents of three hundred and sixty-six books to Enoch through the angel Vrevoil. The ascent is followed by Enoch's thirty-day return to instruct his sons (chapters 39-67) before his final removal to heaven [155].

TERTULLIAN

Late second- and early third-century Christian writer from Roman Carthage, the first major Latin Christian author. Across three separate treatises — On the Apparel of Women, On Idolatry, and On the Veiling of Virgins — Tertullian treats the Genesis 6 Watchers narrative as settled fact, explicitly defends the Book of Enoch's scriptural authority by name, and connects the angels of Genesis 6 to Paul's veiling instruction in 1 Corinthians 11:10 [266] [267] [268].

THAT SON OF MAN (1 ENOCH TITLE)

One of four titles the Parables apply to a single pre-existent heavenly judge, alongside "the Chosen One," "the Righteous One," and "the Messiah"/"the Anointed One" [82]. Concentrated in the second and third parables and the closing ascent narrative (46:1-4; 48:2; 62:5-14; 69:26-29; 71:14, 17), the figure sits "on the throne of his glory," judges "the kings and the mighty of the earth," and is described as having been named before creation itself (48:2-3; 62:7). In the closing chapters an angel identifies Enoch himself as this figure (71:14), a claim scholars read either as a late addition to the text or as its intended climax [85]. The title's relationship to the New Testament Gospels' "Son of Man" sayings for Jesus remains a genuinely open scholarly question, not resolved by this book.

THE BOOK WHICH TELLS THE TRUTH

Claude Vorilhon's 1974 account of his claimed encounter with an extraterrestrial being, published in France as Le Livre qui dit la verite and in English as Space Aliens Took Me to Their Planet; the founding text of the Raelian movement [374].

THE CHIEFS OF TENS (1 ENOCH 6:7)

The subordinate commanders under whom the chapter organizes its two hundred Watchers, traditionally rendered "leaders of tens" and implying twenty officers of ten Watchers each, though the surviving Ethiopic and Aramaic name-lists both preserve only nineteen names total, Shemihazah's own included [13]. The Ethiopic list runs Shemihazah, Araqiel, Rameel, Kokabiel, Tamiel, Ramiel, Daniel, Ezeqeel, Baraqijal, Asael, Armaros, Batarel, Ananel, Zaqiel, Samsapeel, Satarel, Turel, Yomyael, and Sariel; the independent Aramaic fragments from Qumran give a parallel but non-identical roster, and the Greek excerpts preserved by Syncellus diverge further still [14].

THE CHOSEN ONE (1 ENOCH TITLE)

The most frequently used of the Parables' four titles for its heavenly judge, appearing across all three parables (among other places, 39:6; 45:3-4; 49:2; 51:3; 55:4; 61:5, 8), almost always in scenes of the judge seated "on the throne of his glory" separating the righteous from sinners [82].

THE DIOSCURI (CASTOR AND POLYDEUCES)

Twin sons of Leda, unequal in parentage like Heracles and Iphicles before them: Castor mortal, son of Tyndareus, and Polydeuces divine, son of Zeus, born of the same night and the same mother. Their asymmetry motivates the later tradition of Castor's mortal death and the brothers' arrangement to share Polydeuces' immortality between them [308].

THE OTHER NAMED WATCHER-TEACHERS

Seven further Watchers named in 1 Enoch 8:3 alongside Shemihazah, each credited with a distinct forbidden discipline: Armaros (the resolving, or undoing, of enchantments), Baraqijal (astrology), Kokabel (the constellations), Ezeqeel (the knowledge of the clouds), Araqiel (the signs of the earth), Shamsiel (the signs of the sun), and Sariel (the course of the moon). Between this roster and Azazel's separate catalogue in 8:1, the text assigns an illegitimate angelic origin to essentially the full range of ancient technical and divinatory knowledge. The precise spelling and ordering of these names is not perfectly stable across the Ethiopic, Greek, and Aramaic manuscript witnesses, though the substance of the eight-part division is consistent across all of them [205].

THE POETIC EDDA

An anonymous collection of Old Norse mythological and heroic poems, preserved chiefly in the thirteenth-century Codex Regius manuscript, including Voluspa, Vafthrudnismal, and Grimnismal. Cited here in Carolyne Larrington's translation; it independently confirms much of the genealogical material the Prose Edda narrates in prose [328] [331] [335].

THE PROSE EDDA

Snorri Sturluson's thirteenth-century compilation (also called the Younger Edda or Snorra Edda), comprising a Prologue, Gylfaginning, Skaldskaparmal, and Hattatal. The fullest connected narrative source for the Jotunn-Aesir genealogies this chapter traces, cited here in Anthony Faulkes's translation; its status as a Christian-era, pedagogically shaped compilation is a live source-critical caution rather than a settled transcription of pre-Christian belief [339].

THE SEVEN ARCHANGELS (1 ENOCH 20)

The formal roster of seven named angels — Uriel, Raphael, Raguel, Michael, Sariel (Saraqael), Gabriel, and Remiel — each assigned a specific cosmic portfolio at the opening of the book's second guided tour (20:1-8). The list expands an earlier roster of only four named angels (9:1) and is not itself textually stable: the Greek witness preserves all seven while part of the Ethiopic tradition lacks the seventh name, Remiel [56] [57] [58]. The book of Tobit independently attests a tradition of seven angels standing before God, naming only Raphael and the number seven (Tobit 12:15) [59].

THEMIS

Greek goddess personifying divine law and right order, consulted by Zeus in the Cypria's summary as he devises the plan to end the demigod generation and relieve the overburdened earth through the Trojan War [310].

THEOGONY (HESIOD)

Archaic Greek genealogical poem by Hesiod, the earliest surviving systematic account of the Greek gods' origins and family relationships. Its closing catalogue records specific unions between gods and mortals, including Zeus with Semele and Zeus with Alcmene, cited in this chapter as the primary early evidence for the divine-mortal union pattern in Greek tradition [304].

THEOPHANY (1 ENOCH 1)

The vision, announced in 1 Enoch 1:3-9, of God departing his heavenly dwelling and arriving with an army of "holy ones" to execute judgment on the whole earth. Scholarship reads the passage as an anthology assembled chiefly from Deuteronomy 33:2 and Habakkuk 3:3-6, two older Hebrew Bible theophany texts, repurposed from scenes of God blessing or defending Israel specifically into a scene of universal judgment [5]. This same verse is quoted by name, and attributed to Enoch, in the New Testament letter of Jude 14-15 [8].

THOMAS AQUINAS

Dominican friar and scholastic theologian (1225-1274) whose Summa Theologiae, Part I, Question 51, addresses whether angels can assume bodies and whether demons can father children. His proposed succubus-then-incubus mechanism became the standard scholastic account of how demonic conception could occur without demons possessing true generative power of their own [354] [355].

THOR

Son of Odin and the giantess Jord, and the Aesir's most active giant-slayer — himself half-giant through his mother. Thor later fathers the god Magni by the giantess Jarnsaxa [332] [336].

TREE OF LIFE (1 ENOCH 24-25)

A tree of unmatched fragrance shown to Enoch on a mountain resembling a throne-seat, reserved until the final judgment for the righteous and the chosen, whose fruit will then grant them life (24:1-25:6), explained to Enoch by the angel Michael. Widely read as an eschatological counterpart to Eden's tree of life (Genesis 2:9; 3:22-24) and an antecedent to Revelation 22:2, though at least one specialist study argues its earliest resonance within the Book of the Watchers leans closer to a wisdom symbol than to a literal Eden restaging [64].

TURFAN

An oasis in the low desert basin of China's Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, a major staging point on the Silk Road's northern route. The ruined Manichaean temple libraries of nearby Qocho, excavated by four German expeditions between 1902 and 1914, yielded Middle Persian, Parthian, Sogdian, and Old Uyghur fragments of the Manichaean Book of Giants, the far downstream descendant of the Jewish Book of Giants found at Qumran [390].

TWO POWERS IN HEAVEN

A named rabbinic heresy category — the charge that scripture or tradition implies a second, co-equal divine power alongside God — given its standard scholarly treatment in Alan F. Segal, Two Powers in Heaven (1977). The Babylonian Talmud's account of Elisha ben Abuyah seeing Metatron seated and drawing this conclusion (b. Hagigah 15a) is one instance of a broader rabbinic anxiety that the category also addressed in relation to early Christian and Gnostic claims about exalted intermediary figures [170] [168].

URIEL

One of the seven named angels of 1 Enoch 20, set over the world and over Tartarus (20:2). Some manuscript traditions identify Uriel with Sariel, the figure elsewhere assigned oversight of spirits who sin against the spirit; other witnesses treat them as distinct [56].

URIEL (ANGEL OF THE LUMINARIES)

The angel who guides Enoch through the Astronomical Book, introduced as "their leader" over the sun, moon, and stars (72:1). Distinct from Uriel's earlier appearance among the four archangels who intercede over the earth's corruption, this is a specifically instructional office: the angel who explains how time and the heavens actually work [94].

URUK

A Sumerian city, today the mound of Warka roughly 30 km east of Samawah in Iraq's Al-Muthanna Governorate. A Seleucid-era cuneiform tablet excavated there in 1959-60, the Uruk List of Kings and Sages, pairs seven antediluvian kings with seven antediluvian sages, the tradition this book compares to 1 Enoch's Watchers in its twenty-sixth chapter [386].

URUK LIST OF KINGS AND SAGES

A Seleucid-era cuneiform tablet excavated at Uruk in the 1959-60 season and first published by Jan van Dijk in 1962, analyzed at length by Alan Lenzi (2008). It pairs each of seven antediluvian kings with a corresponding apkallu-sage, Oannes/Uanna foremost among them, then continues into the post-flood period pairing historical kings with human ummanu-scholars rather than sage-beings. It is the clearest surviving cuneiform evidence, independent of and likely earlier than Berossus's later Greek retelling, that Mesopotamian scholars themselves traced their professional lineage back to these seven pre-flood culture-bringers in their own native written record [318].

VAFTHRUDNISMAL

A poem of the Poetic Edda staging a wisdom-contest between Odin and the giant Vafthrudnir. Stanza 21 gives the giant's own account of the world's creation from Ymir's body, independently confirming Gylfaginning's prose version [331].

VANIR

The second family of Norse gods, including Njord; folded into the Aesir's household after an earlier war between the two groups. Njord's marriage to the giantess Skadi crosses the Aesir/Vanir divide and the god/giant divide at once [333].

VE

One of the three sons of Bor and the giantess Bestla, brother of Odin and Vili. With them he kills the giant Ymir and helps shape the world from his body [329] [330].

VILI

One of the three sons of Bor and the giantess Bestla, brother of Odin and Ve. With them he kills the giant Ymir and helps shape the world from his body [329] [330].

VISHVAMITRA

A sage (rishi) whose accumulating tapas draws Indra's intervention in two separate epic episodes: in the Mahabharata's Adi Parva, the Apsara Menaka is sent to seduce him, producing a daughter, Shakuntala; in the Ramayana's Balakanda, the Apsara Rambha is sent on a similar mission and is refused and cursed. Vishvamitra is counted among the tradition's great sages despite, or in the epics' own telling partly because of, both encounters [342] [350].

VOLUSPA

The poem opening the Poetic Edda, spoken by a seeress reciting the world's creation and eventual destruction to Odin. Stanzas 3-4 narrate the pre-creation void and the raising of Midgard by Bor's sons [328].

VORTIGERN

The British king in Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae whose collapsing tower requires, his advisers claim, the blood of a fatherless boy for its foundation. The search for that boy brings Merlin and his mother before Vortigern's court, where her testimony about the boy's conception is given and glossed by Maugantius [359].

WAYNE A. GRUDEM

New Testament scholar, author of 1 Peter (Tyndale New Testament Commentaries, 1988), a leading defender of the reading of 1 Peter 3:19's "spirits in prison" as the disobedient human generation of Noah's day rather than fallen angels [287].

WHITE BULL (1 ENOCH 90:37-38)

A bull with great horns, born at the very end of the Animal Apocalypse, feared and petitioned by all other beasts and birds; all other animals present are then said to be transformed into white bulls in turn, echoing the vision's opening image of Adam (85:3). Scholars remain divided over the figure's identity — a restored Adam or Seth, a Davidic messianic figure, or (per a more recent proposal) a "Josephite messiah" tied to Deuteronomy 33:17's wild-ox imagery for Joseph — and this book does not adjudicate between the readings [120].

WILLIAM J. DALTON

New Testament scholar, author of Christ's Proclamation to the Spirits (Analecta Biblica 23, 2nd ed. 1989), the standard monograph defending the reading of 1 Peter 3:19's "spirits in prison" as the fallen Watchers of the Enochic tradition [287].

WOE ORACLE

A prophetic form — "Woe to you who..." followed by an indictment and a coming judgment — borrowed by the Epistle of Enoch from Israelite prophetic literature, where it structures denunciations such as Isaiah 5:8-23 and the "Book of Woes" in Amos 5-6. The Epistle uses the form dozens of times across chapters 94-104 to indict the rich and powerful for specific offenses: luxury consumption, unjust wealth, perjury, and building "houses... with the stones and bricks of sin" (99:13) [128].

WORKS AND DAYS (HESIOD)

Archaic Greek didactic poem by Hesiod, containing the Five Races schema of human history — gold, silver, bronze, a race of heroes/demigods, and iron — in which the demigod race is destroyed by war at Thebes and Troy rather than by any of the mechanisms (metal decay, divine curse) that end the other races [305].

XBALANQUE

Twin brother of Hunahpu, son of One Hunahpu and Xquic, who together with his brother defeats the Lords of Xibalba and ascends into the sky, identified in the Popol Vuh with the moon, though some students of Classic Maya iconography read one twin's celestial role as Venus rather than the moon specifically [418] [419].

XIBALBA

The K'iche' Maya underworld, ruled by a council of death-lords including Hun-Came and Vucub-Came, reached by a road that also passes near the site of the ballgame that draws One Hunahpu and Seven Hunahpu, and later their sons, to their respective confrontations there [411]. Permanently subdued when the Hero Twins trick its two chief lords into requesting, and receiving, the same ritual death the twins had staged and reversed on themselves and others, this time without reversal [417].

XMUCANE

Primordial diviner grandmother, mother of One Hunahpu and Seven Hunahpu and, by extension, grandmother of the Hero Twins. Initially refuses to accept the pregnant Xquic's claim of kinship, setting her a series of tests, including an impossible maize harvest, before accepting her into the household where the twins are subsequently born and raised alongside their half brothers Hunbatz and Hunchouen [416].

XQUIC (BLOOD MOON)

Daughter of the Xibalba lord Cuchumaquic, impregnated without intercourse when the transformed, gourd-like head of One Hunahpu spits into her open hand [413] [414]. Sentenced to death by the Xibalba lords once her pregnancy is discovered, she escapes execution by tricking her owl escorts with tree sap in place of her heart, flees to the earth's surface, passes a series of tests set by her mother-in-law Xmucane, and gives birth to the Hero Twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque [415] [416].

YMIR

The first living being in Norse cosmology, a frost-giant who condenses out of the meeting of heat and rime in the primordial void Ginnungagap. Fed by the cow Audhumla, he is later killed by Odin, Vili, and Ve, who build the world from his body — earth from his flesh, sea from his blood, mountains from his bones, sky from his skull [327] [330] [328] [331].

YOM KIPPUR SCAPEGOAT RITUAL (AZAZEL)

The Day of Atonement rite of Leviticus 16:8-26, in which one of two goats chosen by lot is driven into the wilderness "for Azazel." Babylonian Talmud, tractate Yoma 67b, records a Baraita reading "Azazel" as a description of the ritual's destination, a rugged mountain or cliff, and, separately, a minority etymology attributed to the school of Rabbi Ishmael connecting the name to "the deeds of Uzza and Azael" without further explaining who those figures are [252] [253]. The identification of Uzza and Azael as the Genesis 6 fallen angels is supplied only later, by the medieval commentator Rashi, and not by the Talmud text itself [254].

ZAMZUMMIM

The Ammonite name for the same giant population elsewhere called Rephaim: "Rephaim formerly lived there — but the Ammonites call them Zamzummim" (Deuteronomy 2:20-21). Like Emim, the word appears only in this one passage, and the text explicitly identifies it as an outsider-name for the same category rather than a separate people [233].

ZECHARIA SITCHIN

A popular-nonfiction author (1920-2010), not an Assyriologist, Sumerologist, or credentialed ancient Near Eastern scholar of any kind, whose The 12th Planet (1976) and its many sequels reinterpret the Anunnaki, the real Mesopotamian deity term, as extraterrestrial beings from a supposed planet Nibiru who genetically engineered humanity as a mining workforce [324]. His specific translations and etymologies, most famously his gloss of "Anunnaki" as "those who from heaven to Earth came" and his reading of cylinder seal VA 243 as a solar-system diagram, have been examined and rejected in detail by credentialed specialists in Sumerian and Akkadian; mainstream Assyriology treats his work as pseudo-scholarship built on serious mistranslation, not as a minority position within the field [325] [326]. Sitchin drew on the same Mesopotamian corpus this book's chapter on the Seven Sages surveys in connection with the Apkallu tradition, and professional Assyriologists and Sumerologists reject his underlying translations there as unsupported by the attested philological record [372].

ZEUS

King of the Olympian gods and, across the Greek tradition, the most prolific father of demigod heroes on mortal women — Heracles (by Alcmene), Perseus (by Danae), Helen and Polydeuces (by Leda), Dionysus (by Semele), among many others named in Hesiod's own Theogony [304]. In the Cypria, a lost epic of the Trojan Cycle, Zeus is credited with engineering the Trojan War specifically to end the demigod generation and relieve an overburdened earth, after considering and rejecting outright destruction by thunderbolt or flood [310] [312].
